As the market reassessed inflation risks in the United States, global financial markets experienced renewed volatility at the beginning of the year. In February, global stock markets fell sharply from their late-January highs, completely erasing the significant gains made earlier in the year, while the benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury yield rose to a four-year high. Over the past two years, global stock markets had risen steadily amid low volatility, underpinned by market expectations of an ideal scenario of sustained robust economic growth alongside low inflation and interest rates. However, these expectations are now facing risks stemming from tightening global monetary conditions, rising trade protectionist sentiment, and geopolitical tensions. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened, but the market continued to function in an orderly manner. In the second half of 2017, total loans continued to increase, albeit at a slower pace. Following a modest slowdown earlier in the year, both property price increases and transaction volumes rebounded in the fourth quarter of 2017. Looking ahead, the recurrence of volatility in global and local financial markets may add fluctuations to capital flows in Hong Kong. Given the uncertainties in financial markets, as well as the ongoing normalization of U.S. monetary policy and persistent geopolitical risks, banks should remain vigilant against heightened interest rate volatility and potential capital outflows. In particular, given the continued rise in corporate leverage and the high level of household debt burdens, banks should assess the potential impact on asset quality should interest rates rise more than expected. Following a period of more than two years during which the Chicago Board Options Exchange Volatility Index (VIX) lingered at low levels, global financial markets saw a return of volatility at the start of the year. Global equity markets dropped significantly from their late-January peaks, with the S&P 500 index falling by more than 10% at one point, fully offsetting the notable gains recorded in early January. Market sentiment shifted amid signs that the global economic recovery could put pressure on long-suppressed U.S. wages and prices, potentially prompting the Federal Reserve to accelerate its pace of interest rate hikes. The benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury yield also climbed to a four-year high. The sustained rally in global stock markets over the past two years was predicated on market expectations that economic conditions would remain favorable. In the second half of 2017, global economic growth momentum continued to strengthen, with economic activity in both advanced and emerging market economies picking up in tandem. Toward the end of the year, the U.S. Congress passed a tax reform package, which included tax cuts and comprehensive reforms to corporate and individual tax codes, fueling market hopes that the strong U.S. economic recovery would receive additional cyclical stimulus in the near term. Despite the pickup in activity, core inflation in major advanced economies remained subdued, further reinforcing market expectations that global interest rates would stay low for an extended period. Against this backdrop, global asset markets rallied significantly in 2017, with U.S. equities in particular hitting record highs repeatedly. However, following the release of stronger-than-expected U.S. wage growth data for January, global stock markets began to reassess inflation risks. After the short-term financial market volatility subsides, the risk of tightening global monetary conditions may continue to cast a shadow over the global economic outlook. In the United States, as the economy has already reached its output potential, the anticipated cyclical boost to domestic demand from tax cuts could accelerate a rebound in inflation, thereby prompting the Federal Reserve to tighten monetary policy at a faster pace. Meanwhile, as tax cuts are expected to widen the fiscal deficit, the U.S. government may issue more Treasury bonds in the future; this is likely to exert upward pressure on long-term bond yields even as the Federal Reserve continues to normalize its balance sheet. Outside the United States, strengthening growth momentum in other major advanced economies has led markets to expect that their central banks may scale back their quantitative easing programs. If implemented, this would result in a synchronized tightening of global monetary conditions. Policy and event risks arising from international political and geopolitical tensions could also cloud the global economic growth outlook. The U.S. administration appears increasingly inclined to adopt trade protectionist measures to shield domestic industries from competition, as evidenced recently by the announcement of import tariffs on solar panels, washing machines, steel, and aluminum. These moves have raised concerns about whether trading partners might respond with retaliatory measures. Furthermore, any unexpected escalation of geopolitical tensions could disrupt global trade and exacerbate volatility in global financial markets. Given the aforementioned uncertainties surrounding the global economic outlook, the sustainability of currently elevated valuations in global asset markets is called into question. From a fundamental perspective, it remains to be seen whether cyclical growth in global demand and the projected widening of the U.S. fiscal deficit due to tax cuts will push up the natural rate of interest (R*); coupled with the expectation that the Federal Reserve's balance sheet normalization will lead to higher term premiums, long-term interest rates could rise, thereby weighing on asset market valuations. In East Asia, regional economies have also enjoyed a favorable environment of steady growth and moderate inflation. Buoyed by solid economic performance and optimistic prospects, capital inflows accelerated, lifting financial markets concurrently. However, this positive outlook faces downside risks due to several factors: tightening global liquidity resulting from synchronized monetary policy normalization by major central banks; the U.S. administration's inward-looking trade policies; geopolitical tensions; and the potential tightening of offshore U.S. dollar liquidity caused by massive repatriation of profits by U.S. corporations in response to the one-time "deemed repatriation" provision under the country's tax reform. Should credit and financial markets face any shocks, a reversal of capital flows could be triggered, with highly leveraged sectors and economies being most vulnerable to tightening financial conditions. On the Mainland China front, supported by resilient consumption, robust infrastructure investment, and a rebound in industrial spending toward year-end, the Mainland economy performed well in the second half of 2017. At the same time, signs of the rise of the "New Economy" became increasingly evident; over the past few quarters, high-value-added industries such as manufacturing and services have demonstrated strong momentum in business expansion. Looking ahead, the near-term economic growth outlook remains positive, though uncertainties persist. In particular, it remains to be seen to what extent the rapid growth of the New Economy can help offset the short-term drag on growth arising from further structural reforms. Mainland authorities announced in 2018 that they would maintain a proactive fiscal policy stance, which could help cushion adverse economic developments if necessary. During the period under review, progress was made in both structural reforms and the containment of systemic risks. Notably, following the introduction of tightening measures, the Mainland property market showed signs of cooling during the review period, particularly in first-tier cities. Meanwhile, as banks tightened lending standards, their exposure to enterprises in overcapacity industries remained contained, and shadow banking activities slowed amid financial deleveraging. Beyond these positive developments, our analysis also suggests that capital allocation efficiency in Mainland China appears to have improved. Specifically, borrowing constraints faced by state-owned enterprises with weaker repayment capacity seem to have tightened, possibly reflecting reduced support from local governments (see Box 2 on page 28 for details). On the external front, amid stabilizing economic conditions and receding risks, capital outflow pressures remained mild for most of 2017. The Hong Kong economy maintained its quarter-on-quarter growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Real GDP grew by 3.8% for the full year of 2017, marking the fastest pace in nearly six years. Supported by favorable employment and income conditions as well as rising asset prices, private consumption continued to grow steadily in the second half of 2017. Overall investment expenditure also rebounded, driven by increased business capital spending. Externally, benefiting from improved global trade growth and a gradual recovery in inbound tourism, Hong Kong's export performance improved further. Nevertheless, as import growth outpaced export growth, net exports of goods remained a drag on GDP growth, while net exports of services contributed positively. Economic growth is expected to remain steady in 2018, with private consumption, building and construction activity, and exports continuing to underpin growth. Given that Hong Kong dollar interest rates will eventually rise, Box 3 examines the impact of higher mortgage repayment burdens on private consumption. Both the Government and market consensus forecast real GDP growth for 2018 to be in the range of 3–4% and 3.0%, respectively. However, Hong Kong’s growth outlook remains subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including the external environment mentioned above, Mainland China’s economic performance amid tightening financial conditions, and trends in the local asset market. Although the unemployment rate fell to a near 20-year low of 2.9%, domestic inflationary pressures remained contained. That said, quarter-on-quarter inflation momentum showed slight signs of picking up in recent months, with prices of both tradable goods and services rising. Looking ahead, underlying inflation may edge up slightly but remain moderate, partly reflecting the pass-through effect of higher fresh private residential rentals. Affected by funding requirements related to initial public offering activities and seasonal funding needs, liquidity conditions tightened, and increased squaring of short positions in the Hong Kong dollar prompted the spot exchange rate to strengthen between September and November 2017. As liquidity conditions eased and carry trade activities resumed, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened again starting in December 2017. In early 2018, despite turbulence in global financial markets—particularly equity markets—the Hong Kong dollar remained broadly stable. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened further in early March 2018, but the Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered. The Hong Kong Dollar Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) faced upward pressure between September and December 2017, primarily due to funding demands from IPO activities and banks’ prudent approach to liquidity management approaching year-end. By December, the average overnight and three-month HIBORs had risen by 14 and 50 basis points respectively compared to six months earlier, reaching 0.25% and 1.26%. After dipping slightly in early January 2018, HIBORs remained largely stable and were unaffected by the recent adjustments in global financial markets. Despite intense competition in mortgage lending, banks’ average new mortgage lending rate tracked the rise in short-term HIBORs, climbing to 2.16% in December. On the other hand, retail banks’ funding costs remained generally low after a brief uptick in October due to IPO-related funding needs, with the composite interest rate closing at 0.38% in December. Looking ahead, as U.S. monetary policy continues to normalize, Hong Kong dollar interest rates may face greater upward pressure; meanwhile, any sharp shift in global financial market sentiment could increase volatility in capital flows. For the full year of 2017, total bank loans grew steadily by 16.1%. Following robust growth of 10.2% in the first half, loan growth slowed to 5.3% in the second half. Growth in domestic loans and loans for use outside Hong Kong decelerated across most sectors. Foreign currency loan growth slowed, partly due to rising U.S. dollar funding costs. Meanwhile, Hong Kong dollar loans continued to record rapid growth, supported by improving local economic conditions and relatively low Hong Kong dollar funding costs. As Hong Kong dollar loan growth outpaced deposit growth, the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio rose in the second half of 2017, reaching 82.7% by year-end, the highest level since March 2015. Conversely, due to relatively slower growth in foreign currency loans, the foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio declined to 63.1% at year-end. Both onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates against the U.S. dollar showed signs of stabilization between September and November 2017. Subsequently, as the U.S. dollar weakened significantly against most major currencies, both onshore and offshore renminbi strengthened against the U.S. dollar starting in December. Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi funding pool (comprising total renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit) edged up in the second half of the year following a slight decline in the first half, broadly reflecting shifts in market expectations regarding the renminbi exchange rate. As for other offshore renminbi businesses, although renminbi loans continued to decrease, the value of renminbi trade settlement handled by banks in Hong Kong rebounded in the second half. The average daily turnover of the Renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system remained at a high level. Looking ahead, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi business is poised to benefit from the advancement of the Belt and Road Initiative and the continued internationalization of the renminbi.

The synchronized strengthening of the global economy since late 2016 has shown no signs of abating. Improved growth prospects drove global equity markets higher throughout 2017 and into early 2018. However, as markets reassessed U.S. inflation risks, a sell-off and sharp volatility in global stock markets in February marked the end of the calm that had characterized financial markets over the preceding two years. Looking ahead, risks of tightening global financial conditions, along with a range of policy and event risks, will continue to cast a shadow over the global outlook. Amid a tight labor market, U.S. tax cuts could accelerate a cyclical rebound in inflation, prompting the Federal Reserve to tighten monetary policy at a faster pace. As the Fed continues to normalize its balance sheet, increased issuance of U.S. Treasury securities to finance tax cuts may add upward pressure on long-term bond yields. The specter of rising trade barriers, as well as any unexpected escalation of geopolitical tensions, could also threaten the nascent recovery in global trade. In East Asia, real economic growth continued to rise in the second half of 2017, supported by strong export performance and stable domestic demand. However, despite an optimistic economic outlook, the region faces multiple downside risks, including potentially greater-than-expected tightening of global monetary conditions, inward-looking U.S. trade policies, and geopolitical tensions. Should these downside risks materialize, the risk of capital flow reversals would also increase. Policymakers face multiple challenges: they must guard against risks to economic growth while simultaneously limiting the impact of prolonged accommodative financial conditions on inflation and balance sheet vulnerabilities. In Mainland China, economic performance was solid in the second half of 2017. During the period under review, some progress was made in structural reforms and containing systemic risks. The near-term growth outlook remains positive, though uncertainties persist; this will depend partly on the extent to which rapid growth in the "new economy" can offset the short-term drag on growth from further structural reforms. As economic conditions stabilized and risks subsided, capital outflow pressures remained moderate for most of 2017. As the momentum of cyclical economic improvement has become increasingly entrenched since late 2016, growth in both advanced and emerging market economies accelerated synchronously in 2017. Among major advanced economies, the United States saw robust increases in investment and exports, driven by improving private sector sentiment and a significant depreciation of the U.S. dollar, while the euro area and Japan also recorded broad-based cyclical recoveries. Exports from emerging market economies also benefited from stabilizing global commodity prices and increased import demand from major advanced economies. In the near term, following the passage of tax reform in the United States, investment and consumption are expected to receive a further boost from reductions in corporate and personal income taxes. Given the current cyclical economic upswing and the expansionary effects of U.S. tax reform, the International Monetary Fund projected in January that global economic growth would accelerate from an estimated 3.7% in 2017 to 3.9% in 2018 (Chart 2.1). Chart 2.1 Real GDP Growth Forecasts As growth momentum strengthened in the euro area and Japan, market expectations that global monetary policy divergence would narrow, coupled with a more optimistic global growth outlook, spurred higher risk appetite and capital inflows into emerging market economies, thereby putting pressure on the U.S. dollar. Despite the Federal Reserve raising interest rates three times during the year and beginning to normalize its balance sheet, the U.S. Dollar Index still recorded a decline of nearly 10% in 2017. Meanwhile, despite a broad-based acceleration in economic growth, core inflation in major advanced economies remained subdued and below central bank targets, leading markets to expect until recently that global interest rates would remain low (Chart 2.2). Against this backdrop, global equity markets continued to rally through 2017 and into early 2018, with the S&P 500 index hitting record highs repeatedly, pushing the cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings ratio to 33.8 in January 2018, the highest level since the "dot-com bubble" in early 2000. Chart 2.2 Core Inflation in Major Advanced Economies However, since the second half of 2017, market concerns that tax cuts could lead to larger fiscal deficits and higher inflation have caused U.S. long-term Treasury yields to climb steadily, raising questions about the sustainability of increasingly elevated asset market valuations. Following the release of U.S. data showing a higher-than-expected increase in average hourly earnings in January 2018, markets reassessed U.S. inflation risks, triggering a correction in global equity markets in early February 2018. The S&P 500 index fell more than 10% from its January 26 peak, completely erasing its significant gains earlier in the year, and remained under pressure after the U.S. government announced a new round of trade protectionist measures in early March. The benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury yield also rose to a four-year high in mid-February. Market volatility surged, with the CBOE Volatility Index briefly spiking to a two-year high of 37.3, marking the end of the low-volatility environment that had persisted over the past two years (Chart 2.3). Chart 2.3 CBOE Volatility Index (VIX) Looking ahead, following the recent bout of stock market volatility, U.S. inflation risks, upside risks to U.S. long-term bond yields, and potential monetary tightening by other major central banks could all lead to a tightening of global financial conditions, thereby casting a shadow over the global economic outlook. First, regarding U.S. inflation risks, the recently enacted tax reform includes several provisions expected to provide short-term cyclical stimulus to private consumption and investment. Key measures involved in the tax reform include: (1) reductions in corporate and personal income tax rates; (2) temporary full expensing of capital investments; and (3) a one-time "deemed repatriation" provision designed to reduce incentives for U.S. corporations to keep overseas earnings abroad. While it remains uncertain how tax cuts will affect domestic demand and inflation, with the U.S. economy now operating at its potential output, tax cuts could push U.S. output beyond its potential, leading to economic overheating and a cyclical rebound in inflation. If inflationary pressures rise more than expected, it could prompt the Federal Reserve to tighten monetary policy at a faster pace. Currently, financial markets' projected path for the federal funds rate is flatter than the projections released by the Federal Reserve. However, should inflation rebound unexpectedly, the risk of a sudden repricing of rate hike expectations cannot be ruled out (Chart 2.4). Chart 2.4 Federal Funds Rate Projections Second, given that tax reform could exacerbate the fiscal deficit, U.S. Treasury issuance is expected to increase going forward. As the Federal Reserve continues its balance sheet normalization program, which is expected to raise term premiums, increased Treasury issuance under these circumstances could intensify upward pressure on long-term bond yields. Furthermore, as market expectations regarding the likelihood of passing U.S. tax cuts increased, U.S. inflation expectations have risen steadily since the second half of 2017 (Chart 2.5). Consequently, after hovering at low levels for much of 2017, the benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury yield has risen by more than 70 basis points since the third quarter, partly reflecting market concerns over increased supply pressure on Treasuries and rising inflation expectations. Chart 2.5 5-Year 5-Year Forward Inflation Expectations Moreover, a key question is whether the natural rate of interest (R*), a major component of long-term interest rates, will remain persistently low as widely expected. Although estimates of R* vary, there is a general consensus that it has declined significantly since the Global Financial Crisis (Chart 2.6). Nevertheless, due to (1) an expected decline in the national savings rate resulting from larger fiscal deficits, and (2) a potential rise in the investment rate driven by corporate tax cuts and more favorable tax treatment of capital expenditures, U.S. R* may face upside risks in the future. A rise in R*, combined with an expected increase in term premiums due to Fed balance sheet normalization, could signal higher long-term interest rates, thereby creating headwinds for asset market valuations. Chart 2.6 Estimated U.S. R* Based on the Laubach-Williams Model Third, strengthening growth momentum in the euro area and Japan has led markets to anticipate that their central banks may scale back monetary easing measures. Should this occur, it could signal a synchronized tightening of global financial conditions. In the euro area, member economies have recorded broad-based cyclical expansion (Chart 2.7). As for Japan, the economic recovery has also gained traction, with real GDP posting its eighth consecutive quarter of positive growth in Q4 2017. Although the European Central Bank (ECB) and the Bank of Japan have continued to signal their commitment to maintaining accommodative monetary policies amid weak inflation, clearer growth prospects in Europe and Japan (along with continued tightening in Japan's labor market) have led some market participants to predict that they will further taper their quantitative easing programs in the near future. Chart 2.7 Real GDP of Selected Euro Area Member States Policy and event risks stemming from international political and geopolitical tensions could also pose threats to the nascent global economic growth and trade recovery. The U.S. administration appears increasingly inclined toward inward-looking trade policies to protect domestic industries; recent examples include the imposition of import tariffs on solar panels and washing machines announced in January 2018, and the announcement of import tariffs on steel and aluminum in early March, raising concerns about potential retaliatory measures from trading partners. Meanwhile, negotiations between the United Kingdom and the rest of the European Union regarding post-Brexit trade arrangements are currently underway, a process fraught with numerous uncertainties. If these developments lead to increased trade friction, global trade flows could be hindered and global productivity reduced. Furthermore, any unexpected escalation of geopolitical tensions (such as military conflict on the Korean Peninsula, political instability in the Middle East, and latent risks of terrorist attacks) could increase volatility in global financial markets. In East Asia, economic growth momentum strengthened further in the second half of 2017, culminating in a strong performance for the full year. Real growth accelerated to 4.3% in 2017, the fastest pace since 2012. External trade remained the primary engine of growth, while domestic demand provided steady support (Chart 2.8). Accelerated recovery in advanced economies, stronger-than-expected growth in Mainland China, and a rebound in global demand for technology products all boosted regional exports. Chart 2.8 East Asia: Domestic Demand and Exports Inflationary pressures have remained subdued thus far. In the second half of 2017, headline inflation in East Asia moderated, affected by declining food price inflation and stable energy prices (Chart 2.9). Meanwhile, due to slow wage growth in several economies, core consumer price inflation (excluding food and energy) remained at relatively low levels. Sources: CEIC and respective central banks. Improving economic conditions, accompanied by substantial capital inflows, led to significant increases in financial asset prices in 2017 and early 2018 (blue and pink bars in Chart 2.10). Capital inflows into regional markets rebounded significantly in 2017, with total portfolio investment inflows reaching their highest level since 2010. Valuations across various financial assets in the region also rose alongside market gains. Indeed, credit risk premiums in the region narrowed further in the second half of 2017, and benchmark equity indices across the entire region rose broadly. Regional currencies generally appreciated against the U.S. dollar.

With robust domestic demand and improved export performance, the Hong Kong economy maintained steady growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Economic growth is expected to remain steady in 2018. However, the local economic outlook remains subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including monetary policy normalization by major central banks, stability of global financial markets, rising protectionist sentiment, and escalating geopolitical tensions. In the near term, although local inflationary pressures should remain moderate, some upside risks persist. The Hong Kong economy sustained its growth momentum in the second half of 2017. The seasonally adjusted real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) grew by 0.8% quarter-on-quarter in both the third and fourth quarters, similar to the average growth rate of 0.9% in the preceding two quarters (Chart 3.1). Compared with the first half of the year, private consumption continued to grow steadily and remained one of the key drivers of GDP growth. Consumption growth was underpinned by favourable employment and income conditions, sustained optimistic consumer sentiment, and the positive wealth effect arising from rising asset prices. Although building and construction activity moderated, business capital expenditure increased, leading to a notable rise in overall investment spending in the last quarter after remaining broadly stable for three consecutive quarters. On the external front, benefiting from improved global trade growth and a gradual recovery in inbound tourism, Hong Kong's export performance further improved (Chart 3.2). Nevertheless, as import growth outpaced export growth, net exports of goods continued to drag on GDP growth, while net exports of services made a positive contribution. Chart 3.1 Real GDP Growth Rate and Contributions of Major Expenditure Components Chart 3.2 Real Imports and Exports Sustained economic growth momentum led to an increase in employment in the second half of 2017. Total employment rose by approximately 0.7% during the period to over 3.85 million, with the most significant increases recorded in the construction sector, financing and business services sector, and public administration, social and personal services sector. As real GDP growth exceeded employment growth, labour productivity showed further signs of improvement. Economic growth is expected to remain steady in 2018. On the external front, Hong Kong's export performance will continue to benefit from improved prospects for global economic growth and a gradual recovery in inbound tourism. Domestically, private consumption is expected to continue growing, primarily due to ideal labour market conditions. Given that Hong Kong dollar interest rates will eventually rise, Box 3 examines the impact of higher mortgage repayment burdens on private consumption. As for local fixed capital formation, building and construction activity should grow steadily, benefiting from increased housing supply and ongoing infrastructure projects. While an improved business environment will stimulate business capital expenditure, potential interest rate hikes may have a negative impact. The Government forecasts real GDP growth of 3% to 4% for 2018, while growth forecasts by international organizations and private sector analysts range from 2% to 4%. However, Hong Kong's growth outlook remains subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including those mentioned in previous chapters regarding the external environment, Mainland China's economic performance amid tightening financial conditions, and trends in the local asset market. Local inflationary pressures remained contained in the second half of 2017, but sequential inflation momentum showed slight signs of picking up in recent months. Year-on-year, the underlying Composite Consumer Price Index (CCPI) rose by 1.7% and 1.6% in the third and fourth quarters respectively, similar to the average increase of about 1.7% in the first half of the year. However, the annualized three-month underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, edged up to 2.8% in January 2018 (Chart 3.3). Prices of both tradable goods and services increased. The rebound in fresh private residential rentals since mid-2016 may also have added to inflation momentum to some extent (Chart 3.4). In addition, labour cost pressures remained moderate in recent quarters (Chart 3.5). Chart 3.3 Various Indicators Reflecting Consumer Price Inflation Chart 3.4 Rent Component of CCPI and Market Rentals Chart 3.5 Unit Labour Cost and Average Pay Per Person With global inflation remaining mild and local cost increases staying steady, inflationary pressures in Hong Kong are expected to remain moderate in 2018, although the underlying inflation rate may gradually pick up from the eight-year low of 1.7% in 2017. For instance, inflationary pressures may increase somewhat in the second half of 2018 due to the pass-through effect of rising fresh private residential rentals. Market consensus forecasts headline inflation at a moderate 2.2% for 2018, while the Government forecasts underlying inflation at 2.5%. Despite the moderate inflation outlook, upside risks remain. Externally, any larger-than-expected surge in global inflation or commodity prices could add to local inflation momentum. Domestically, the labour market has tightened further recently; the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate fell from 3.4% in 2016 to 2.9% in December 2017, dropping below 3% for the first time in nearly 20 years (Chart 3.6). The current output gap is estimated to be close to zero; if the labour market tightens significantly, it could exert additional upward pressure on inflation. Chart 3.6 Unemployment Rate Following the 2008 Global Financial Crisis, prolonged low interest rates led to an increase in mortgage debt among Hong Kong households. As US dollar interest rate normalization progresses, Hong Kong dollar interest rates will eventually follow suit, increasing household mortgage repayment burdens accordingly and thereby weighing on household consumption. Therefore, this box examines the impact of increased mortgage repayment burdens on private consumption in Hong Kong. Mortgage repayment burden refers to the ratio of mortgage debt servicing payments (i.e., interest payments plus principal repayments) to income. Chart B3.1 illustrates the role of mortgage repayment burden in the transmission of interest rate shocks to private consumption. In addition to the substitution effect, income effect, wealth effect, and collateral effect arising from asset price changes generally discussed in economic theory, in the presence of mortgage repayment burdens, interest rate shocks also affect private consumption by altering mortgage interest payments and consequently changing households' disposable income. This impact will be amplified as outstanding mortgage loans increase. Furthermore, principal repayments vary with changes in outstanding mortgage loans, which also affects private consumption through changes in household disposable income. Chart B3.1 Determinants of Private Consumption To measure the impact of mortgage repayment burden on private consumption, we estimated the Outstanding Mortgage Debt Servicing Ratio (OMDSR) based on outstanding mortgage liabilities. Unlike existing mortgage repayment burden indicators that apply only to newly originated mortgages, OMDSR covers all outstanding mortgage liabilities of households as a whole, which are more closely related to total private consumption. Broadly following the methodology used by the Bank for International Settlements, we measure OMDSR using the standard formula for fixed installment payments: where Dt is the amount of outstanding residential mortgage loans in the banking sector, Yt is the total income of owner-occupier households (proxied by the median income of owner-occupier households multiplied by the number of owner-occupier households), and rt and st are the average interest rate and tenor of outstanding mortgage loans, respectively. To assess whether OMDSR can reliably measure the mortgage repayment burden of the entire household sector, it is useful to compare OMDSR with two commonly used repayment burden indicators. Chart B3.2 shows the estimated OMDSR from 1985 to mid-2017, alongside the median Mortgage Payment and Loan Repayment-to-Income Ratio estimated by the Census and Statistics Department based on quinquennial population censuses. Both ratios trended downward in the early 2000s, consistent with the decline in overall household mortgage borrowing following the bursting of the property bubble in 1997 and the sharp drop in mortgage rates during the same period. Despite significant increases in property prices after the Global Financial Crisis, both ratios remained stable, as macro-prudential measures implemented by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) on bank mortgage lending curbed overall household mortgage leverage. Additionally, the extension of tenors for new mortgage loans reduced the actual amount of mortgage repayments. Chart B3.2 OMDSR and Median Mortgage Payment and Loan Repayment-to-Income Ratio We also compared OMDSR with banks' Debt Servicing Ratio (DSR), which represents the actual debt servicing-to-income ratio of new mortgage applicants. As shown in Chart B3.3, OMDSR is lower than banks' DSR, partly because OMDSR covers not only new mortgages but also existing ones. Since existing mortgages were originated when property prices were lower, their repayments are correspondingly lower than those of new mortgages. Consequently, an indicator covering both existing and new mortgages (i.e., OMDSR) is lower than an indicator covering only new mortgages (i.e., banks' DSR). Moreover, banks' higher DSR is also attributable to compliance with HKMA prudential requirements, which mandate the inclusion of non-mortgage loan repayments in DSR calculations. Both OMDSR and banks' DSR remained stable after the Global Financial Crisis, mainly due to HKMA's prudential supervision of mortgage lending, which imposed a cap on banks' DSR, a measure that also helped stabilize OMDSR. Chart B3.3 OMDSR and Banks' New Mortgage Debt Servicing Ratio Overall, OMDSR is broadly consistent with commonly used repayment burden indicators, but it offers greater timeliness and reflects the burden of total outstanding mortgage liabilities rather than just new ones. Therefore, we believe OMDSR is suitable for assessing the impact of mortgage repayment burden on private consumption. To evaluate the impact of mortgage repayment burden on private consumption in Hong Kong, we estimated an error-correction model following the approaches of Lai and Lam (2002) and Kang (2016). In this model, the long-run relationship between real private consumption (proxied by real average private consumption per household) and its determinants is captured by an error-correction term in the short-run equation. Based on existing theoretical and empirical evidence, we include real income (proxied by median household income, deflated by the CCPI), real housing and financial wealth (proxied by residential property prices and the Hang Seng Index respectively, deflated by the CCPI), and OMDSR as long-run determinants of private consumption.

The Hong Kong dollar weakened, while the local interbank market continued to function in an orderly manner. In the second half of 2017, total loans continued to increase, albeit at a slower pace than in the first half. Looking ahead, as US monetary policy continues to normalize, HKD interest rates may face greater upward pressure. Should global financial market sentiment shift abruptly, volatility in capital flows could increase. In the second half of 2017, the HKD/USD spot exchange rate fluctuated between 7.799 and 7.827 (Chart 4.1). The HKD spot rate strengthened briefly from September to November 2017, hovering around the 7.80 level. This was mainly due to increased funding demand for IPO activities and banks' prudent liquidity management ahead of month-end and year-end dates, which led to tighter liquidity conditions, thereby slowing interest rate arbitrage activities and increasing short-covering of the HKD. As HKD liquidity tightness eased and commercial demand for USD rose towards year-end, the HKD spot rate softened again in mid-December 2017. Entering 2018, despite increased volatility in global financial markets, particularly equity markets, the HKD continued to function in an orderly manner. During the reporting period, the HKD/USD exchange rate weakened, but the Weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1 HKD Exchange Rate Chart 4.2 Capital Flow Indicators The nominal effective exchange rate index of the HKD fluctuated slightly in the second half of 2017 but has recently faced greater downward pressure amid further weakening of the US dollar (Chart 4.3). This was broadly consistent with the movement of the USD against most major currencies. Given the minimal inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners and its limited impact on the real effective exchange rate index, the real effective exchange rate index of the HKD continued to track closely the movements of the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.3 Nominal and Real Effective Exchange Rates Non-resident portfolio investment recorded inflows in the second half of 2017. The latest Balance of Payments statistics show that both resident and non-resident equity portfolio investment recorded inflows in the third quarter, reflecting improved regional economic prospects and optimistic market sentiment (Table 4.A). Non-resident debt securities investment recorded inflows in the third quarter of 2017, offsetting outflows in resident debt investment. A survey of global mutual funds also indicated that both equity and debt investments recorded inflows in the fourth quarter of 2017, driven by optimistic market views on economic prospects and corporate earnings. In recent weeks, data from the same survey showed that despite adjustments in global financial markets, equity investment still recorded inflows, while bond investment saw minor net outflows (Chart 4.4). Chart 4.4 Market Survey on Equity and Bond-related Capital Flows Looking ahead, as the normalization of US monetary policy continues, the negative interest rate differential between the HKD and USD is expected to widen, potentially leading to increased arbitrage activities. Therefore, the possibility of the Weak-side Convertibility Undertaking being triggered should not be ruled out. This would be a normal process under the Linked Exchange Rate System. Meanwhile, given the uncertain pace of US monetary policy normalization and rapidly changing global macro-financial conditions and market sentiment, volatility in HKD capital flows and the HKD exchange rate may increase. The HKMA will continue to fully guarantee the stability of the HKD exchange rate in accordance with the Currency Board mechanism. Despite the Federal Reserve raising interest rates and continuing to shrink its balance sheet, Hong Kong's monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2017 and recently. The HKD Monetary Base rose further by 1.4% in the second half of 2017, mainly driven by growth in Certificates of Indebtedness issued for banknote issuance (Chart 4.5). As the Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered, the Aggregate Balance and the total amount of outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes remained largely unchanged in the second half, standing at approximately HK$1,226.8 billion. Specifically, the Aggregate Balance contracted somewhat, while outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes increased correspondingly. This was due to the additional issuance of Exchange Fund Bills (totaling HK$80 billion) to meet banks' substantial demand for liquidity management. Entering 2018, despite stock market corrections, the Monetary Base remained stable. Chart 4.5 Components of the Monetary Base Meanwhile, HKD money supply grew further in the second half of 2017, but at a slower pace. Growth in broad HKD money supply (HKD M3) decelerated from 8.9% in the first half to 2.5% in the second half. As a major component of HKD M3, HKD deposits edged up by 2.2% in the second half (Chart 4.7). Among them, demand deposits grew faster in the second half, partly due to buoyant asset markets and rising investment demand. Counterpart analysis shows that the growth in HKD M3 was supported by robust growth in HKD loans on one hand (Chart 4.6), but dragged down by net outflows of HKD funds from the non-bank private sector and a contraction in banks' net foreign currency assets on the other. Chart 4.6 Changes in HKD M3 and Its Counterparts On the other hand, foreign currency deposit growth was mixed. Partly reflecting the depreciation of the USD against most major currencies, the growth rate of USD deposits slowed from 3.0% in the first half to 2.4% in the second half (Chart 4.7). In contrast, other foreign currency deposits rebounded significantly in the second half, rising by 8.4%, after declining continuously for more than two years. This was mainly driven by the recent recovery in RMB deposits. Due to slower growth in both HKD and USD deposits, total deposits of authorized institutions increased slightly by 3.0% in the second half, compared to a growth rate of 5.6% in the first half. For 2017 as a whole, total deposits grew moderately by 8.7%, broadly similar to the figure for 2016. Chart 4.7 Deposit Growth From September to December 2017, increased funding demand for IPO activities and banks' prudent liquidity management ahead of month-end and year-end dates exerted upward pressure on HKD HIBOR (Chart 4.8). Compared with six months earlier, overnight and 3-month HIBOR rose by 14 and 50 basis points respectively, reaching 0.25% and 1.26% respectively in December (monthly averages). The negative interest rate differentials between HKD and USD HIBOR for maturities ranging from one month to three months narrowed accordingly. Chart 4.8 HKD and USD HIBOR Meanwhile, the HKD yield curve shifted upwards but flattened, broadly mirroring the trend of the USD yield curve. In the second half, the yield on 3-year Hong Kong Government Bonds rose by 63 basis points to close at 1.52% at end-2017, while the yield on 10-year bonds rose by a smaller margin of 33 basis points to close at 1.83% at end-2017 (Chart 4.9). Chart 4.9 Government Bond Yields Composite Interest Rate and Average Mortgage Rate for New Loans Entering 2018, the HKD interbank market continued to function in an orderly manner. As year-end funding demand subsided, HKD HIBOR retreated in early January. Thereafter, despite corrections in global and local equity markets, HKD HIBOR remained largely stable. Overnight and 3-month HIBOR closed at 0.43% and 1.08% respectively at end-February 2018. On the retail front, although banks' lending rates rose alongside the surge in HIBOR, banks' funding costs generally remained low due to a large deposit base. Despite intense competition in mortgage lending, the average mortgage rate for new loans rose gradually by 36 basis points to 2.16% in December (Chart 4.9), broadly tracking the rise in 1-month HIBOR. On the other hand, the composite interest rate, which measures retail banks' HKD funding costs, although rising briefly in October due to increased funding demand for IPO activities, remained soft for most of the second half, closing at 0.38% at end-December. Looking ahead, as US monetary policy continues to normalize and other major economies may embark on interest rate normalization, HKD interest rates may face greater upward pressure. At the same time, fluctuations in global market sentiment and rapidly changing macro-financial conditions may increase volatility in capital flows. However, the substantial HKD Monetary Base can serve as a buffer to help mitigate any excessively rapid rise in HKD interest rates. Furthermore, banks' prudent liquidity management and access to the Discount Window also help curb excessive volatility in interbank interest rates. Bank credit grew strongly throughout 2017. Loan growth reached 10.2% in the first half before slowing to 5.3% in the second half (Chart 4.10). In the second half of 2017, growth in both loans for use in Hong Kong and loans for use outside Hong Kong slowed. Analyzed by currency, driven by an improving local economic environment and relatively lower HKD funding costs, HKD loans continued to grow rapidly by 9.5% in the second half, while foreign currency loans edged up by only 0.1%. Notably, USD loan growth slowed to 1.8%, partly due to rising USD funding costs. For 2017 as a whole, total loans recorded robust growth of 16.1%, compared to 6.5% in 2016. Chart 4.10 Loan Growth Growth in loans for use in Hong Kong (including trade financing) decelerated from 9.4% in the first half to 5.6% in the second half, with performance varying across major sectors (Chart 4.11). Loan growth in construction and property development and investment slowed in the second half, partly because authorities required banks to strengthen risk management regarding loans to property developers starting June 2017. Despite further improvements in merchandise trade and retail sales, loans for trade financing and the transport sector recorded only relatively modest increases, while loans for the wholesale and retail trade sector declined. Conversely, loan growth for financial and finance-related firms remained strong, partly reflecting the steady expansion of the financial services sector. Chart 4.11 Domestic Loan Growth by Sector Household debt grew by 6.5% in the second half of 2017, compared to an increase of 5.0% in the first half. Within household debt, growth in personal loans (including credit card advances and other personal loans) accelerated further, reaching 12.4% in the second half. The robust growth in personal loans was mainly driven by borrowing from private banking and wealth management clients secured against financial assets. The growth of these loans was broadly in line with the continued expansion of client assets under management by banks. The risks associated with such secured lending are considered manageable. Moreover, the HKMA issued guidelines to banks in January 2014 on risk management of personal loans, requiring banks to adopt prudent risk management measures, including caps on loan tenors and borrowers' debt servicing ratios. On the other hand, although residential transaction volumes increased, the average loan-to-value ratio of newly approved mortgages decreased, and growth in residential mortgage loans slowed slightly to 3.8% in the second half. Overall, the ratio of household debt to GDP rose from 68.2% in the second quarter of 2017 to 70.2% in the fourth quarter (Chart 4.12).

Mainly benefiting from growth in net interest income, retail banks' earnings improved in the second half of 2017 compared to the same period in 2016. Capital and liquidity positions remained sound. After strong growth in the first half of 2017, credit growth moderated in the second half, while asset quality remained robust by historical standards. Despite a significant rise in Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBOR), retail banks' Hong Kong dollar funding costs remained low due to low retail deposit rates. However, banks should remain vigilant against risks of increased interest rate volatility and potential capital outflows amid US monetary policy normalization, as well as geopolitical risks. Given rising corporate leverage and high household debt burdens, banks should assess the potential impact on asset quality should interest rates rise more than expected. To enhance banks' resilience to systemic risks, the Countercyclical Capital Buffer ratio in Hong Kong will be raised to 2.5% effective January 1, 2019. In the second half of 2017, retail banks' aggregate pre-tax operating profit increased by 13.6% year-on-year. This was mainly driven by a substantial increase in net interest income and lower loan impairment provisions, which more than offset the decline in non-interest income. However, as asset growth outpaced earnings growth, retail banks' return on assets dipped slightly from 1.17% in the first half to 1.15% in the second half of 2017. Nevertheless, the return on assets in the second half of 2017 remained higher than the 1.11% recorded in the same period of 2016 (Chart 5.1). For 2017 as a whole, retail banks' aggregate pre-tax operating profit grew by 15.8%, while the return on assets rose from 1.09% in 2016 to 1.16%. Chart 5.1 Retail Banks' Earnings Retail banks' net interest margin widened further to 1.5% in the fourth quarter of 2017, from 1.34% in the same period of 2016 (Chart 5.2). Evidence suggests that the improvement in net interest margins is consistent with the widening of average spreads on Hong Kong dollar corporate loans in the Hong Kong syndicated loan market (Chart 5.3). Chart 5.2 Retail Banks' Net Interest Margin Chart 5.3 Average Spread on Hong Kong Dollar Syndicated Loans HIBORs rose across the board since September 2017, mainly driven by liquidity needs related to initial public offerings and banks' year-end funding requirements, as well as expectations of US interest rate hikes. Notably, the 3-month HIBOR reached a post-financial crisis high of 1.31% at end-December 2017, up 53 basis points from end-June, though still low by historical standards (blue line in Chart 5.4). Entering 2018, HIBORs appeared to stabilize as banks' year-end liquidity needs eased. Despite the recent rise in HIBORs, retail banks' Hong Kong dollar funding costs remained stable, mainly due to low retail deposit rates during the review period. Against this backdrop, the composite interest rate, which reflects the average Hong Kong dollar funding cost of retail banks, remained at a low level of around 0.3% for most of the second half of 2017, before edging up slightly to 0.38% at end-December (green line in Chart 5.4). A similar trend was observed in the overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong. In the second half of 2017, banks' average non-deposit market funding costs for Hong Kong dollars and US dollars rose by 35 basis points, while average deposit funding costs increased slightly by 12 basis points. Overall, the average total Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks rose by 22 basis points (red line in Chart 5.5). Chart 5.4 Interest Rates Chart 5.5 Hong Kong Dollar and US Dollar Funding Costs and Maturities of Licensed Banks The rise in HIBORs exceeded the increase in the banking sector's overall funding costs, which may help improve margins on HIBOR-linked assets. However, this improvement could be partially offset by intense competition in the mortgage market. In particular, market information indicates that some banks have reduced their mortgage rate spreads over benchmark rates or introduced fixed-rate mortgage terms to attract new customers. Given expectations of further US rate hikes this year, banks may soon face greater upward pressure on funding costs. Amid intense competition in the loan market, if increased funding costs cannot be fully passed on to customers, banks' net interest margins could come under pressure. The consolidated capital adequacy ratios of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained well above international minimum standards, indicating that the Hong Kong banking sector remains strongly capitalized. At end-December 2017, the total capital ratio increased to 19.1% from 18.7% at end-June (Chart 5.6), while the Tier 1 capital ratio also rose to 16.6%, of which 15.4% was Common Equity Tier 1 capital. Chart 5.6 Capital of Locally Incorporated Authorized Institutions The HKMA recently published a consultation paper on proposed rules for loss-absorbing capacity requirements applicable to authorized institutions under the Financial Institutions (Resolution) Ordinance. While enhancing authorized institutions' loss-absorbing capacity helps reduce the likelihood of financial crises, thereby benefiting society, it inevitably entails costs. Box 5 presents a cost-benefit assessment of the potential impact of loss-absorbing capacity requirements on Hong Kong. Our assessment indicates that implementing these requirements would yield net benefits to the Hong Kong economy. Measured by the Basel III Liquidity Coverage Ratio requirement, the banking sector's liquidity position remained robust during the review period. The average Liquidity Coverage Ratio of Category 1 institutions rose from 144.2% in the second quarter of 2017 to 155.1% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 80% applicable in 2017. Although the average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio of Category 2 institutions declined slightly from 49.7% in the second quarter of 2017 to 49.4% in the fourth quarter, it remained well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Authorized institutions' ample liquidity demonstrates that the Hong Kong banking sector is capable of withstanding liquidity shocks arising from potential capital outflows from Hong Kong. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio The Net Stable Funding Ratio, as part of the Basel III liquidity standards, was implemented in Hong Kong on January 1, 2018. This requirement aims to reduce banks' medium- to long-term funding risk by requiring them to maintain sufficient stable funding sources to finance their business activities. Specifically, Category 1 institutions must maintain a Net Stable Funding Ratio of no less than 100% at all times. Customer deposits remained the primary funding source for authorized institutions, reflecting a stable funding structure in the banking system. At end-December 2017, customer deposits accounted for 56.2% of total liabilities of all authorized institutions, broadly unchanged from six months earlier (Chart 5.8). Chart 5.8 Liability Structure of All Authorized Institutions The Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions rose from 77.1% at end-June 2017 to 82.7% at end-December (Chart 5.9), reflecting faster growth in Hong Kong dollar loans and advances relative to deposits during the review period. Meanwhile, as foreign currency deposit growth outpaced loan growth, the foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio fell from 65.5% at end-June 2017 to 63.1% at end-December. Overall, the loan-to-deposit ratio in all currencies rose from 71.4% six months earlier to 73.0%. Banks should assess the implications of the rising loan-to-deposit ratio for their liquidity management. Chart 5.9 Average Loan-to-Deposit Ratio of All Authorized Institutions Interest rate risk exposures of locally incorporated licensed banks remained low. We estimate that under an assumed parallel 200-basis-point upward shock in interest rates, the potential decline in the economic value of interest rate positions of locally incorporated licensed banks would amount to 3.45% of their total capital base at end-December 2017 (Chart 5.10). Nevertheless, given expectations that the Federal Reserve will continue to raise interest rates and commence balance sheet normalization, banks should assess the implications for their interest rate risk management. Chart 5.10 Impact of Interest Rate Shock on Locally Incorporated Licensed Banks In the second half of 2017, amid a moderate yet favorable economic environment, the growth rate of total loans and advances of all authorized institutions slowed to 5.3%, down from the robust 10.2% growth recorded in the first half. Following two years of slower growth, total loans grew solidly by 16.1% for 2017 as a whole. Asset quality of banks' loan portfolios remained robust and continued to improve in the second half of 2017. At end-December 2017, the overall specific classified loan ratio and overdue and rescheduled loan ratio of all authorized institutions fell to 0.67% and 0.52% respectively, compared with 0.84% and 0.61% at end-June. For retail banks, the overall specific classified loan ratio and overdue and rescheduled loan ratio also declined to 0.54% and 0.4% respectively (Chart 5.11). However, given the rapid growth in loans for use outside Hong Kong in recent years, banks' asset quality may have become more sensitive to external developments, and banks should therefore closely monitor their credit risk. Chart 5.11 Asset Quality of Retail Banks As banks have become more optimistic about near-term credit growth, strong credit expansion is expected to persist. The HKMA's December 2017 "Credit Conditions Outlook Survey" showed that 29% of respondent authorized institutions expected loan demand to increase over the next three months, while the remaining 71% expected loan demand to remain unchanged (Table 5.A). Credit risk associated with personal lending remained low during the review period. Banks' mortgage loan portfolios remained sound, with the delinquency ratio staying low at 0.03% at end-December 2017. The average loan-to-value ratio of newly approved mortgages fell further from 50.1% in the second quarter of 2017 to 48.8% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.12). This loan-to-value ratio is significantly lower than the 64% recorded prior to the introduction of the first round of countercyclical macro-prudential measures by the HKMA in September 2009.

The global economy maintained its growth, but the momentum has weakened as uncertainties increased due to ongoing trade frictions, tightening financial conditions, and other idiosyncratic and cyclical headwinds. The Federal Reserve adjusted its monetary policy stance, emphasizing that decisions would be "data-dependent" and require "patience," leading investors to rule out the possibility of further rate hikes. However, financial markets may become more sensitive to subsequent data releases, particularly those that could prompt a tightening of monetary policy, such as rising U.S. inflation. In Hong Kong, although the Weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered in March, trading in the Hong Kong dollar continued to be smooth and orderly. In the second half of 2018, total loan growth narrowed slightly, reflecting reduced credit demand amid headwinds such as the ongoing U.S.-China trade conflict and slowing global economic growth. The residential property market also cooled in the second half of 2018, with transaction volumes declining significantly and property prices retreating, before showing signs of stabilization in early 2019. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector faces multiple headwinds due to increasing uncertainties in the external environment. If these uncertainties intensify and persist for a prolonged period, they could significantly dampen business confidence and credit demand, thereby exerting downward pressure on bank profitability. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage, banks should prudently assess the impact that a potential deterioration in the external environment could have on the credit risk of their related corporate loans. In the second half of 2018, the global economy maintained its growth. However, while the U.S. economy grew steadily, growth momentum in other regions slowed. Among advanced economies, Japan and several major euro area countries experienced slower growth and low inflation. Slowing global trade and a significant decline in oil prices posed cyclical headwinds to emerging market economies. In light of the slowing global growth momentum, the International Monetary Fund lowered its global growth forecasts for 2019 and 2020 in January by 0.2 and 0.1 percentage points, respectively, compared to its October 2018 projections. Due to dimming growth prospects and escalating trade frictions, global equity markets experienced significant volatility at the end of 2018. The U.S. Treasury yield curve flattened to levels not seen since the Global Financial Crisis, sparking market concerns about an impending recession in the United States. However, U.S. economic fundamentals remain solid, and the probability of a recession in the near term is low. Nevertheless, the global economic outlook remains fraught with uncertainties. On the U.S. front, although moderate inflation has given the Federal Reserve room to pause rate hikes, the Fed's data-dependent policy inclination suggests that financial markets may become more sensitive to subsequent data releases, particularly data such as rising U.S. inflation that could prompt monetary policy tightening. Meanwhile, the outcomes of trade negotiations between the U.S. and China, as well as between the U.S. and the EU, remain uncertain. In the UK, it remains unclear whether a plan to avoid a "hard Brexit" can be realized. In East Asia, financial markets have stabilized as the U.S. dollar's rally has moderated and markets anticipate a pause in Fed rate hikes, but a deteriorating external environment could weigh on regional economic growth. Indeed, weakening global trade momentum has already dragged down economic growth in several East Asian economies, and inflationary pressures have also subsided. While this shift may alleviate the policy dilemma faced by regional central banks between supporting growth and containing inflation, financial imbalances, such as high private sector debt in some countries within the region, remain severe. As detailed in Box 1 (page 16), another challenge facing the East Asian region is that unexpected shifts in the Federal Reserve's monetary policy could trigger spillovers to sovereign bond markets in emerging market economies, including those in East Asia. In Mainland China, growth slowed further in the second half of 2018 due to increased external uncertainties and a slight moderation in domestic demand. Looking ahead, the economic outlook remains uncertain pending the outcome of U.S.-China trade negotiations. Financing difficulties faced by private enterprises, especially small firms, have intensified over the past few quarters due to a significant contraction in shadow financing activities. Coupled with weakening economic confidence, this may also exert pressure on business activity. In this challenging economic environment, policymakers need to continue striking a balance between stabilizing the economy and preventing potential systemic risks by adopting accommodative yet targeted measures, such as targeted reserve requirement ratio cuts. At the same time, authorities have implemented additional supply-side measures to boost productivity growth, such as promoting competition among companies of different ownership structures, and to provide a better social safety net for individuals. The official growth target for 2019 has also been lowered from around 6.5% in 2018 to a range of 6.0% to 6.5%. In 2018, risk aversion dominated Mainland financial markets. Bank asset quality deteriorated slightly during the review period, while leverage among listed non-financial corporations rose marginally. However, banks' loan impairment provisions increased further in the second half of 2018, and their exposure to off-balance-sheet wealth management products continued to decline; both developments help shield the banking system from potential deterioration in credit quality. Another positive development is that leverage among listed companies in industries with overcapacity—a key source of bank credit risk—declined further in the first three quarters of 2018. Box 2 (page 32) provides an in-depth analysis of the factors driving the recent improvement in business performance in industries with overcapacity. Compared with the first half of 2018, economic activity in Hong Kong softened in the second half. Quarter-on-quarter GDP growth stalled, and year-on-year growth also slowed, dragging full-year economic growth down from 3.8% in 2017 to 3.0% in 2018. The weakening of economic activity was mainly due to consumption and exports being weighed down by the direct and indirect effects of the U.S.-China trade conflict. Private consumption growth slowed, possibly reflecting increased economic uncertainties and the negative wealth effect arising from adjustments in local asset prices. Externally, Hong Kong's merchandise export performance also deteriorated, particularly in the fourth quarter after both the U.S. and China implemented additional tariffs. Box 3 examines more closely the impact of the U.S.-China trade conflict on Hong Kong's merchandise trade performance and explores the near-term outlook and associated risks. Mainly due to slowing global economic growth, economic growth in 2019 is expected to slow further. Amid the interplay of multiple factors, Hong Kong's export performance is expected to remain under pressure. Domestically, supported by a low unemployment rate and rising household incomes, private consumption is expected to continue underpinning economic growth, although the outlook for overall investment spending may become more uncertain. The government forecasts real GDP growth of 2% to 3% for 2019, while the average of private sector analysts' latest growth forecasts stands at 2.3%. These forecasts are subject to the various uncertainties and risks mentioned above. Local inflation edged up in the second half of 2018 but remained moderate. The slight increase in inflation was partly attributable to earlier increases in fresh private residential rentals. Meanwhile, although the unemployment rate remained low at 2.8%, its lowest level in over two decades, growth in total employment showed signs of slowing. Looking ahead, as domestic economic growth momentum weakens, local inflationary pressures are expected to remain moderate in 2019. Following the triggering of the Weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in late August, the HKD exchange rate moved away from 7.8500 and fluctuated between 7.8062 and 7.8499 until the Weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered four more times in March 2019 (as of March 19). The HKD exchange rate strengthened in September and November, partly reflecting the unwinding of carry trades amid tightening liquidity. Entering 2019, the HKD depreciated against the USD, partly due to the re-establishment of carry trade positions. Despite the re-triggering of the Weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in March, HKD trading continued to be smooth and orderly. Due to the triggering of the Weak-side Convertibility Undertaking, the Aggregate Balance declined slightly to HK$70.9 billion (as of March 19). HKD HIBORs generally rose in the second half of 2018, mainly reflecting expectations of U.S. rate hikes. Compared with June 2018, the 3-month and 12-month HIBORs rose by approximately 30 basis points to 2.32% and 2.74% respectively in December (monthly averages). Entering 2019, HKD HIBORs generally fell due to waning seasonal demand. The Composite Interest Rate, which measures the average HKD funding cost of retail banks, rose from 0.62% at end-June 2018 to 0.83% at end-January 2019. In light of rising funding costs, following the upward adjustment of the U.S. Federal Funds target range at end-September, retail banks raised their Best Lending Rates by 12.5 to 25.0 basis points. At end-January 2019, the average mortgage rate for newly originated mortgages rose in tandem with the Best Lending Rate to approximately 2.45%. Given the persistence of uncertainties related to U.S.-China trade frictions and Brexit negotiations, volatility in capital flows may intensify. Moreover, the significant negative interest rate differential between HKD and USD rates could stimulate carry trade activities, leading to capital outflows. Under such circumstances, both capital outflows and the potential triggering of the Weak-side Convertibility Undertaking represent normal operations under the Linked Exchange Rate System. Since the beginning of 2018, both offshore and onshore RMB exchange rates have faced depreciation pressures due to market concerns over escalating U.S.-China trade frictions. However, buoyed by optimism driven by the resumption of high-level trade talks between the U.S. and China, both offshore and onshore RMB exchange rates stabilized in November. Although U.S.-China trade frictions persist, they have not yet had a significant impact on liquidity conditions in the offshore interbank market. Overnight CNH HIBOR remained below 4% for most of 2018, while 3-month CNH HIBOR hovered around 4%. Meanwhile, Hong Kong's offshore RMB capital pool expanded steadily in the second half of the year, with RMB customer deposits growing by 5.2% in the second half of 2018. Average daily turnover in the RMB Real Time Gross Settlement system remained at high levels, rising further to RMB 1,010.1 billion in 2018. Despite lingering concerns over U.S.-China trade frictions, Hong Kong's offshore RMB business is expected to continue expanding, driven by Mainland China's capital account liberalization, the development of Stock Connect and Bond Connect schemes, and regional economic cooperation promoted under the Belt and Road Initiative and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiative. The local stock market experienced a roller-coaster ride over the past six months. During the early part of the review period, the market fell sharply due to continued tightening of U.S. monetary policy, significant disagreements between the two sides in U.S.-China trade negotiations, and increasing signs of weakening economic growth in the Mainland. Subsequently, as the U.S. economic outlook weakened and became more uncertain, the Federal Reserve shifted to a "patient" monetary policy stance. Meanwhile, during the trade war truce, China took additional measures to reduce its trade surplus with the U.S. and open its markets to foreign investors. Although the U.S. filed highly politicized legal charges against a Chinese telecommunications company, both sides struck a conciliatory tone, signaling determination to reach a trade deal. Against this backdrop, the local stock market rebounded sharply earlier this year. However, considerable uncertainty remains as both sides discuss the details of a potential agreement, and future developments regarding the U.S. federal government's prosecution could complicate matters, particularly in the high-tech sector. The HKD debt market grew slightly last year. Yields declined, and performance improved towards year-end as market expectations of a slower pace of U.S. monetary policy normalization strengthened. Consequently, fund flows into bond funds reversed course in the second half of the year and saw a modest increase. Issuance in Hong Kong's offshore RMB market rebounded strongly after three consecutive years of decline. However, total issuance remained below maturing debt as Mainland companies continued to deleverage. Looking ahead, the local debt market remains challenging, with its outlook contingent on global economic developments, particularly those in the Mainland.

During the period under review, the global economy continued to expand, but growth momentum weakened amid a combination of idiosyncratic and cyclical headwinds, particularly in regions outside the United States. In light of the dimming growth outlook, the Federal Reserve adjusted its monetary policy stance, emphasizing that decisions would be "data-dependent" and require "patience," and ceased providing forward guidance on further rate hikes. Given the Fed's data-dependent policy inclination, financial markets may become more sensitive to subsequent data releases and may perceive monetary policy as becoming more uncertain. Meanwhile, heightened uncertainties over global trade policies and escalating geopolitical risks could continue to cast a shadow over the global economic outlook. In East Asia, financial markets have largely stabilized since late 2018, as signs of a slowdown in the U.S. rate hike cycle emerged and the U.S. dollar stabilized. However, due to a deteriorating external environment—namely the unresolved U.S.-China trade conflict and weakening growth in advanced economies—the region may face a broad-based slowdown. In Mainland China, growth momentum slowed further in the second half of 2018, and uncertainty over the growth outlook has risen amid the U.S.-China trade conflict and financing difficulties faced by small enterprises. Consequently, policymakers have adopted more targeted measures to stabilize the economy and support private and small businesses. Faced with these challenges, policymakers will need to strike a delicate balance between continuing to prevent and control systemic risks and supporting enterprises and the real economy. In the second half of 2018, the global economy continued its broad-based expansion. However, while the U.S. economy remained generally robust, some signs of slowing emerged. There were also clear indications that growth momentum outside the U.S. had moderated. Idiosyncratic shocks in specific countries—including natural disasters in Japan, the implementation of new auto emission standards in Germany, a surge in Italian government bond yields due to a fiscal standoff with the EU, and social unrest in France—all weighed on economic activity in advanced economies (Chart 2.1). In addition, a cyclical slowdown in global import growth posed headwinds to industrial production in emerging market economies (Chart 2.2). The sharp drop in oil prices in the fourth quarter also presented new challenges to commodity-exporting emerging market economies. Given the deceleration in growth momentum in the second half of 2018, the International Monetary Fund lowered its 2019 global growth forecast by 0.2 percentage points to 3.5% in January. Chart 2.1 Composite Purchasing Managers’ Index for Selected Advanced Economies Chart 2.2 Global Import Volume and Industrial Production in Emerging Market Economies In the fourth quarter, global equity markets underwent significant corrections amid slowing global growth momentum, heightened trade policy uncertainties, market concerns over the sustainability of U.S. corporate earnings growth, and the Fed’s rhetoric signaling continued monetary tightening. As financial market sentiment deteriorated, the U.S. Treasury yield curve flattened to levels unseen since the Global Financial Crisis, sparking fears among some market participants of an impending U.S. recession (Chart 2.3). Chart 2.3 Spread Between 10-Year and 3-Month U.S. Treasury Yields and Probability of a U.S. Recession Nevertheless, the probability of a U.S. recession in the near term remains low. U.S. economic fundamentals remain solid; in particular, the tight labor market is expected to continue supporting private consumption. Meanwhile, the U.S. output gap is estimated to have turned positive only last year, making it less likely that economic overheating would prompt the Fed to tighten monetary policy aggressively. However, possibly taking into account the significant tightening of financial conditions since the fourth quarter, senior Fed officials began emphasizing in early January that monetary policy would be data-dependent, noting that muted inflation pressures allowed them to be "patient" in determining future policy adjustments. Furthermore, following its January meeting, the Federal Open Market Committee ceased providing forward guidance on further rate hikes and announced that it "is prepared to adjust any of the details for completing balance sheet normalization in light of economic and financial developments." This shift triggered a rebound in global equity markets (Chart 2.4). Chart 2.4 S&P 500, MSCI World ex-U.S. Index, and MSCI Emerging Markets Index Despite the Fed’s recent "dovish" signals, the outlook for U.S. monetary policy remains highly uncertain, contingent upon inflation and other developments. Inflation pressures have been muted thus far, giving the Fed room to proceed gradually with monetary normalization. Inflation expectations have remained anchored in recent years, supporting the view that the Fed "can afford to be patient" (Chart 2.5). Moreover, as Fed Chair Powell noted in January, the U.S. economic outlook faces multiple headwinds, including slowing growth outside the U.S. and trade policy uncertainties. In light of these developments, the Fed may need to adopt a more cautious monetary policy stance. Chart 2.5 Market-Based and Survey-Based Measures of U.S. Inflation Expectations However, the tight labor market is expected to continue supporting overall U.S. economic performance. Against this backdrop, wage growth may accelerate, which typically implies that inflation could pick up going forward (Chart 2.6). Therefore, market expectations that have essentially priced out the possibility of Fed rate hikes in 2019 may be overly optimistic (Chart 2.7). Chart 2.6 Average Hourly Earnings and Core PCE Inflation Chart 2.7 Futures-Implied Probability of the Federal Funds Rate Target Range Remaining Unchanged in 2019 Versus At Least One Rate Hike In summary, a prolonged pause in Fed rate hikes is not a foregone conclusion.
