To minimize policy errors, the Fed has increasingly emphasized that its decisions will be data-dependent as a risk management strategy. It follows that financial markets may become more sensitive to subsequent data releases, especially those that could prompt monetary tightening. Monetary policy outlooks at other major central banks are also uncertain. In the Eurozone, the European Central Bank ended its asset purchase program in December while continuing to reinvest principal payments from maturing securities purchased under the program in full, and reaffirmed its forward guidance that key interest rates would remain at their present levels at least through the summer of 2019. However, in January, the ECB downgraded its near-term growth assessment, stating that risks to the growth outlook had "moved to the downside." The implications of this downward revision for monetary policy remain to be seen. In Japan, the Bank of Japan indicated at its recent policy meeting that it would ease its monetary policy stance if necessary amid increasing downside risks. However, resistance to further monetary easing could be strong, as its effectiveness is questioned and the side effects of maintaining an ultra-low interest rate environment for a prolonged period are becoming increasingly apparent; for instance, regional banks' capital adequacy ratios declined from 10.6% in 2015 to 9.7% in 2018 as persistently low yields weighed on profitability. Consequently, the BOJ has very limited room to adjust monetary policy in the near term. Beyond uncertainties related to the global monetary policy outlook, uncertain outcomes of future trade negotiations and escalating geopolitical risks constitute two major sources of risk to the global economic outlook. The U.S. administration announced in early December that it would not increase tariffs on imports from China for 90 days, and extended the deadline again in late February, but whether the two sides can reach a long-term trade deal remains to be seen. Meanwhile, trade negotiations between the U.S. and the EU have made little progress at this stage. Uncertainty surrounding the outcomes of these trade negotiations could continue to cloud the global economic outlook. Policy and geopolitical risks are also prominent. In the U.S., partisan disagreements over border security funding led to a 35-day federal government shutdown from late December 2018 to late January 2019. Although the impact of the shutdown on economic growth should be transitory, tensions between the Trump administration and the Democratic-controlled House of Representatives could lead to further policy gridlock going forward. In the UK, after Prime Minister Theresa May’s Brexit deal was overwhelmingly rejected in mid-January, risks associated with Brexit and its spillover effects surged, and it remains uncertain whether a solution can be crafted at the eleventh hour to avoid a disruptive "hard Brexit." Elsewhere, geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, such as renewed U.S. sanctions on Iran, could also create uncertainty regarding oil prices, thereby affecting the global growth outlook. In East Asia, financial markets largely stabilized in the fourth quarter after experiencing volatility during the first three quarters of last year. The stabilization of the U.S. dollar since October and signs that the Fed would remain patient regarding further rate hikes eased currency depreciation and capital outflow pressures facing East Asian economies. Several currencies in the region appreciated slightly against the U.S. dollar in the fourth quarter, and portfolio investment flows returned to net inflows (Chart 2.8). Chart 2.8 East Asia: Currency Indices and Capital Flows Despite financial market stability, there are growing signs that the region faces a broad-based slowdown. Weakening global trade momentum resulting from the U.S.-China trade conflict has dampened export growth in the region, causing real GDP growth in most East Asian economies to slow in the second half of last year. Indeed, the new export orders sub-index of the Purchasing Managers’ Index for several regional economies—a gauge of near-term external trade performance—has fallen into contraction territory since the fourth quarter, suggesting that near-term growth momentum may weaken further (Chart 2.9). Chart 2.9 Markit PMI New Export Orders Index for East Asian Economies Amid slowing growth and declining oil prices recently, inflationary pressures in East Asia have subsided (Chart 2.10). Chart 2.10 East Asia: Headline Inflation Rates and Oil Prices With both recent inflationary pressures and upward pressure on the U.S. dollar relatively moderate, central banks in East Asia face no pressing need to raise interest rates, alleviating the policy dilemma involving trade-offs between fostering economic growth and curbing inflation and capital outflows. However, as private sector debt in some East Asian countries remains high by emerging market standards, central banks still face challenges related to financial imbalances (Chart 2.11).

The Hong Kong economy softened in the second half of 2018, reflecting a slowdown in private consumption growth and weaker export performance amid the US-Mainland trade dispute. With global growth slowing, real GDP growth is expected to moderate in 2019. The local growth outlook is clouded by numerous uncertainties and risks, including trade protectionism, the future direction of US monetary policy, and economic performance on the Mainland. Local inflationary pressures should remain mild in 2019, though the outlook faces both upside and downside risks. Economic activity in Hong Kong softened in the second half of 2018. Specifically, economic activity failed to sustain the strong momentum seen in the first half, and the quarter-on-quarter GDP growth rate turned slightly negative in the second half (Table 3.A and Chart 3.1). On a year-on-year basis, economic growth also slowed, with the fourth-quarter growth rate at 1.3%, below trend growth, dragging down full-year growth from 3.8% in 2017 to 3.0% in 2018.* *Calculated based on the expenditure-based seasonally adjusted real GDP volume index. Chart 3.1 Real GDP Growth Rate and Contributions of Major Expenditure Components The weakening of economic activity was mainly due to consumption and exports being dragged down by the direct or indirect effects of the US-Mainland trade conflict. Private consumption growth slowed, possibly due to increased economic uncertainty and the negative wealth effect resulting from adjustments in local asset prices (Chart 3.1). Total investment spending declined significantly amid fragile business sentiment. Hong Kong's external merchandise trade performance also deteriorated, particularly after the US and the Mainland implemented additional tariffs in the fourth quarter (Chart 3.2). Nevertheless, as total imports decelerated faster than total exports, net trade still made a positive contribution to GDP in the fourth quarter. Box 3 examines Hong Kong's merchandise trade performance in greater detail and explores the near-term outlook and associated risks. Chart 3.2 Real Imports and Exports As economic activity weakened, employment growth appeared to slow in the second half of 2018. Total employment increased by only 0.1% to approximately 3,873,000 by end-2018, lower than the 0.8% increase in the first half of 2018. Due to weak output and employment growth, labour productivity remained broadly flat, showing no signs of significant improvement. With global economic growth slowing further, local economic growth is expected to moderate in 2019. Facing challenges in the external environment, Hong Kong's export performance is expected to remain under pressure. Domestically, although low unemployment and rising household incomes will continue to support private consumption, consumption growth is expected to slow, partly affected by weakening consumer confidence and the negative wealth effect caused by earlier asset price adjustments. As for gross domestic fixed capital formation, the outlook may become more uncertain. While building and construction activities are expected to grow steadily as housing supply increases, businesses may become more cautious about capital investment amid rising economic uncertainty. Business sentiment indicators, such as the Hong Kong Purchasing Managers' Index, continued to hover in contractionary territory; forecasts of future economic growth derived from this index suggest a further slowdown in year-on-year GDP growth in the near term. The Government forecasts real GDP growth of 2–3% for 2019, while the latest growth forecasts by private sector analysts range from 1.5% to 2.7%. The local growth outlook is subject to the multiple uncertainties and risks discussed in the previous two chapters. Although local inflationary pressures have continued to build up in recent months, they remain mild. Year-on-year, the underlying Composite Consumer Price Index rose by 2.8% and 2.9% in the third and fourth quarters of 2018 respectively, higher than the average increase of 2.4% in the first half. The three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, also picked up recently, rising from 2.5% in July 2018 to 2.6% in January 2019 (Chart 3.3). The slight increase in inflation momentum was driven by rises in certain service prices. Earlier increases in fresh private residential rentals and accelerated rises in dining-out prices continued to push up services inflation (Chart 3.4). However, labour cost pressures have remained largely mild over the past few quarters (Chart 3.5). Chart 3.3 Various Measures of Consumer Price Inflation Chart 3.4 Rent Component of CCPI and Market Rentals Chart 3.5 Unit Labour Costs and Wages Per Employee Looking ahead, local inflationary pressures should remain mild in 2019, mainly reflecting weaker local growth momentum. However, earlier increases in private residential rentals will continue to feed through to consumer price inflation. Market consensus forecasts a moderate overall inflation rate of 2.2% for the year, while the Government forecasts an underlying inflation rate of 2.5%. The above inflation outlook faces both upside and downside risks. On the downside, the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate remained at around 2.8%, the lowest level in over 20 years (Chart 3.6). If the labour market were to deteriorate unexpectedly, the current near-zero output gap would turn negative, potentially exerting additional downward pressure on inflation. Conversely, if US-Mainland trade tensions ease, leading to better-than-expected local economic performance, local inflation could be pushed higher. Chart 3.6 Unemployment Rate The US-Mainland trade conflict escalated gradually in the second half of 2018: the US imposed additional 25% tariffs on US$34 billion and US$16 billion worth of imports from the Mainland on July 6 and August 23 respectively. Following these two moves, the Mainland responded by imposing additional 25% tariffs on an equivalent value of US goods. The US escalated further on September 24, imposing additional 10% tariffs on US$200 billion worth of imports from the Mainland. The Mainland immediately responded by imposing additional 5–10% tariffs on US$60 billion worth of US goods. Subsequently, the two sides entered negotiations to avoid further tariff hikes. As Hong Kong has traditionally been an entrepôt between these two economies, additional tariffs inevitably have a direct impact on Hong Kong through trade channels. Therefore, the US-Mainland trade dispute has important implications for Hong Kong's macroeconomic and financial stability. This box reviews Hong Kong's recent merchandise trade performance and explores its near-term outlook. We also attempt to use more granular data to identify trade goods directly affected by additional tariffs, thereby examining the impact of tariff hikes more closely. To analyse the impact of tariffs, we first extracted six sets of Hong Kong re-export data corresponding to the various rounds of tariff hikes described in the previous section. In the first two rounds of tariff hikes, the US mainly imposed tariffs on capital goods and semi-manufactures, while the Mainland primarily targeted agricultural products, chemicals, medical equipment, and energy equipment. In the third round, the scope of affected goods expanded to cover more consumer goods. For brevity, we refer to the goods affected by these three rounds of tariff hikes as List 1, List 2, and List 3 accordingly. After collecting these more granular trade data, we focused our analysis on year-on-year changes in Hong Kong re-export values to adjust for seasonal effects. In addition, readers should exercise caution when analysing September 2018 data, as trade activities that month were disrupted to some extent by Super Typhoon Mangkhut. Overall, the findings in this section should be regarded only as preliminary evidence of the impact of additional tariffs. Hong Kong Re-exports of Mainland Origin Affected by Tariffs Shortly after the imposition of additional tariffs, relevant goods re-exported from the Mainland via Hong Kong to the US appeared to have declined significantly or seen growth slow (Chart B3.1). For example, re-export growth for Lists 1 and 2 slowed in the first month after tariff implementation, while re-exports for List 3 recorded negative growth. Moreover, re-exports for all three lists recorded negative growth in December. Chart B3.1 Value of Goods Re-exported from the Mainland via Hong Kong to the US, 2018 Hong Kong Re-exports of US Origin Affected by Tariffs In contrast, goods re-exported from the US via Hong Kong to the Mainland showed mixed performance (Chart B3.2). Re-exports for List 1 appeared to decline significantly in the months following tariff implementation but rebounded towards the end of the year. Re-exports for List 2 remained largely in negative growth territory throughout the year, while growth for List 3 appeared broadly stable. Chart B3.2 Value of Goods Re-exported from the US via Hong Kong to the Mainland, 2018 Front-loading Due to the time lag between tariff announcements and final implementation (or simply due to the threat of additional tariffs), firms may increase shipments of affected goods ahead of anticipated effective dates. Indeed, anecdotal evidence and news reports suggest that such front-loading behaviour was quite prevalent. Some private sector analysts also attribute part of the strong overall trade figures prior to tariff implementation to this behaviour. More granular trade data indicate some signs of front-loading for certain listed goods, but this appears limited to goods re-exported from the Mainland to the US (Chart B3.1). Re-export growth rates for Lists 1 and 2 both rose in the months preceding their respective tariff effective dates. On the other hand, growth rates for re-exports from the US via Hong Kong to the Mainland (Chart B3.2) show no clear evidence of significant front-loading by firms. Hong Kong Re-exports Not Affected by Additional Tariffs It is worth noting that Hong Kong re-exports (by value) directly affected by additional tariffs account for only about 4–5% of total Hong Kong re-exports. To gain a more complete picture of Hong Kong's trade performance, we should also examine re-exports not affected by additional tariffs. We found that re-exports unaffected by additional tariffs recorded negative growth in the last two months of 2018 (Chart B3.3). Furthermore, growth in tariff-affected re-exports (red line) has shown a markedly larger decline since the third quarter, reflecting the significant impact of tariffs. The slowdown in growth of re-exports unaffected by additional tariffs partly reflects broader weakening in external demand. As ongoing trade frictions lead to increased uncertainty, tightening global financial conditions, and rising geopolitical risks, external demand is likely to come under broader pressure. In particular, the trade conflict has weighed on global economic sentiment and activity, as reflected in corrections in major equity markets. Import demand from other economies has thus been dragged down, dampening Hong Kong's external trade performance. Chart B3.3 Value of Hong Kong Re-exports, 2018 Even if US-Mainland trade tensions ease, the near-term outlook for Hong Kong's merchandise trade remains challenging. Global growth is likely to slow in 2019 (see Chapter 2), which will further weigh on Hong Kong's export performance. Various business sentiment indicators suggest that firms of all sizes are pessimistic about their business outlook (Chart B3.4), with sentiment in the trade sector particularly subdued. Other trade-related sectors, such as logistics, may also be affected. Chart B3.4 Survey on Business Prospects for Hong Kong's Import/Export Sector

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened in September and November, partly reflecting the unwinding of carry trades amid tightening liquidity driven by anticipated seasonal funding demand. Entering 2019, partly due to the repatriation of IPO proceeds by corporations and the re-establishment of carry trade positions in the market, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate gradually weakened, triggering the Weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in March. Nevertheless, trading in the Hong Kong dollar remained smooth and orderly. The Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) generally rose in the second half of 2018, reflecting expectations of US interest rate hikes and seasonal funding demand, before retreating in January 2019. Looking ahead, amid uncertainties such as the continued US-China trade friction, Brexit negotiations, and the increasingly unpredictable pace of US monetary policy normalization, capital flows in the Hong Kong dollar may become more volatile. If the interest rate differential between Hong Kong and the US remains wide, market carry trade activities may persist, causing the Hong Kong dollar to remain weak for some time and potentially triggering the Weak-side Convertibility Undertaking again, which is consistent with the design of the Linked Exchange Rate System. Following the triggering of the Weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in late August, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate moved away from 7.8500 and fluctuated between 7.8062 and 7.8499 until it triggered the Weak-side Convertibility Undertaking four times in total in March 2019 (as of March 19) (Chart 4.1). The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate rose briefly in September, partly reflecting the unwinding of carry trades amid tightening liquidity, but subsequently declined gradually in October. The Hong Kong dollar stabilized again after November as year-end funding demand led to tighter liquidity and the unwinding of carry trades. Entering 2019, the spot exchange rate weakened, partly reflecting the repatriation of IPO proceeds by corporations and the re-establishment of carry trade positions in the market. As the interest rate differential between Hong Kong and the US widened after the turn of the year, market participants engaged in carry trades by buying US dollars and selling Hong Kong dollars, driving the Hong Kong dollar gradually weaker and triggering the Weak-side Convertibility Undertaking again in March. Despite the triggering of the Weak-side Convertibility Undertaking, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly. The Aggregate Balance has remained at around HK$76 billion since August (Chart 4.2), declining slightly to HK$70.9 billion following the triggering of the Weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in March (as of March 19). Capital outflows from the Hong Kong dollar since April 2018 represent only a small fraction of the approximately HK$1 trillion inflows recorded since 2008. Chart 4.1 Hong Kong Dollar Exchange Rate Chart 4.2 Capital Flow Indicators The nominal effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar broadly tracked movements in the US dollar and continued to rise during the review period (Chart 4.3). Given the minimal inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners, which had limited impact on the real effective exchange rate index, the trend of the real effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar largely mirrored that of the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.3 Nominal and Real Effective Exchange Rates The latest balance of payments statistics indicate that portfolio investment continued to record net outflows in the third quarter of 2018. Amid weak market sentiment and increased stock market volatility, outflows in equity portfolio investment by local residents accelerated, more than offsetting the inflows in portfolio investment by non-residents in the third quarter (Table 4.A). In contrast, both local and non-resident debt securities portfolio investments recorded inflows in the third quarter. Looking ahead, amid uncertainties such as the continued US-China trade friction, Brexit negotiations, and the increasingly unpredictable pace of US monetary policy normalization, capital flow volatility may intensify. Furthermore, the significant negative interest rate differential between Hong Kong dollar and US dollar rates may stimulate carry trade activities, leading to capital outflows. Under the Linked Exchange Rate System, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate may weaken, and the Weak-side Convertibility Undertaking may be triggered again. Both capital outflows and the potential triggering of the Weak-side Convertibility Undertaking are normal operations under the Linked Exchange Rate System. Despite the ongoing process of US interest rate normalization and the multiple triggering of the Weak-side Convertibility Undertaking from April to August, Hong Kong's monetary conditions remained accommodative in the second half of 2018. The Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base contracted slightly by 0.7% in the second half, standing at HK$1,632.9 billion at end-2018 (Chart 4.4). The contraction in the Monetary Base was mainly attributable to the triggering of the Weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in August 2018, which caused the Aggregate Balance to decrease from HK$109.5 billion at end-June 2018 to HK$76.4 billion at end-2018, while Certificates of Indebtedness, government-issued currency notes and coins in circulation, and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes increased slightly. The Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base remained broadly stable in the first two months of 2019, with the Aggregate Balance showing no significant change since August. Subsequently, due to the triggering of the Weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in March, the Aggregate Balance declined slightly to approximately HK$70.9 billion (as of March 19). Chart 4.4 Components of the Monetary Base Regarding broader measures of Hong Kong dollar money supply, money supply growth generally slowed in the second half, partly reflecting increased uncertainties in the macroeconomic and financial environment. Broad Hong Kong dollar money supply (HKD M3) grew by 3.6% in the first half but only edged up by 0.1% in the second half (Chart 4.5). As a major component of HKD M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits remained largely unchanged compared with end-June (Chart 4.6). Within Hong Kong dollar deposits, demand and savings deposits fell, partly due to reduced investment-related transactions in the second half; on the other hand, time deposits continued to record robust growth amid higher deposit rates. Counterpart analysis shows that the slower growth in HKD M3 was attributable to changes in banks' capital and reserves (included in "Net Other Items"). Chart 4.5 Changes in HKD M3 and Its Counterparts Foreign currency deposits accelerated in growth during the second half. Driven by an increase in deposits attracted after banks raised their preferential US dollar deposit rates, US dollar deposits grew strongly by 8.8% in the second half, becoming the main driver of foreign currency deposit growth (Chart 4.6). Other foreign currency deposits rose slightly by 1.4% in the second half, with Renminbi deposits continuing to record growth. Overall, total deposits of Authorized Institutions grew moderately by 3.3% in the second half, slightly faster than the 1.6% increase in the first half. Chart 4.6 Deposit Growth Although the Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base and deposit base remained substantial, HIBOR began to face certain upward pressure in the second half of 2018, mainly reflecting US interest rate hikes. Seasonal liquidity demand occasionally pushed up short-term HIBORs, making them more volatile than long-term HIBORs (Chart 4.7). The 3-month and 12-month HIBORs averaged 2.32% and 2.74% respectively in December, about 30 basis points higher than their June averages. Entering 2019, HIBORs generally declined as seasonal demand subsided. The 3-month and 12-month HIBORs fell to average 1.65% and 2.39% respectively in February. Chart 4.7 HIBORs and USD LIBORs The Hong Kong dollar yield curve shifted downward in the second half of 2018, broadly tracking movements in the US dollar yield curve. Compared with end-June 2018, yields on 3-year and 10-year Hong Kong Government Bonds fell by 45 and 37 basis points respectively to 1.56% and 1.83% at end-February 2019 (Chart 4.8). Chart 4.8 Government Bond Yields, Composite Interest Rate, and Average Lending Rate on New Mortgages During the review period, the Composite Interest Rate, which measures the average Hong Kong dollar funding cost of retail banks, rose slightly. Reflecting changes in interbank and deposit funding costs, the Composite Interest Rate increased from 0.62% at end-June to 0.89% at end-December 2018, before retreating to 0.83% at end-January 2019 (Chart 4.8). In light of rising funding costs, following the upward adjustment of the target range for the US federal funds rate in September, retail banks raised their Best Lending Rates by 12.5 to 25.0 basis points. After the target range for the US federal funds rate was raised again in December, retail banks did not adjust their Best Lending Rates further. Meanwhile, the average lending rate on new mortgages followed the rise in Best Lending Rates, reaching approximately 2.45% at end-January 2019. Looking ahead, US dollar interest rate trends, capital flows, and local financial market activities (such as IPO subscription activities) will continue to be key drivers of Hong Kong dollar interest rates. Given the still-large Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base and the substantial holdings of Exchange Fund Bills by the banking system—since banks can use Exchange Fund Bills as collateral to borrow Hong Kong dollar funds through the Discount Window—the pace of increase in Hong Kong dollar interest rates should be relatively moderate. Against the backdrop of escalating US-China trade friction, both offshore and onshore Renminbi exchange rates depreciated against the US dollar since early 2018 (Chart 4.9). However, buoyed by optimism driven by the resumption of high-level trade talks between China and the US, both offshore and onshore Renminbi exchange rates stabilized in November. Meanwhile, the spread between onshore and offshore Renminbi was not significant during the review period. Chart 4.9 Onshore and Offshore Renminbi Exchange Rates Currently, the ongoing US-China trade friction has not yet had a significant impact on liquidity conditions in the offshore interbank market. With liquidity conditions remaining broadly stable, the overnight CNH HIBOR stayed below 4% for most of the review period, rising only occasionally due to seasonal factors (Chart 4.10). The 3-month CNH HIBOR hovered around 4% from September to December 2018, before falling to 3.02% at end-February 2019, possibly reflecting recent monetary easing measures introduced by the People's Bank of China. Nevertheless, it remains to be seen how progress in US-China trade negotiations will affect liquidity in the offshore Renminbi interbank market in 2019. Chart 4.10 Overnight and 3-Month CNH HIBORs Pricing Hong Kong's offshore Renminbi liquidity pool expanded steadily in the second half of 2018. Outstanding Renminbi customer deposits and Certificates of Deposit grew by 3.7% in the second half to RMB 657.7 billion at end-2018, slightly faster than the 2.6% increase in the first half (Chart 4.11 and Table 4.B). This was mainly driven by Renminbi customer deposits, which grew by 4.5% in the first half and recorded a 5.2% increase in the second half. Among these, corporate customer deposits grew faster than personal customer deposits. However, outstanding Certificates of Deposit fell further by 14.1% in the second half, mainly due to reduced issuance and a relatively large amount of Certificates of Deposit maturing in October.

Mainly benefiting from an increase in net interest income, the profitability of retail banks continued to improve in the second half of 2018 compared with the same period in 2017. Capital and liquidity positions also remained sound. Reflecting the upward pressure on the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) and retail deposit rates amid US interest rate normalization, the overall HKD funding cost of retail banks rose notably but remained at a relatively low level. Against a backdrop of external uncertainties, bank credit contracted moderately in the second half of 2018. Nevertheless, credit growth has shown signs of stabilization since November, and asset quality remained sound by historical standards. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will face multiple headwinds due to continued uncertainties in US-China trade relations, a slowdown in the global economy, uncertainty over the pace of the US monetary policy tightening cycle, and geopolitical risks. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage, banks should remain vigilant about the potential impact on the credit risk of their related corporate loans should the external environment deteriorate further. The aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks increased by 14.3% compared with the same period in 2017, while the return on assets also rose from 1.14% to 1.23% (Chart 5.1). This strong performance was mainly driven by a substantial increase in net interest income, which was sufficient to offset increases in loan impairment allowances and operating expenses. For 2018 as a whole, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks grew by 19.4%, while the return on assets rose from 1.16% in 2017 to 1.27%. Chart 5.1 Profitability of Retail Banks The net interest margin of retail banks widened further to 1.67% in the fourth quarter, compared with 1.5% in the same period last year (Chart 5.2). Chart 5.2 Net Interest Margin of Retail Banks Largely reflecting further US interest rate hikes and a decline in interbank HKD liquidity following the triggering of the Weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in August 2018, the funding costs of Hong Kong banks continued to face upward pressure in the second half of 2018. Specifically, the 3-month HIBOR rose by 23 basis points in the second half of 2018 (Chart 5.3). As banks generally raised time deposit rates to secure long-term stable funding, HKD retail deposit rates also increased during the review period. In addition, following the US interest rate hike decision at the end of September, banks raised their best lending rates and correspondingly increased their savings deposit rates. Given the rise in both wholesale and retail funding costs, the composite interest rate (a measure of the average HKD funding cost of retail banks) increased from 0.62% in June 2018 to 0.89% in December, but remained at a relatively low level by historical standards. Chart 5.3 Interest Rates (a) End-of-period figures. (b) Period-average figures for newly approved loans. On a broader level, the overall HKD and USD funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong continued to show an upward trend. In the second half of 2018, the average overall HKD and USD funding cost of banks rose by 36 basis points, following a 40-basis-point increase in the first half (red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4 HKD and USD Funding Costs and Maturity Profile of Licensed Banks The cumulative increase in HIBOR exceeded the rise in the overall funding cost of Hong Kong banks, which may have had a positive impact on retail banks' HIBOR-based mortgage loans, a product the industry has actively promoted in recent years. However, future improvements in net interest margins may become more limited, as most HIBOR-based mortgage loans have already reached their capped rates linked to the best lending rate. Given the unclear timing of future best lending rate adjustments, the continued upward trend in bank funding costs amid US interest rate normalization could weigh on overall net interest margins. Looking ahead, increased external uncertainties could cast a shadow over banks' earnings outlook. In particular, against the backdrop of slowing global economic growth, continued uncertainties in US-China trade relations could dampen business confidence and reduce demand for bank credit. Should this lead to a significant decline in loans and deterioration in asset quality, it could weigh on banks' profitability. The capital position of the Hong Kong banking sector remained strong and well above international minimum standards. At the end of 2018, the consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions (AIs) rose further to 20.3% (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio also increased to 17.9%, of which 16.0% was Common Equity Tier 1 capital. Chart 5.5 Capital Position of Locally Incorporated AIs 1. Consolidated basis. 2. Starting from January 1, 2013, locally incorporated AIs are required to comply with the revised capital framework under Basel III. Therefore, capital ratios from March 2013 onwards are not directly comparable with data up to December 2012. In addition to risk-based capital adequacy ratios, Basel III introduced a non-risk-based leverage ratio requirement to constrain excessive leverage in the banking system. The minimum leverage ratio requirement came into effect in Hong Kong in 2018, and the leverage ratio of locally incorporated AIs remained at a robust level of 8.0% at the end of December 2018, well above the statutory minimum of 3% (Chart 5.6). Chart 5.6 Leverage Ratio of Locally Incorporated AIs Measured by the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) requirement under Basel III, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained sound during the review period. The average LCR of Category 1 institutions rose from 156.6% in the second quarter of 2018 to 167.6% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 90% applicable in 2018. The average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio (LMR) of Category 2 institutions also rose from 51.3% in the second quarter to 54.3% in the fourth quarter, well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio 1. Consolidated basis. 2. Quarterly average figures. The Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR), as part of the Basel III liquidity standards, indicated that the funding positions of AIs were stable. The average NSFR of Category 1 institutions remained at a high level of 135.6% in the fourth quarter of 2018 (Chart 5.8), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average Core Funding Ratio (CFR) of Category 2A institutions remained at a high level of 134.3%, also exceeding the statutory minimum requirement of 50% applicable in 2018. The ample liquidity and sound funding positions of AIs indicate that the Hong Kong banking sector is resilient to various liquidity shocks. Chart 5.8 Net Stable Funding Ratio Customer deposits remained the primary source of funding for AIs, reflecting the stable funding structure of the banking system. At the end of 2018, customer deposits as a share of total liabilities of all AIs edged up from 54.5% six months earlier to 55.7% (Chart 5.9). Chart 5.9 Liability Structure of All AIs 1. Figures may not add up to the total due to rounding. 2. Figures refer to the percentage of total liabilities (including capital and reserves). 3. Debt securities include negotiable certificates of deposit and all other negotiable debt instruments. As total loans and advances declined during the second half of 2018 while total deposits increased over the same period, the loan-to-deposit ratio of all AIs on an all-currency basis fell from 75.7% at the end of June 2018 to 72.6% at year-end (Chart 5.10). Similarly, the foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio of all AIs decreased from 65.2% to 58.3% during the same period. By contrast, as HKD deposit growth lagged significantly behind HKD loan growth, the HKD loan-to-deposit ratio edged up from 85.4% at the end of June 2018 to 86.9% at year-end. Chart 5.10 Average Loan-to-Deposit Ratio of All AIs The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks decreased slightly in the second half of 2018. We estimate that under a shock of a parallel 200-basis-point increase in interest rates across the board, the potential decline in the economic value of interest rate positions of locally incorporated licensed banks would be equivalent to 2.44% of their total capital base at the end of 2018 (Chart 5.11). Nevertheless, given the uncertainty regarding the pace of further US interest rate hikes, banks should pay close attention to their interest rate risk management. Chart 5.11 Impact of Interest Rate Shock on Locally Incorporated Licensed Banks 1. Interest rate shock refers to the impact of a standard parallel interest rate shock of 200 basis points on the institution's interest rate risk exposure. 2. The impact of the interest rate shock refers to the change in the economic value of the banking book and trading book, expressed as a percentage of the bank's total capital base. Against the backdrop of continued uncertainties in the US-China trade conflict, tightening global financial liquidity, and slowing global economic growth, credit growth slowed markedly in the second half of 2018. However, credit growth has shown signs of stabilization since November 2018. On a semi-annual basis, total loans and advances of all AIs declined by 0.9% in the second half of 2018, following a 5.3% increase in the first half (Chart 5.12). This decline was attributable to slower growth in domestic loans (including loans for use in Hong Kong and trade financing) and a decrease in loans for use outside Hong Kong. Domestic loan growth slowed to 0.1% in the second half, while loans for use outside Hong Kong contracted by 3.0% over the same period, compared with growth of 5.3% and 5.2% respectively in the preceding six months. For 2018 as a whole, total loan growth slowed significantly to 4.4% from 16.1% in 2017. Chart 5.12 Loan Growth Looking ahead, credit demand is likely to remain weak in the near term. The HKMA’s "Survey on Credit Conditions Outlook" conducted in December 2018 showed that among all surveyed AIs, 82% expected loan demand to remain unchanged over the next three months, while the proportion expecting a decline in demand rose to 18% (Table 5.A). Despite a slight decline in total loans in the second half of 2018, the asset quality of banks' loan portfolios remained sound. The overall specific classified loan ratio and the overdue and rescheduled loan ratio of all AIs edged down to 0.55% and 0.36% respectively at the end of December 2018, from 0.61% and 0.40% respectively at the end of June 2018. For retail banks, the overall specific classified loan ratio dipped slightly to 0.50%, while the overdue and rescheduled loan ratio rose marginally to 0.32% (Chart 5.13). Both ratios remained low by historical standards. Chart 5.13 Asset Quality of Retail Banks 1. Specific classified loans refer to those classified as "substandard", "doubtful" or "loss". 2. Figures prior to December 2015 reflect the position of retail banks' Hong Kong offices and overseas branches. From December 2015 onwards, coverage has been expanded to include major overseas subsidiaries of retail banks. On a semi-annual basis, personal loan growth slowed from 5.3% in the first half of 2018 to 3.9% in the second half. This was mainly due to slower growth in private loans (including credit card advances and other loans for private use), which offset the rapid growth in residential mortgage loans (Table 5.B). As nominal GDP growth in Hong Kong lagged behind the growth rate of personal loans, the household debt-to-GDP ratio edged up from 71.2% in the second quarter of 2018 to 71.9% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.14).

The coronavirus outbreak that began in early 2020 has dealt a blow to both demand and supply, posing challenges to the global economy distinct from those of previous crises. Although major central banks and some governments have introduced stimulus measures since early March to contain the economic shock caused by the epidemic, financial markets remain volatile and global financial conditions have tightened. Despite uncertainties in the external and domestic environments, Hong Kong's foreign exchange and money markets continued to function smoothly and orderly. Amidst a stronger Hong Kong dollar exchange rate, a stable Aggregate Balance, and moderate growth in total deposits, no significant capital outflows from the Hong Kong dollar or the Hong Kong banking system were observed during the review period. Following a moderate rebound in the first half of 2019, total loan growth slowed in the second half. The residential property market has generally softened since mid-2019, though its trend has been somewhat erratic. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will continue to face multiple downside risks, including uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, future US-China trade relations, geopolitical tensions, and local social incidents. In light of rising corporate leverage and household debt burdens, banks should prudently assess the impact on the asset quality of their loan portfolios should these risk factors intensify. Since the fourth quarter of 2019, global economic growth has shown initial signs of stabilisation, benefiting from intensified monetary easing by major central banks, an easing of US-China trade tensions, and a reduced risk of a "no-deal Brexit" in the UK. However, since late January, the rising number of global coronavirus infections has sparked market concerns and triggered significant volatility in global financial markets. To address the evolving risks of the epidemic, several major central banks have cut interest rates sharply and expanded liquidity facilities, while some governments have also launched targeted measures to support the real economy. Nevertheless, global financial conditions have tightened amid widening credit spreads and plunging stock markets. Looking ahead, downside risks to the global economic outlook have increased. The coronavirus epidemic will dampen global economic activity, and the extent of the economic impact will depend on the severity and duration of the outbreak. Over the medium term, relations between the US and its major trading partners may become tense again, and post-Brexit trade negotiations between the UK and the EU could prove difficult. Weak global demand continued to weigh on economic growth in East Asia. Exports from the East Asian region to various major destinations, including the US, European economies, and Mainland China, remained weak in the second half of 2019. Some major telecommunications equipment exporters in the region recently reported revenue growth, but it remains to be seen whether there will be a broad-based rebound in the technology product cycle. Financial markets reacted positively to the Phase One US-China trade agreement announced in December 2019, and the trade truce has to some extent reduced uncertainties surrounding global trade. Nevertheless, the East Asian region will continue to face headwinds such as weak corporate earnings and high private sector leverage ratios. Meanwhile, the coronavirus outbreak has raised concerns that regional economies could come under further pressure amid persistently weak growth. Travel bans imposed by many economies in the region could hit Asia's tourism industry, particularly those economies more reliant on tourism service exports. Manufacturing may also be affected by the outbreak due to the region's close supply chain linkages with Mainland China. As for Mainland China, economic growth continued to slow in the second half of 2019 due to weak domestic and external demand. Looking ahead, although the signing of the Phase One trade agreement between the US and China has helped temporarily reduce external uncertainties facing the Mainland economy, downward pressure persists amid the coronavirus outbreak, ongoing economic rebalancing, and a slowing global economy. The Central Economic Work Conference held in December 2019 made stabilising the economy a priority for 2020, while also focusing on controlling financial risks. The latest consensus forecast indicates that Mainland economic growth will slow to 5.2% in 2020. During the review period, Mainland authorities continued to announce targeted monetary and fiscal policies to support the private sector, especially small private enterprises. Despite these measures, some media reports and market analysts have pointed out that private industrial enterprises may have faced declining shareholders' equity in recent years, seen as a sign of "private sector retreat." Box 2 examines the drivers behind changes in equity of Mainland industrial enterprises using 2018 listed company data, finding that private or small enterprises are not inherently more susceptible to downsizing or "retreat." While negative profitability was found to be the largest driver, other factors, particularly structural ones, are also noteworthy (see Box 2 for details). Local economic activity contracted significantly in the second half of 2019. Real GDP declined for three consecutive quarters, indicating that the local economy had entered a recession. Dragged down by this, the economy contracted by 1.2% for the full year of 2019, compared to growth of 2.9% in 2018, marking the first annual contraction since 2009. A slowdown in domestic demand, particularly a contraction in private consumption, was the main factor dragging down GDP in the second half of 2019. Local social incidents severely affected consumption activities, leading to a weak economic outlook and thereby undermining consumer and business confidence. With the resurgence of US-China trade friction, slowing global economic growth, and a severe downturn in inbound tourism, Hong Kong's external trade performance remained sluggish. Given the significant headwinds facing the economy, the Government rolled out multiple rounds of economic stimulus measures between August and December 2019. To allow banks greater room to step up support for the local economy and help cushion the economic cycle, the HKMA announced on October 14 a reduction in the Countercyclical Capital Buffer (CCyB) ratio for banks from 2.5% to 2.0%, thereby enabling banks to release an additional lending capacity of HK$200 billion to HK$300 billion to businesses, especially small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Economic performance in 2020 is expected to face significant challenges, and the epidemic has recently brought about notable downside risks. As sectors such as retail, accommodation services, food services, tourism, and transport have yet to recover from the disruption caused by social incidents, the epidemic will deal a double blow to these industries. However, a series of counter-cyclical measures announced in the 2020/21 Budget can provide relief to households and businesses (especially SMEs), including a one-off cash payout to adult permanent residents and special low-interest loans with 100% government guarantee for enterprises under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme. The HKMA further reduced the CCyB ratio for banks from 2.0% to 1.0% on March 16, 2020, which will allow banks greater room to step up support for the local economy, particularly sectors and individuals under greater short-term pressure due to the epidemic. Analysed by GDP component, private consumption and investment are likely to remain weak due to fragile consumer and business sentiment. Although government consumption will support economic growth, public investment expenditure is expected to be relatively subdued following the completion of some major infrastructure projects. On the external front, the Phase One US-China trade agreement is expected to have a slight positive impact on the local economy in the short term. However, weak global economic growth and trade activities will continue to weigh on Hong Kong's external trade performance. In particular, the coronavirus outbreak could lead to disruptions in regional supply chains and a slowdown in cross-border economic activities (such as tourism), thereby constraining Hong Kong's export performance. The Government forecasts real GDP growth for 2020 to range between -1.5% and 0.5%, while the average growth forecast by international institutions and private sector analysts is -1.5%. This weak economic outlook is subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including slowing global economic growth, US-China trade relations, economic performance in Mainland China, and local social incidents. The labour market came under greater pressure in the second half of 2019 and early 2020, with total employment declining, the unemployment rate rising, and the real wage index falling year-on-year. Specifically, the unemployment rate rose from a multi-year low of 2.8% in June 2019 to 3.7% in February 2020, partly reflecting the impact of social incidents and the epidemic outbreak on the retail, accommodation, and food service sectors. Looking ahead, given the weak economic outlook and the coronavirus outbreak, the unemployment rate is set to rise further. Box 3 provides a more detailed discussion of recent developments and the near-term outlook for the labour market. Domestic inflationary pressures continued to build up until the third quarter of 2019, mainly driven by higher fresh pork prices; thereafter, as economic activity weakened, inflation momentum gradually eased. Due to weak economic conditions, consolidation in private residential rentals, and mild imported inflation, inflation is expected to moderate in the near term. Market consensus forecasts overall inflation for 2020 to range between 0.6% and 3.7%, while the Government forecasts underlying inflation at 2.5%. Supported by increased equity-related demand for Hong Kong dollars (including initial public offerings), the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened gradually from mid-October 2019 onwards. Entering December, upward momentum in the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened further, partly due to buoyant IPO activity and partly due to the unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions prompted by tightening liquidity towards year-end. After the Lunar New Year holidays, liquidity conditions eased, and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened slightly towards the end of February. Overall, trading in the Hong Kong dollar remained smooth and orderly during the review period, and the Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered. The Aggregate Balance remained stable at around HK$54 billion. Since the fourth quarter of 2019, short-term Hong Kong Dollar Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) have exhibited volatility, reflecting seasonal funding needs and increased capital market activities such as IPOs. Box 4 examines how market attention to future IPO activity affects 3-month HIBOR. Meanwhile, the Composite Interest Rate rose gradually from 0.94% at end-July 2019 to 1.01% at end-January 2020, reflecting banks continuing to raise preferential deposit rates to attract deposit funding. As some banks raised the interest rate caps linked to the Prime Rate, the average mortgage rate for new mortgages rose to around 2.6% in October, but fell slightly to around 2.5% in January 2020 as the Prime Rate in the market was lowered starting from November. Amidst a stronger Hong Kong dollar exchange rate, a stable Aggregate Balance, and moderate growth in total deposits, no significant capital outflows from the Hong Kong dollar or the Hong Kong banking system were observed during the review period. However, we need to monitor the impact should the coronavirus epidemic worsen further amid an uncertain external environment. With substantial foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system, the HKMA has the capability, resources, and determination to cope with capital outflows and maintain monetary and financial stability in Hong Kong. During the review period, amid market expectations of a US-China trade deal, both offshore and onshore Renminbi exchange rates strengthened, but have faced weakening pressure since late January 2020 due to the coronavirus outbreak. In late 2019, the offshore Renminbi generally traded at a premium to the onshore Renminbi; the discount widened briefly at end-January 2020, but the spread remained modest by historical standards. Hong Kong's offshore Renminbi liquidity pool recovered slightly after a minor decline in the previous review period. As of end-January 2020, Renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit increased to RMB 637.4 billion. Other Renminbi businesses in Hong Kong also grew, with Renminbi bank loans and Renminbi trade settlement business recording strong growth. The average daily turnover of the Renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement System remained at a high level of RMB 1,133.9 billion for the full year of 2019. Despite uncertainties in the external environment, Hong Kong's offshore Renminbi business is expected to benefit from the continued opening up of the Mainland's capital account, increased allocation to Renminbi assets by international investors, and deepening regional economic and financial cooperation under the Belt and Road Initiative and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiative.

At the end of 2019, signs of stabilization in global economic activity raised hopes for a global economic recovery. However, since late January 2020, the rising number of global coronavirus infections has dashed these hopes, deepening investors' concerns about a global recession and triggering a sell-off in global financial markets. In response to the economic shock, major central banks and some governments have introduced stimulus measures since early March. Given the spread of the epidemic, downside risks to the global growth outlook have increased. In East Asia, weak global demand since the second half of 2019 has cast a shadow over the prospects of regional economies. The coronavirus outbreak is expected to weigh on regional economic growth in the near term, with the tourism sector being particularly hard hit. On the other hand, the East Asian region continues to face challenges of weak corporate earnings and high private sector leverage. As for Mainland China, economic growth continued to slow in the second half of 2019 due to weak domestic and external demand. Looking ahead, although the signing of the Phase One trade agreement between China and the United States has helped temporarily reduce external uncertainties, downward pressures remain amid the impact of the coronavirus outbreak, ongoing economic rebalancing, and the global economic slowdown; policy responses by authorities through monetary and fiscal measures will provide some buffer. Amid persistent trade tensions and policy uncertainty, manufacturing and investment remained weak, and global economic growth was still sluggish in the second half of 2019. Nevertheless, growth showed preliminary signs of stabilization in the last quarter (Chart 2.1), partly supported by earlier easing policies from the Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank, as well as an easing of global trade tensions following the signing of the "Phase One" trade agreement between China and the US. Chart 2.1 Manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Indices However, since the end of January, the increasing number of global coronavirus cases and the subsequent economic shock have sparked market anxiety, leading to a sell-off in global financial markets (Chart 2.2). Given that Mainland China is a major global export destination and plays a pivotal role in global supply chains, disruptions to production activities on the Mainland caused by the epidemic, along with the drag on its economic growth, will generate significant spillover effects that could potentially spread globally (Chart 2.3). Since the end of February, the surge in coronavirus cases outside Mainland China may exacerbate supply chain disruptions and pose risks of directly dragging down local economic activities. 5 Chart 2.2 MSCI All Country World Index and Bloomberg Barclays Global Corporate Bond Index Option-Adjusted Spread Chart 2.3 Exports of Goods and Services to Mainland China from Selected Major Advanced Economies in 2018 (% of GDP) To address the potentially severe economic impact of the epidemic, several central banks (including the Federal Reserve, the Bank of Canada, and the Bank of England) have cut interest rates since early March, while some governments have also introduced targeted measures to support households and businesses. However, financial markets continue to face immense selling pressure, resulting in a significant tightening of global financial conditions, which may further intensify downward pressures on the global economy (Chart 2.4). Chart 2.4 Bloomberg Financial Conditions Index for Advanced Economies Beyond the evolution of the epidemic, other downside risks and uncertainties also cloud the global economic outlook. Regarding trade tensions in particular, although policy risks have decreased following the Phase One trade agreement between China and the US, subsequent negotiations could be fraught with difficulties as many thorny structural issues remain unresolved. In Europe, trade negotiations between the EU and the UK are not expected to proceed smoothly, thereby perpetuating post-Brexit uncertainties. Additionally, the sharp drop in oil prices since March will put pressure on major oil-exporting emerging economies. In East Asia, real economic activity remained weak in the second half of 2019 due to subdued global demand. Exports from the East Asian region to various major destinations, including the United States, European economies, and Mainland China, remained weak in the second half of 2019 (Chart 2.5). Despite preliminary signs suggesting that the downcycle in regional technology products is bottoming out—including reports from major regional electronics companies of improved earnings at the end of 2019 6—it remains to be seen whether there will be a substantive rebound in regional tech exports. Chart 2.5 East Asia: Merchandise Exports to Major Destinations Persistent weak economic growth and trade uncertainties have also weighed on investor sentiment, with gross fixed capital formation declining in most East Asian economies in 2019 (Chart 2.6), potentially affecting the region's potential economic growth in the long run. To support economic growth in an environment of moderate inflation, the central banks of Indonesia, the Philippines, and South Korea cut policy rates again in the second half of 2019 after earlier cuts in the first half, while the Bank of Thailand also lowered its policy rate for the first time since 2015. Chart 2.6 East Asia: Gross Fixed Capital Formation The outbreak of the coronavirus has raised concerns that regional economies may come under further pressure amid persistently weak growth. As multiple economies in the region have imposed entry and exit restrictions on travel to and from Mainland China, the tourism sector has borne the brunt; economies more reliant on visitors from Mainland China and tourism service exports have been disproportionately affected by this epidemic (Chart 2.7). The persistence and intensification of the epidemic will also affect supply chains in the region that are closely linked to Mainland China. Chart 2.7 East Asia: Tourism Exports and Chinese Tourists In the near term, the epidemic will continue to affect economic activity and investor sentiment. Drawing on the experience of the 2003 SARS outbreak, these impacts may be transient, but the actual outcome will depend on the severity and geographic spread of the epidemic, as well as the effectiveness of government containment measures. Meanwhile, East Asian economies also face multiple headwinds. First, although corporate earnings are expected to deteriorate in the near term (Chart 2.8), accommodative global monetary conditions have encouraged yield-seeking behavior, pushing up asset prices without fundamental support. Consequently, regional stock markets have become more vulnerable to shifts in investor sentiment. Chart 2.8 Expected Earnings of Benchmark Stock Index Constituents Second, weak corporate earnings and economic growth may make it more difficult for private sector entities in the region to service their debts. While lower domestic interest rates can provide breathing room for indebted corporations and households, they may also sow the seeds for further debt accumulation. Furthermore, as discussed in Box 1, as more index-tracking funds flow into regional financial markets, the risk of private sector debt overhang may also intensify, although this effect is likely confined to firms with stronger financial fundamentals and their long-term borrowing. Third, regarding external factors, East Asian economies may face increased risks in the face of increasingly protectionist U.S. trade policies. Despite recent progress on the Phase One trade agreement between China and the US, trade tensions persist as fundamental trade issues between the two countries remain unresolved. As evidenced by the widening trade surpluses of many regional economies with the United States (Chart 2.9), multinational corporations may continue to seek alternative sourcing channels outside China-centric supply chains to circumvent tariffs. As of November 2019, the cumulative trade surplus of nine emerging Asian economies (excluding China) with the United States had risen to approximately US$167 billion. If trade surpluses with the United States continue to expand, relevant Asian economies could become the next targets of the trade war; for instance, the U.S. government imposed massive tariffs of up to 456% on steel imports from Vietnam in July 2019. 7 In light of this, despite the truce in the Sino-US trade war, the regional trade outlook remains highly uncertain. Chart 2.9 Merchandise Trade Surplus with the United States Over the past decade, intensified integration of international financial markets has led to a significant increase in global cross-border portfolio flows. A recent study indicates that up to 70% of these cross-border investment flows are driven by index-tracking funds. 8 Index-tracking funds include not only funds that closely track investment indices (commonly referred to as passive funds) but also actively managed funds that benchmark against investment indices. 9 By bringing in overseas investors that relevant economies would otherwise be unable to attract or access, these funds help promote financial market development in emerging market economies. Consequently, such funds enable emerging market economies to diversify their investor base, contributing to long-term market growth and stability. However, is there really such a thing as a free lunch? With regard to passive bond funds, there are concerns that investments by such funds may weaken the financial discipline of the corporate bond issuers they invest in, thereby leading to elevated leverage levels at the relevant corporations. 10 Moreover, some argue that the growth of index-tracking funds in recent years has exacerbated the volatility of global portfolio flows, rendering emerging market economies—which are already highly sensitive to global factors and influenced by other common factors—even more vulnerable. 11 This box assesses the impact of index-driven investment on financial stability by examining these two propositions. Passive bond funds allocate their investment capital to constituent bonds based on the weights of those bonds in the benchmark index. Therefore, compared to actively managed bond funds, the mechanical investment decisions adopted by passive bond funds may reduce the incentive for issuers of index constituent bonds to act in the interests of fund investors. 13 Worse still, from a financial stability perspective, such behavior may fuel excessive borrowing, posing significant credit and solvency risks to the corporate sectors of emerging market economies, where leverage ratios rose sharply after the Global Financial Crisis (Chart B1.1). Chart B1.1 Corporate Leverage in Emerging Market Economies Using the weights of corporations from various emerging market economies in a mainstream index tracking emerging market corporate bonds as a proxy for the extent of passive bond fund investment in their bonds, 14 we find that an increase in such investment raises the long-term (rather than short-term) leverage ratios of the relevant corporate bond issuers. The solid blue bars in Chart B1.2 represent the estimated effects. In addition to fostering the development of emerging market corporate bond markets, the expanded long-term bond investor base resulting from passive bond funds also benefits the development of corporations in emerging market economies. We also find that the aforementioned effects are significant only for emerging market corporations with relatively sound fundamentals (particularly those with stronger solvency and lower leverage ratios) (solid green bars in Chart B1.2). Facing higher costs of financial distress, highly leveraged or less solvent firms appear unlikely to fall further into a debt trap as a result of passive bond fund investments. In summary, the above research suggests that the growth of passive bond fund investments may not significantly increase solvency risks in the corporate sectors of emerging market economies.

Due to weakened private consumption, reduced investment expenditure, and poor export performance, the Hong Kong economy contracted in the second half of 2019, entering its first recession since 2009. Economic performance in 2020 is expected to face significant challenges, with the recent coronavirus epidemic also posing substantial downside risks. The economic outlook is being affected by numerous uncertainties and risks, including slowing global economic growth, Sino-US trade relations, economic performance in Mainland China, and developments in local social incidents. Given the various headwinds facing the economy, the unemployment rate is likely to rise further in 2020. Domestic inflationary pressures are expected to ease somewhat, although the outlook faces potential risks on both the upside and downside. The local economy contracted significantly in the second half of 2019. On a year-on-year basis, real GDP contracted by 2.8% and 2.9% in the third and fourth quarters respectively (Table 3.A). Dragged down by the economic contraction in the second half, the full-year economy shrank by 1.2%, worse than the 2.9% growth recorded in 2018, marking the first annual contraction since the Global Financial Crisis in 2009. Chart 3.1 Real GDP Growth Rate and Contributions of Major Expenditure Components On a quarter-to-quarter basis, economic activity slowed markedly in the second half (Chart 3.1). Specifically, real GDP fell successively by 0.4%, 3.0%, and 0.3% in the second, third, and fourth quarters, indicating that the economy had entered a recession. Domestically, private consumption was the main factor dragging down GDP in the third quarter. Local social incidents severely affected consumption activities; as the economic outlook weakened and consumer confidence was dampened, private consumption contracted significantly from the third quarter onwards.33 Due to increasing economic uncertainties and deteriorating business sentiment, overall investment spending remained weak, dragging down GDP in the fourth quarter.34 Externally, amid escalating Sino-US trade frictions, weakening global economic growth, and a sharp decline in visitor arrivals, Hong Kong's external trade performance continued to be sluggish (Chart 3.2).35 Affected by the sharp contraction in exports of services, net exports dragged down GDP in the third quarter but provided support for GDP growth in the fourth quarter, partly reflecting an improvement in the merchandise trade balance. Chart 3.2 Real Imports and Exports In view of the significant headwinds facing the economy, the Government introduced several rounds of measures between August and December 2019 to relieve the financial burden on citizens, safeguard employment, and support enterprises, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and hard-hit sectors such as retail, food services, transport, and tourism.36 To allow banks greater room to step up support for the local economy and help cushion the economic cycle, the HKMA announced on October 14 a reduction in the Countercyclical Capital Buffer (CCyB) ratio for banks from 2.5% to 2.0%, thereby enabling banks to release an additional lending capacity of HK$200 billion to HK$300 billion to enterprises, including SMEs. Hong Kong's economic performance in 2020 is expected to face significant challenges, with the recent epidemic also bringing notable downside risks. As some industries have yet to recover from the disruption caused by social incidents, the epidemic will deal a double blow to these sectors. However, a series of counter-cyclical measures announced in the 2020-21 Budget can provide relief to households and businesses (especially SMEs), including a one-off cash payout to adult permanent residents and special low-interest loans with 100% government guarantee for enterprises under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme.37 The HKMA further lowered the CCyB ratio for banks from 2.0% to 1.0% on March 16, 2020, which will allow banks greater room to intensify support for the local economy, especially for sectors and individuals under greater short-term pressure due to the impact of the epidemic. Analyzed by GDP components, private consumption and investment are likely to remain weak due to fragile consumer and business confidence. While government consumption will support economic growth, public investment expenditure is expected to be relatively subdued following the completion of some major infrastructure projects. On the external front, the Phase One Sino-US trade agreement is expected to have a slight positive impact on the local economy in the near term.38 However, weak global economic growth and trade activities will continue to drag on Hong Kong's external trade performance. In particular, the coronavirus outbreak may lead to disruptions in regional supply chains and a slowdown in cross-border economic activities (such as tourism), thereby constraining Hong Kong's export performance. The Government forecasts real GDP growth for 2020 to range between -1.5% and 0.5%, while the average growth forecast by international organizations and private sector analysts is -1.5%. This weak economic outlook is subject to the numerous uncertainties and risks mentioned in previous chapters. The labour market came under greater pressure in the second half of 2019 and early 2020. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate rose from a multi-year low of 2.8% in June 2019 to 3.3% in December 2019, and climbed further to 3.7% in February 2020 (Chart 3.3). Notably, the unemployment rate in the retail, accommodation, and food services sectors surged to a nearly ten-year high of 6.1%, partly reflecting the severe blow dealt by social incidents.39 As economic momentum weakened, total employment fell by 0.5% year-on-year in the second half of 2019 and continued to decline to 3,768,800 in February 2020. The decline in employment was mainly concentrated in the trade, wholesale, retail, accommodation, food services, and construction sectors. Real wages also fell by 0.3% year-on-year in the third quarter. Looking ahead, given the weak economic outlook described above, the labour market will continue to face more challenges, and the unemployment rate is highly likely to rise further. Box 3 discusses recent developments and the short-term outlook for the labour market in greater detail. Chart 3.3 Labour Market Conditions Domestic inflationary pressures continued to build up until the third quarter of 2019, mainly due to rising fresh pork prices; subsequently, as economic activity weakened, inflation momentum gradually slowed. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying Composite Consumer Price Index (CPI) increased by 3.3% in the third quarter, with the rate of increase easing slightly to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. The three-month annualized underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, also softened from a high of 4.7% in August 2019 to 2.1% in January 2020. The slowdown in inflation momentum was due to reduced price pressures across several CPI components. For traded goods, basic food inflation remained notable due to higher fresh pork prices, though price pressures on consumer goods such as clothing and footwear, as well as durable goods, remained mild. For services, as the growth in newly signed private residential rents slowed earlier, the growth of the rent component of the CPI also showed a downward trend (Chart 3.5). Labour cost pressures edged up slightly but remained moderate in recent quarters (Chart 3.6). Chart 3.4 Various Indicators Reflecting Consumer Price Inflation Chart 3.5 Rent Component of Composite CPI and Market Rents Chart 3.6 Unit Labour Costs Domestic inflationary pressures are expected to ease in the near term. Domestically, weak economic conditions and a widening negative output gap will continue to exert downward pressure on local inflation. With private residential rents continuing to soften, the housing rental component of inflation should ease further. Externally, import inflation is expected to remain moderate due to weak global economic growth and softer energy prices. Market consensus forecasts overall inflation for 2020 to range between 0.6% and 3.7%, while the Government forecasts underlying inflation at 2.5% and overall inflation at 1.7%. This inflation outlook is subject to both upside and downside risks. On the one hand, given that the estimated negative output gap has widened since the third quarter of 2019, if the economic deterioration is more severe than expected (e.g., due to a prolonged coronavirus epidemic), inflation could be further suppressed. On the other hand, if disruptions to the supply of fresh pork become more severe, this would exert upward pressure on inflation. Despite the marked slowdown in the local economy, the unemployment rate remained at a low level of 2.8–2.9% during the first nine months of 2019. It was only as social incidents persisted that the unemployment rate rose more noticeably to 3.3% by end-2019. Affected by the coronavirus epidemic, the labour market will face greater headwinds in 2020. Against this backdrop, this box analyzes recent developments and the short-term outlook for the labour market, including an examination of why the overall labour market remained largely stable in the first three quarters of 2019 (with little change in the unemployment rate) and what implications this holds for future developments. This article also reviews risk factors that could lead to a sharp rise in unemployment. It is worth noting that the unemployment rate is a lagging indicator, partly because adjusting labour demand entails costs. In fact, the unemployment rate typically lags behind the year-on-year growth rate of real GDP by about two to three quarters (Chart B3.1). This lagging nature explains why the unemployment rate remained low at around 2.9% even as real economic activity deteriorated sharply in the third quarter. Chart B3.1 Real GDP Growth Rate and Unemployment Rate On the labour demand side, although Sino-US trade tensions and local social incidents dealt heavy blows to employment in trade-related and retail and tourism-related sectors respectively, several key sectors managed to sustain the overall labour market. Specifically, employment in finance, business services, public administration, social and personal services continued to grow in 2019, partially offsetting the decline in employment in the trade and retail sectors (Chart B3.2). Despite the economy entering a recession, Hong Kong’s financial system remained robust, and financial activities related to fintech development and IPOs were very active. These factors likely helped support the job market in the financial and business services sectors. Moreover, public administration, social and personal services—including education, healthcare, and social work activities—appear to be less sensitive to the economic cycle. Correlation analysis shows that while employment in many sectors is highly correlated with real GDP, public administration, social and personal services exhibit a relatively neutral response to the economic cycle. In other words, employment in these sectors may not be significantly affected by cyclical fluctuations even during an economic downturn. Chart B3.2 Changes in Employment by Industry in 2019 On the labour supply side, the labour force participation rate40 declined from 61.2% in 2018 to 60.5% in 2019, providing a buffer against rising unemployment. Chart B3.3 illustrates the various supply and demand factors affecting changes in the unemployment rate (blue line). As shown in the chart, the labour force participation rate (green bars) exerted downward pressure on the unemployment rate in 2019.41 Meanwhile, the increase in employment in the first half of 2019 (purple bars) also helped contain the unemployment rate. However, the significant economic contraction in the second half led to a decrease in employment, exerting upward pressure on the unemployment rate. Overall, although employment decreased during the recession, the lower labour force participation rate helped mitigate the upward pressure on the unemployment rate in the second half of 2019. Chart B3.3 Factors Contributing to Changes in the Unemployment Rate Some structural changes in the labour market are also noteworthy. In particular, the rising proportion of voluntary part-time employees may help firms retain staff. Indeed, while the shares of self-employed persons and underemployed persons in total employment have fallen to 6% and 1% respectively in recent years, the number of voluntary part-time employees has continued to rise, making them the second-largest group in total employment (about 7% in 2017).42 Consequently, firms may be able to retain or hire more staff by adjusting the working hours of part-time employees. Our calculations show that average weekly working hours have decreased from a recent high of 48 hours in 2010 to approximately 44 hours currently, partly reflecting a larger share of part-time workers in the current employed population.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has strengthened since October, with upward momentum further intensifying in December, keeping the exchange rate at the strong side of the Convertibility Zone for several months. The strong demand for the Hong Kong dollar was partly driven by equity-related demand and partly by the unwinding of short positions amid tightening liquidity towards year-end. Overall, the foreign exchange and money markets in Hong Kong continued to function smoothly and orderly.
