Chart 3.3 Labour Market Conditions Chart 3.4 Various Indicators Reflecting Consumer Price Inflation Domestic inflationary pressures continued to ease over the eight-month period from mid-2020 to February 2021. The underlying consumer price inflation rate declined markedly on a year-on-year basis to 0.3% and 0.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2020 respectively, and further to -0.5% and -0.1% in January and February 2021 respectively (Chart 3.4). The three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, fluctuated slightly in recent months but remained at a relatively low level. Specifically, price pressures on basic foodstuffs eased, and costs for dining out decreased noticeably, reflecting more restaurants offering takeaway discounts during periods when dine-in services were restricted. Price pressures on other traded goods (such as durable goods) remained moderate. On the services side, the rent component of the Composite Consumer Price Index remained soft as private residential rents underwent consolidation (Chart 3.5). Labour cost pressures have also moderated in recent quarters (Chart 3.6). Chart 3.5 Rent Component of Composite CPI and Market Rents Chart 3.6 Unit Labour Costs Given the challenging global and local economic conditions, domestic inflationary pressures are expected to remain mild in the near term. In particular, local inflation will continue to be contained due to the earlier slowdown in fresh private residential rental growth. Market consensus forecasts a moderate overall inflation rate of 1.4% for 2021, while the Government projects an underlying inflation rate of 1% and an overall inflation rate of 1.6% for 2021. As the novel coronavirus pandemic ravaged the region, inbound tourism rapidly fell into depression, raising concerns about the scarring effect this crisis may have on the future recovery of the labour market. To this end, this box empirically analyses the impact of the boom in inbound tourism on the local labour market to explore the potential implications of the current downturn in tourism. Since 2000, inbound tourism has experienced significant ups and downs (Chart B2.1). Specifically, visitor arrivals declined during the SARS (Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome) outbreak in 2003. Following the introduction of the Individual Visit Scheme (IVS) in July of the same year, visitor numbers began to surge. Under the initial IVS, Mainland residents could apply to visit Hong Kong as individuals once or twice a year, with each stay not exceeding seven days. The scheme was expanded in April 2009 to allow eligible Shenzhen household registration holders to apply for multiple-entry IVS endorsements valid for one year ("one trip per week"). Since then, the number of Mainland visitors has increased substantially. Driven by new cross-boundary infrastructure connecting with Mainland China, visitor arrivals reached historic highs from late 2018 to early 2019. Subsequent local social incidents halved visitor numbers in the second half of 2019, and the novel coronavirus pandemic brought inbound tourism to a virtual standstill from late January 2020 onwards. Chart B2.1 Visitor Arrivals and Related Policies Using the tourism boom triggered by the IVS as a case study, we examine the impact of inbound tourism on local employment and earnings. We consider the introduction of the IVS in 2003 akin to a random economic shock, as it was nearly exogenous in timing and unanticipated by the local population. Our primary data source is population data from Hong Kong Population Censuses and By-censuses. Specifically, we utilise the 5% samples from the 1996, 2001, 2006, 2011, and 2016 Population Censuses and By-censuses. Furthermore, we define tourism-related industries as catering, retail, hotel, and transport sectors. First, we adopt a difference-in-differences framework to compare the differences in employment outcomes between younger workers (aged 20–40) in the treatment group and older workers (aged 41–65) in the comparison group before and after the implementation of the IVS. We classify the younger cohort as the treatment group because they are still in the early stages of their careers and can adjust their employment choices more flexibly in response to the exogenous growth in inbound tourism. As the impact of the IVS-induced tourism boom on the labour market may evolve over time, we also employ an event study approach to identify time-varying effects. Our empirical results indicate that, compared to the older cohort, younger workers (especially women and those with only secondary education) were more likely to enter tourism-related industries following the implementation of the IVS. Notably, the effect of the IVS on the probability of young women working in tourism-related industries was particularly significant and persistent, remaining at nearly 5 percentage points (in terms of the average differential in entry probability relative to the older cohort) from 2006 onwards (Chart B2.2). We also used a similar methodology to compare earnings between those employed in tourism-related industries (treatment group) and non-tourism-related industries (comparison group). Estimation results show that following the implementation of the IVS, earnings growth for workers in tourism-related industries exceeded that of employees in non-tourism-related industries. Moreover, compared to similar employees in other industries, female workers and lower-educated workers in tourism-related industries experienced higher and rising earnings premiums (ranging from 3 to 20 percentage points) (Chart B2.3). Chart B2.2 Impact of the IVS on Female Employment Chart B2.3 Impact of the IVS on Earnings of Female and Lower-Educated Workers These findings are broadly consistent with international experience, highlighting tourism as a vital source of employment, particularly for young people, women, and lower-educated workers. In the context of Hong Kong, our results align with previous analyses indicating that robust growth in inbound tourism increased demand for lower-skilled labour, thereby enhancing the resilience of the lower-skilled segment of the labour market. As inbound tourism falls from its peak to a trough, these worker groups are likely to be disproportionately affected, warranting close monitoring.

The HKD exchange rate continued to stay close to the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking, which was triggered multiple times during September and October 2020. The strong demand for HKD was mainly driven by equity-related funding needs, including those arising from buoyant IPO activities and southbound capital inflows via the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect. As the Aggregate Balance increased to over HK$450 billion, HIBORs across all tenors retreated. Despite uncertainties related to the development of the COVID-19 pandemic, the pace of economic recovery, and continued tensions in China-US relations that could exacerbate capital flow volatility, Hong Kong possesses ample foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system, enabling it to withstand pressures from capital flow volatility. The HKD exchange rate stayed close to the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking, mainly driven by equity-related funding needs, including those from buoyant IPO activities and southbound capital inflows via the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect (Chart 4.1). Although some proceeds raised from IPOs were converted out of HKD, the HKD exchange rate traded within a narrow range of 7.7505 to 7.7544 in November and December, supported by improving sentiment in the local stock market and market expectations of rising funding needs towards year-end. With fundraising activities remaining active in the first two months of 2021 (Chart 4.2), the HKD/USD exchange rate closed at 7.7568 on 26 February 2021. Overall, trading in the HKD market continued to be smooth and orderly. During the review period, the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered multiple times, leading to an increase in the Aggregate Balance, reflecting substantial capital inflows into HKD. Between September and October 2020, the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered 47 times. In accordance with the design of the Linked Exchange Rate System, the HKMA sold a total of HK$263.3 billion, increasing the Aggregate Balance from HK$193.1 billion at end-August to HK$457.5 billion at end-February (Chart 4.3). For the full year of 2020, the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered a total of 85 times, resulting in cumulative inflows of HK$383.5 billion. From a cross-border perspective, total deposits increased, indicating no signs of significant capital outflows from the local banking system. Meanwhile, the latest Balance of Payments statistics showed that non-residents’ direct investment continued to flow into Hong Kong in the fourth quarter of 2020, with no indication of any abnormal capital flows. Chart 4.1 HKD Exchange Rate Chart 4.2 Equity Funds Raised on the Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited (HKEX) Chart 4.3 Aggregate Balance and Outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes During the review period, the nominal effective exchange rate index of the HKD generally declined, tracking the weakening of the USD against major currencies (Chart 4.4). As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was minimal and had limited impact on the real effective exchange rate index, the movement of the HKD real effective exchange rate index broadly tracked that of the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.4 Nominal and Real Effective Exchange Rates Looking ahead, uncertainties related to the development of the pandemic, the pace of economic recovery, and continued tensions in China-US relations may exacerbate capital flow volatility. As an international financial centre, Hong Kong hosts various fundraising activities (such as IPOs), resulting in substantial capital inflows and outflows. On one hand, these fundraising activities can attract international investors to transfer funds to Hong Kong. On the other hand, funds raised by listed companies may subsequently be transferred out of Hong Kong due to business needs. Hong Kong possesses ample foreign exchange reserves and a sound banking system, capable of withstanding capital flow volatility without compromising financial stability. Amid continuous capital inflows into HKD, the local monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2020 and in recent months. Over the eight months since end-June 2020, the HKD Monetary Base increased by 20.8% (Chart 4.5). Analysed by component, the increase in the Monetary Base during this period reflected the rise in the Aggregate Balance caused by multiple triggers of the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking. On the other hand, other components, including Certificates of Indebtedness, government-issued currency notes and coins in circulation, and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes, remained relatively stable. Chart 4.5 Components of the Monetary Base During the review period, large-scale IPO activities led to an increase in HKD deposits derived from IPO subscription loans, causing HKD broad money (HKD M3) and its HKD deposit component to rise significantly during July–October 2020 and January 2021 (Chart 4.6). Following the conclusion of IPO activities and the repayment of IPO subscription loans by customers, HKD deposits and broad money returned to normal levels at end-2020. Entering January 2021, HKD M3 surged again, mainly driven by a large-scale IPO at end-January. Overall, over the seven-month period since end-June, HKD M3 grew by 21.7%; excluding the impact of the end-January IPO, HKD M3 registered a moderate growth of 9.1%. Based on counterpart analysis, excluding IPO subscription loans, the growth in HKD M3 was mainly attributable to the expansion of the Monetary Base driven by triggers of the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking (Chart 4.7). As a major component of HKD M3, HKD deposits rose by 22.9% over the same period; excluding the impact of the end-January IPO, HKD deposits grew moderately by 9.1%. Although HKD time deposits recorded a decline due to low deposit rates, this was fully offset by rapid growth in demand and savings deposits, partly driven by investment demand. Chart 4.6 Authorized Institutions' Deposits by Currency Chart 4.7 Changes in HKD M3 and Counterparts Total foreign currency deposits grew steadily by 3.6% over the seven-month period since end-June. USD deposits edged down by 0.3%, partly reflecting USD weakness, while other foreign currency deposits grew strongly by 15.5% over the same period, mainly reflecting an increase in RMB deposits. Overall, due to short-term fluctuations in HKD deposits caused by IPO activities, total deposits of authorized institutions rose significantly by 13.2% during the review period (Chart 4.6). Excluding the end-January IPO, total deposits grew moderately by 6.4%. It should be noted that monthly monetary statistics may fluctuate due to various short-term factors (such as seasonal and IPO-related funding needs, as well as business and investment-related activities), and therefore should be interpreted with caution. With the increase in the Aggregate Balance, HIBORs generally remained at very low levels during the review period (Chart 4.8). Despite large-scale IPO activities in the second half of 2020, HIBORs did not exhibit significant volatility due to ample liquidity in the banking system. Overall, the local interbank market continued to function normally. Chart 4.8 HKD and USD Interbank Interest Rates The HKD yield curve broadly tracked the movement of the USD yield curve, steepening during the review period as short-term bond yields declined while long-term bond yields rose (Chart 4.9). Compared with end-June, the yield on 3-year Hong Kong Government Bonds dipped slightly by 4 basis points to 0.23% at end-February, while the yield on 10-year Hong Kong Government Bonds rose by 67 basis points to 1.30% over the same period. Chart 4.9 Government Bond Yields, Composite Interest Rate, and Average Lending Rate on New Mortgages Retail HKD interest rates mainly followed the decline in HIBORs. The composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of HKD funds for retail banks, fell further from 0.71% at end-June to 0.23% at end-February 2021 (Chart 4.9). Driven by lower funding costs, the average lending rate on new mortgages also decreased from 2.02% in June 2020 to 1.56% in January 2021, broadly tracking the movement of the 1-month HIBOR. On the other hand, retail banks' best lending rates remained unchanged during the review period, ranging from 5.00% to 5.50%. Under the Linked Exchange Rate System, HKD interest rates are influenced by USD interest rates. Given the prolonged low US interest rates, HKD interest rates are expected to remain low, with occasional fluctuations due to capital market activities and seasonal liquidity needs. Facing a highly uncertain macro-financial environment, ample liquidity in the banking system should provide a sufficient buffer to maintain Hong Kong's monetary and financial stability. Both offshore RMB (CNH) and onshore RMB (CNY) exchange rates against the USD strengthened since end-May (Chart 4.10), broadly reflecting Mainland China’s better economic outlook compared to the rest of the world and USD weakness. FTSE Russell’s announcement at end-September to include Mainland government bonds in the World Government Bond Index further supported the RMB rally through investment demand. For most of the review period, the CNH exchange rate traded at a premium to the CNY exchange rate, with an average premium of about 100 pips in the fourth quarter, which remains modest by historical standards. Chart 4.10 Onshore and Offshore RMB Exchange Rates During the review period, liquidity conditions in the offshore RMB interbank market remained stable. Although overnight CNH HIBOR experienced brief fluctuations due to occasional northbound remittance needs and seasonal liquidity demand towards year-end, it stayed below 4% for most of the time (Chart 4.11). The 3-month CNH HIBOR followed onshore RMB rates to retreat in late December, before rising again in late January, partly due to tightening onshore liquidity and seasonal factors. Chart 4.11 Overnight and 3-Month CNH HIBORs In the second half of 2020, Hong Kong’s offshore RMB funding pool continued its growth trend. Since the fourth quarter, the growth of RMB deposits accelerated, partly reflecting RMB appreciation and relatively higher RMB interest rates compared to other currencies. Compared with end-June 2020, the growth of RMB customer deposits and certificates of deposit accelerated, reaching RMB826.3 billion at end-January 2021, an increase of 21.9% (Chart 4.12 and Table 4.A). Among them, RMB customer deposits grew by 24.7%, mainly driven by strong growth in corporate customer deposits. On the other hand, outstanding certificates of deposit decreased by 25.0% over the same period. Chart 4.12 RMB Deposits and Certificates of Deposit in Hong Kong Regarding other RMB businesses, over the seven-month period since end-June 2020, outstanding RMB loans declined by 2.4% to RMB159.2 billion. On the other hand, RMB trade settlement in Hong Kong continued to grow strongly. During the seven-month period from July 2020 to January 2021, banks in Hong Kong processed transactions totaling RMB3,769.5 billion, up 16.7% from the same period last year. Among these transactions, remittances from Hong Kong to the Mainland grew faster than remittances from the Mainland to Hong Kong (Chart 4.13). Hong Kong maintains a sizable RMB funding pool, sufficient to continue supporting substantial RMB payments and financial transactions. For the full year of 2020, the daily average turnover of the RMB Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system reached RMB1,191.5 billion, compared to RMB1,133.9 billion in 2019.

Due to the prolonged economic downturn caused by recurring waves of the novel coronavirus pandemic, coupled with the impact of a prolonged low-interest-rate environment, Hong Kong's retail banks saw further declines in profitability and a slight deterioration in asset quality in the second half of 2020. Nevertheless, the banking sector remained resilient, underpinned by strong capital and liquidity positions. During the period under review, to continue supporting the broader economy through these difficult times, the HKMA decided to extend various relief measures. Looking ahead, although the rollout of vaccines has raised hopes that the global pandemic may be brought under control and economic activities resumed, the pace of economic recovery remains uncertain. The aforementioned uncertainties, along with ongoing geopolitical tensions, will weigh on business activities and continue to pose challenges to the local banking sector. In particular, as the pandemic weakens the repayment capacity of corporates and households, the banking sector should remain vigilant regarding the impact of relevant downside risks on its asset quality. In the second half of 2020, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell by 38.5% compared to the same period in 2019. Accordingly, the return on assets declined to 0.62% in the second half of 2020, down from 1.13% in the same period of 2019 (Chart 5.1). The net interest margin of retail banks narrowed from 1.63% in the second half of 2019 to 1.01% in the same period of 2020 (Chart 5.2), resulting in a decrease in net interest income that outweighed the modest growth in non-interest income, thereby leading to lower profitability. For the full year of 2020, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks decreased by 29.4%, and the return on assets fell from 1.19% in 2019 to 0.77%. Chart 5.1 Retail Bank Profitability Chart 5.2 Net Interest Margin of Retail Banks Broadly speaking, Hong Kong dollar liquidity became more abundant due to substantial fund inflows driven largely by stock market activity. The Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) softened further in the fourth quarter of 2020. Notably, the three-month HIBOR dropped by 43 basis points in the second half of the year to 0.35% at end-2020 (blue line in Chart 5.3). The Composite Interest Rate (a measure of the average HKD funding cost for retail banks) followed a broadly similar trend, declining significantly from 0.71% at end-June 2020 to 0.28% at end-2020 (green line in Chart 5.3). The decline in the Composite Interest Rate mainly reflected lower interbank funding costs and reductions in time deposit rates by some major retail banks. Chart 5.3 Interest Rates From a broader perspective, the average overall HKD and USD funding costs of locally incorporated licensed banks moderated downward by 53 basis points in the second half of 2020 (red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4 HKD and USD Funding Costs and Maturity Profile of Licensed Banks Looking ahead, as the global low-interest-rate environment is likely to persist and continue to weigh on banks' net interest margins, the earnings outlook for the banking sector will remain challenging. Moreover, despite breakthroughs in vaccine development boosting market optimism about the global economic outlook, the trajectory of economic recovery remains highly uncertain given considerable uncertainties surrounding vaccine distribution and efficacy. These risk factors will continue to affect loan quality and profitability in the banking sector in the near term. The capital position of the Hong Kong banking sector remained robust and well above international minimum standards. The consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions stood at 20.7% at end-December 2020, well above the international minimum requirement of 8% (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio was 18.7% during the period, of which 16.7% was Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital. Furthermore, the leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained at a robust level of 8.2% at end-December 2020, exceeding the statutory minimum of 3% (Chart 5.6). Chart 5.5 Capital Position of Locally Incorporated Authorized Institutions Chart 5.6 Leverage Ratio of Locally Incorporated Authorized Institutions Measured by the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) requirement under Basel III, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained sound during the period under review. The average LCR of Category 1 institutions was 155.1% in the fourth quarter of 2020 (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. Over the same period, the average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio (LMR) of Category 2 institutions was 57.9%, also well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio The latest ratio figures under the Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) requirement also indicated stable funding positions of authorized institutions. The average NSFR of Category 1 institutions and the average Core Funding Ratio (CFR) of Category 2A institutions remained high at 138.6% and 139.5% respectively in the fourth quarter of 2020 (Chart 5.8), well above their respective statutory minimum requirements of 100% and 75%. The ample liquidity and stable funding positions of authorized institutions demonstrate the resilience of the Hong Kong banking sector against liquidity shocks. Chart 5.8 Net Stable Funding Ratio Customer deposits remained the primary source of funding for authorized institutions, reflecting a stable funding structure within the banking system. At end-2020, customer deposits accounted for approximately 56.1% of total liabilities of all authorized institutions, similar to the level six months earlier (Chart 5.9). Chart 5.9 Liability Structure of All Authorized Institutions As total deposits of all authorized institutions increased in the second half of 2020 while total loans decreased over the same period, the average loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions across all currencies fell from 76.0% at end-June 2020 to 72.3% at end-2020 (Chart 5.10). The increase in total deposits broadly reflected growth in both HKD and foreign currency deposits. Correspondingly, as of end-2020, the average HKD loan-to-deposit ratio and foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio declined to 83.5% and 61.0% respectively, compared with 86.4% and 65.5% six months earlier. Chart 5.10 Average Loan-to-Deposit Ratio of All Authorized Institutions The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks remained at a relatively low level in the fourth quarter of 2020. Under an assumed shock of a 200-basis-point rise in both HKD and USD interest rates, the estimated potential decline in the economic value of interest rate positions of locally incorporated licensed banks would amount to 1.41% of their total capital base at end-December 2020 (Chart 5.11). Chart 5.11 Impact of HKD and USD Interest Rate Shocks on Locally Incorporated Licensed Banks Against the backdrop of a sustained economic downturn caused by recurring pandemic waves and tightened social distancing measures, total loans and advances moderated downward in the second half of 2020. However, for the full year of 2020, total credit extended by the banking sector still recorded positive growth, though the growth rate slowed markedly from 6.7% in 2019 to 1.2%. On a semi-annual basis, after growing by 3.0% in the first half of 2020, total loans and advances of all authorized institutions contracted by 1.8% in the second half (Chart 5.12). The decline in total loans was attributable to decreases in both domestic loans (including loans for use in Hong Kong and trade financing) and loans for use outside Hong Kong. Specifically, total domestic loans edged down by 0.9% in the second half, while total loans for use outside Hong Kong contracted by 3.9%, following increases of 2.6% and 4.2% respectively in the preceding six-month period. Chart 5.12 Loan Growth Analyzed by currency, after declining by 2.0% in the first half, HKD loans remained broadly unchanged at end-2020 compared to the level at end-June. Following a significant surge of 10.6% in the first half of 2020, foreign currency loans decreased by 4.5% in the second half, partly reflecting weaker demand for USD loans amid improved global liquidity conditions. The banking sector turned slightly more optimistic about the outlook for short-term credit demand compared to six months ago. The HKMA’s "Survey on Credit Conditions Outlook" conducted in December 2020 showed that the proportion of respondent authorized institutions expecting loan demand to increase over the next three months rose to 37%, while those expecting a decline fell to 13% (Table 5.A). Due to the adverse impact of the pandemic on the repayment capacity of households and firms, bank loan quality deteriorated slightly but remained sound by historical and international standards. Moreover, the pace of deterioration in loan quality also slowed in the second half of 2020. The aggregate specific classified loan ratio of all authorized institutions rose moderately from 0.79% six months earlier to 0.9% at end-2020, while the overdue and rescheduled loan ratio of all authorized institutions increased from 0.49% at end-June 2020 to 0.57% at end-2020. For retail banks, the aggregate specific classified loan ratio and the overdue and rescheduled loan ratio rose to 0.82% and 0.48% respectively (Chart 5.13).

Entering 2022, global economic performance remained weak, yet inflationary pressures continued to intensify across various regions, particularly in the United States. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook faces significant uncertainties, including the risk of large-scale pandemic outbreaks and the possibility that monetary policy tightening could be more aggressive than expected if U.S. inflation proves more persistent and broad-based than anticipated. Should the Federal Reserve tighten monetary policy significantly, leading to tighter global financial conditions, it would place pressure on the recovery of relatively vulnerable emerging market economies. Recently, the military conflict between Russia and Ukraine has emerged as a factor that could significantly impact the global economy through trade and financial channels, further complicating the global monetary policy outlook. During the period under review, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened somewhat, but trading continued to be smooth and orderly. Total deposits grew moderately during the review period, with no significant signs of capital outflows from the local banking system. For 2021 as a whole, total bank loan growth accelerated. On the other hand, the residential property market has softened since mid-2021. Looking ahead, the rapid spread of the Omicron variant poses a threat to sustained economic recovery. Coupled with the possibility that the pace of U.S. monetary policy normalization may be faster than expected, these risk factors will pose challenges to banks' credit risk management. Banks should remain vigilant and carefully assess the potential impact of relevant risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios. The global economy began to slow down in late 2021, with weakness extending into 2022, as the spread of the highly transmissible Omicron variant led to increased restrictions on mobility worldwide, while persistent supply bottlenecks continued to weigh on production. Meanwhile, amid supply-demand imbalances and labor shortages, global inflationary pressures have continued to intensify, spreading to a broad range of goods and services in major advanced economies, particularly the United States. More recently, following the outbreak of military conflict between Russia and Ukraine, surging commodity prices could further exacerbate the threat of global inflation, while heightened financial market volatility could lead to an undesirable tightening of global financial conditions, further complicating the global monetary policy outlook. Looking ahead, there are significant uncertainties regarding the global economic outlook. In the near term, should large-scale outbreaks occur, the reimposition of lockdown measures and a renewed worsening of supply bottlenecks cannot be ruled out. In the United States, as the risk of inflation being more persistent and broad-based than expected grows, the Federal Reserve has adopted a more hawkish stance, accelerating the timeline for tapering asset purchases and interest rate hikes, and has begun discussions on balance sheet reduction. If the Federal Reserve needs to tighten monetary policy significantly, global financial conditions could also tighten, deteriorating borrowers' debt-servicing capacity, and disorderly capital outflows would put pressure on the recovery of relatively vulnerable emerging market economies. More recently, the military conflict between Russia and Ukraine risks keeping global commodity prices elevated, exacerbating industrial supply shortages and increasing financial market volatility. Heightened market volatility could also trigger redemption pressures on open-ended funds, increasing their liquidity risks. Box 1 discusses whether swing pricing—a liquidity management tool for open-ended funds—can mitigate liquidity risks for these funds during times of market stress, and examines the potential limitations of this tool. In Emerging Asia, economic recovery continued in the second half of 2021, although momentum slowed temporarily in some Southeast Asian economies due to the reimposition of strict pandemic containment measures in the third quarter, while technology-exporting economies in the region (South Korea and Singapore) continued to benefit from strong global demand for tech products. Although a broad-based recovery in Emerging Asia is widely expected in 2022, the region's near-term economic outlook faces multiple headwinds. First, new variants remain a concern, especially for economies in the region with lower vaccination rates and strained public health resources. Second, the Federal Reserve's accelerated policy normalization could trigger capital outflows from the region and exacerbate currency depreciation pressures; for regional economies that still need to maintain accommodative monetary policies to support economic recovery, the trade-off between curbing capital outflow pressures and supporting economic activity will become more difficult. Third, slowdowns in major economies, coupled with a potential shift in demand from goods to services as the global economy gradually reopens, will weigh on trade growth prospects. Fourth, rising prices of various commodities triggered by the Russia-Ukraine conflict will feed into regional inflation while simultaneously dampening consumption. Coupled with increased global economic uncertainty, monetary policy normalization decisions by central banks in the region will become more complex. Central banks in economies with weaker growth momentum and inflation more sensitive to energy prices will face particularly difficult trade-offs. In the longer term, to rebuild a sustainable and robust growth model, investors need to place greater emphasis on Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) factors in their investment considerations. Box 2 examines the sensitivity of equity returns to changes in climate risk and how such sensitivity is influenced by corporate environmental performance. Mainland China's economic growth slowed in the second half of 2021, affected by a new wave of COVID-19 outbreaks, power rationing measures, and tightening measures in the real estate market. Looking ahead, due to the continued downturn in the real estate market and the outbreak of the Omicron variant, the Mainland economy may continue to face downward pressure in the near term. Consequently, Mainland authorities have made stabilizing growth their top priority this year and have introduced a series of fiscal and monetary support measures. Both the total amount of onshore bond defaults and onshore bond defaults by state-owned enterprises (SOEs) decreased in the second half of 2021; Box 3 discusses whether the pricing of SOE bonds has improved in recent years. Overall risks in the banking sector remain manageable, as Mainland banks (especially systemically important banks) have limited exposure to developer loans, low non-performing loan ratios, and high provision coverage ratios. The Hong Kong economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021, albeit at a slower pace than in the first half. Supported by the continued recovery of the global economy, improvements in the local labor market, and the government's Consumption Voucher Scheme, which boosted merchandise exports and private consumption, seasonally adjusted real GDP grew moderately. Year-on-year, economic growth was 5.1% in the second half of 2021, compared to 7.8% in the first half. For 2021 as a whole, the economy grew by 6.4%, marking the first full year of positive growth since 2019. Entering 2022, a new wave of local epidemic cases and the consequent tightening of social distancing measures have weighed on local economic activity. The Government launched the fifth and sixth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund and introduced additional counter-cyclical measures under the 2022-23 Budget to support the economy. To support cash flow, enhancements have been made to the "100% Personal Loan Guarantee Scheme" and various guarantee products under the "SME Financing Guarantee Scheme," including higher maximum loan amounts and extended application and repayment periods. The HKMA, together with the banking sector, has also extended the "Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme" to end-October 2022. The Scheme also offers borrowers an option to repay part of the principal over a one-year period, which is also applicable to loans under the "SME Financing Guarantee Scheme." The Hong Kong economy is expected to continue its recovery throughout 2022, though at a slower pace than in 2021, partly reflecting slowing global growth amid the ongoing pandemic and a higher base effect. Specifically, Hong Kong's merchandise exports will continue to benefit from global economic expansion. The Government's push for multiple capital works and infrastructure projects will also provide support to the economy. The Government forecasts real GDP growth of between 2.0% and 3.5% for 2022, while the average growth forecast by international organizations and private sector analysts is 1.6%. However, the strength and pace of the economic recovery are subject to a number of uncertainties and risks discussed in previous sections, particularly the epidemic situation and the pace of U.S. monetary policy normalization. Alongside the economic recovery, the labor market further improved in the second half of 2021, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate falling to 3.9% by year-end. Total employment rebounded but remained below pre-pandemic levels. In early 2022, official data indicated that labor market pressures resurfaced amid a new wave of local infections. Furthermore, a decline in online job advertisements reflected a reduction in new job vacancies. The new wave of local infections and tightened anti-epidemic measures will exert some pressure on the local labor market in the near term, particularly in sectors involving face-to-face contact. Over the longer term, labor market conditions will depend on the development of the local epidemic and the pace of local economic recovery. Local inflationary pressures have generally increased in recent months but remain mild. Year-on-year, underlying consumer price inflation edged up to 1.1% and 1.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2021 respectively, remaining at 1.2% in January 2022. The three-month annualized underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, has also picked up in recent months, partly due to higher prices for dining out and certain energy-related items. Looking ahead, driven by rising import prices and logistics disruptions caused by the pandemic, local inflation is expected to rise slightly in the near term. However, soft rentals and mild local labor cost pressures should contain overall price pressures. Market consensus forecasts overall inflation for 2022 at 2.4%, while the Government projects overall inflation at 2.1% and underlying inflation at 2.0% for 2022. Since September 2021, the Hong Kong dollar has gradually softened against the U.S. dollar amid risk aversion in the local stock market. Despite a slight rebound in October 2021, the Hong Kong dollar subsequently lost upward momentum, mainly due to weak southbound net buying via Stock Connect and market expectations that the U.S. dollar would strengthen alongside the Federal Reserve's monetary policy normalization. Overall, the Hong Kong dollar traded mostly in the strong side of the Convertibility Zone, and trading continued to be smooth and orderly. Total deposits grew moderately during the review period, with no significant signs of capital outflows from the local banking system. Transactions in the Hong Kong interbank market continued to be smooth and orderly. Due to ample interbank liquidity, the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) remained low during the review period. The average mortgage rate for newly approved mortgages rose slightly from 1.48% in July 2021 to 1.56% in January 2022. Best lending rates quoted by major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging from 5.00% to 5.50%. Offshore Renminbi (RMB) banking business continued to thrive. In particular, the offshore RMB liquidity pool in Hong Kong continued to expand; as of end-January 2022, RMB customer deposits and certificates of deposit increased to RMB 1,113.5 billion. While RMB loans outstanding declined, RMB trade settlement in Hong Kong continued to grow. Average daily turnover of the RMB Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system rose to RMB 1,522.6 billion in 2021. Looking ahead, leveraging Hong Kong's efficient financial infrastructure, the two-way Northbound and Southbound Stock Connect, Bond Connect, and Cross-boundary Wealth Management Connect, as well as the continued opening up of the Mainland's capital account, increasing international investor demand for RMB assets, and deepening regional economic and financial cooperation under the Belt and Road Initiative and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiative, Hong Kong's offshore RMB business is expected to benefit. Stimulated by government monetary and fiscal policies, the global economic recovery and strong corporate earnings drove major global equity markets generally higher in the last quarter of 2021, pushing the MSCI World Index to a record high of 3,262 points on January 4, 2022. However, growing market concerns over the tightening stance of major central banks in advanced economies amid surging inflation risks, soaring commodity prices, and escalating Russia-Ukraine tensions have led to consolidation in major global equity markets since early January 2022.

Due to the rapid global spread of variant viruses (Delta and Omicron) and persistent production bottlenecks, the global economy slowed markedly in late 2021, with growth momentum remaining weak entering 2022. Global inflationary pressures have continued to intensify and have broadened across a wide range of goods and services in major advanced economies, particularly the United States. Rising inflation concerns have prompted a shift toward a more hawkish monetary policy stance by the Federal Reserve, exacerbating the risk that premature tightening of global financial conditions could weigh on currently elevated asset valuations and adversely affect emerging markets where recoveries remain generally lagging. More recently, the conflict between Russia and Ukraine has driven up energy and other commodity prices and triggered volatility in global financial markets, further compounding some of the aforementioned risks. In Emerging Asia, despite the spread of the Delta variant within the region, economic recovery continued in the second half of 2021, with major technology-exporting economies continuing to outperform others. While the current Omicron variant is unlikely to severely derail the regional economic recovery, any uncertainties associated with new variants will continue to cast a shadow over the region's economic outlook. Additionally, the normalization of Federal Reserve policy may trigger adjustments in regional asset prices, while slowing growth in major economies could also drag down regional merchandise export growth. The conflict between Russia and Ukraine, on the one hand, has led to rising commodity prices and increased inflation risks; on the other hand, it will dampen consumption and increase global economic uncertainty, thereby complicating monetary policy normalization decisions for central banks in the region. Economic growth in Mainland China slowed in the second half of 2021, affected by a fresh wave of COVID-19 outbreaks, power rationing, and tightening measures in the real estate market. Looking ahead, the Mainland economy may continue to face downward pressure from a cooling property market and Omicron outbreaks. In light of this, the government has made stabilizing growth its top priority for this year, and macroeconomic policies will provide greater support. The global economic recovery slowed noticeably in the last quarter of 2021 as the highly transmissible Omicron variant overlapped with the spread of the Delta variant, triggering a new wave of infections and leading to tightened mobility restrictions worldwide. Moreover, supply chain issues—such as shipping bottlenecks and shortages of key production inputs like semiconductors—continued to constrain production. Entering 2022, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) projected in January that global GDP growth would slow from 5.9% in 2021 to 4.4% in 2022, reflecting the continued drag from the pandemic and supply constraints, reduced policy support in the U.S. and other major advanced economies, and slowing growth momentum in Mainland China offsetting an anticipated rebound in growth elsewhere in Asia (Chart 2.1). Chart 2.1 IMF Real GDP Growth Forecasts Alongside the slowdown in global economic growth, inflationary pressures continued to build during the period under review. Core inflation (excluding food and energy prices) rose significantly in major advanced economies, especially in the U.S., which had implemented larger-scale policy stimulus since the onset of the pandemic. Amid supply bottlenecks, pent-up demand being released, and labor shortages, inflationary pressures have broadened across a wide range of goods and services (Chart 2.2). Furthermore, the recent military conflict between Russia and Ukraine has pushed up prices of various commodities, potentially exacerbating already elevated global inflationary pressures. Chart 2.2 Core Consumer Price Index Inflation Rates of Selected Economies (1) Latest data for the U.S., U.K., and Euro Area are for January 2022; for others, December 2021. (2) "Advanced Asian Economies" includes Australia, New Zealand, Japan, South Korea, Hong Kong, and Singapore. (3) "Emerging Asian Economies" includes Mainland China, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, and Thailand. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook faces significant uncertainty with considerable downside risks, and will depend on the evolution of the pandemic and associated supply chain disruptions, how geopolitical tensions impact global trade, inflation, and financial market sentiment, and the policy responses of major central banks to inflation. On the pandemic front, most governments have so far adopted targeted measures in response to the recent surge in Omicron cases, focusing on restricting high-risk activities, encouraging remote work, and promoting vaccination. Compared with previous lockdowns, these relatively milder measures should help mitigate supply chain disruptions, which have shown preliminary signs of improvement since late 2021 (Chart 2.3). However, should large-scale outbreaks occur, lockdown measures cannot be ruled out, which could lead to a renewed worsening of supply bottlenecks. Chart 2.3 Purchasing Managers' Index – Supplier Delivery Times Sub-index If the pandemic remains under control, supply bottlenecks are expected to ease gradually, providing some relief to goods inflation. However, several developments could make the current episode of elevated global inflation more persistent than expected, including the risk that the military conflict between Russia and Ukraine and sanctions on Russian energy imports will push up commodity prices, the delayed pass-through of rising production costs to final selling prices, the earlier sharp rise in global residential property prices potentially driving subsequent rent increases, upside risks to wage growth from tight labor markets, and rising inflation expectations. Notably, given that U.S. inflation recorded its largest increase in decades, the Federal Reserve shifted to a more hawkish policy stance at its December 2021 Federal Open Market Committee meeting, no longer characterizing high inflation as "transitory," and doubled the pace of its asset purchase tapering from $15 billion per month to $30 billion, aiming to conclude its asset purchase program by March 2022 and begin discussions on balance sheet reduction. Indeed, recent market pricing suggests that the Fed may raise interest rates multiple times in 2022. By contrast, given the Euro Area's closer trade and financial linkages with Russia and Ukraine, the European Central Bank may face more significant policy trade-offs. Against this backdrop, and with global debt levels and asset valuations remaining elevated following prolonged accommodative policies, if persistent inflationary pressures compel the Fed to tighten policy faster than expected, borrowers' debt-servicing capacity could deteriorate, potentially triggering financial market volatility. Recently, amid escalating geopolitical tensions in Eastern Europe, risk aversion in financial markets has risen, and signs of U.S. dollar funding stress have emerged, including widening cross-currency basis swaps. Under conditions of premature tightening of global financial conditions, emerging market economies with weaker fundamentals still grappling with the pandemic may be vulnerable to renewed growth slowdowns, currency depreciation, and capital outflow pressures. Heightened market volatility could also trigger redemption pressures on open-ended funds, increasing their liquidity risks. Box 1 examines whether swing pricing—a liquidity management tool for open-ended funds—can reduce liquidity risks for these funds during periods of market stress, and discusses the potential limitations of this tool. In Emerging Asia, economic recovery continued in the second half of 2021, but the spread of the Delta variant dampened growth momentum in the third quarter, particularly in some Southeast Asian economies (Chart 2.4). Meanwhile, as major regional exporters of technology products, South Korea and Singapore continued to benefit from robust global demand for tech products, further widening the unevenness of the recovery across the region. Furthermore, inflationary pressures in many Emerging Asian economies remained moderate. Chart 2.4 Manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Indices Markets broadly expect a widespread recovery in Emerging Asia in 2022, but the region's near-term economic outlook faces multiple headwinds: First, although the Omicron variant has been spreading in the region since late 2021, its economic impact has been milder than previous infection waves; however, some regional economies with lower vaccination rates and tighter public health resources will continue to face threats from the emergence of new variants. Second, Federal Reserve policy normalization could trigger capital outflows and exert depreciation pressure on regional currencies. For regional economies that still need to maintain accommodative monetary policies to support economic recovery, the trade-off between curbing capital outflow pressures and supporting economic activity will become more difficult. At the long end of the yield curve, given their historically high correlation (Chart 2.5), the risk of a sudden spike in U.S. long-term yields could spill over to long-term bond yields in Emerging Asia, heightening the risk of adjustments in regional asset markets. Chart 2.5 Correlation Between Asian 10-Year Sovereign Bond Yields and Corresponding U.S. Treasury Yields Third, the outlook for regional merchandise trade faces uncertainties stemming from slowing growth in major economies and the possibility that demand may shift from goods to services as the global economy gradually reopens, factors that could dampen regional export growth. Chart 2.6 U.S.: Imports from Emerging Asia and Real GDP Fourth, although regional economies have relatively limited trade and financial linkages with Russia and Ukraine, the rise in commodity prices triggered by the conflict will feed into regional inflation while simultaneously dampening consumption. Coupled with increased global economic uncertainty, monetary policy normalization decisions by regional central banks will become more complex. Central banks in some regional economies with weaker growth momentum and inflation more sensitive to energy prices will face particularly difficult trade-offs. The pandemic has also underscored the long-term need for regional economies to rebuild more sustainable and resilient growth models to prepare for other risks such as climate change. To this end, investors need to place greater emphasis on Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) factors in their investment considerations. Box 2 examines whether stock market returns are affected by changes in climate risk and how such sensitivity is influenced by corporate environmental performance. The COVID-19 pandemic caused massive shocks to global financial markets in March 2020. During this period of market turmoil, some open-ended funds experienced substantial outflows (Chart B1.1), straining their liquidity management. Chart B1.1 Outflows from Selected Open-Ended Funds During the March 2020 Episode Beyond investors' liquidity needs, another reason for large outflows may have been investors exercising a "first-mover advantage" by redeeming early to avoid bearing redemption costs that could escalate under stressed market conditions. To curb outflows driven by first-mover advantage, some open-ended funds adopted swing pricing—a pricing mechanism designed to reduce investors' first-mover advantage. Although many open-ended funds employed swing pricing during this episode, there has been no empirical research demonstrating whether swing pricing effectively reduces outflows from open-ended funds. Against this background, this box conducts an empirical study to assess whether swing pricing reduced fund outflows during the March 2020 episode, thereby mitigating liquidity risks. Additionally, this box identifies factors that may limit the effectiveness of swing pricing during periods of market stress. Based on these assessments, we offer policy recommendations regarding financial stability. First-mover advantage refers to investors redeeming ahead of others, thereby passing redemption costs onto remaining investors. This advantage primarily exists in open-ended funds using traditional pricing rules, where subscription and redemption costs borne by fund investors (e.g., transaction costs arising from portfolio adjustments) are reflected in the fund price only after transactions occur. Under this pricing mechanism, investors who redeem shares first do not bear these transaction costs. This creates an incentive for them to redeem early, especially when large redemption costs are anticipated. Consequently, during periods of market stress, first-mover advantage becomes more pronounced as expected redemption costs rise. This amplifies redemption pressures and liquidity risks faced by open-ended funds.

With continued growth in goods exports and private consumption, the Hong Kong economy sustained its recovery in the second half of 2021, recording positive annual growth for the first time since 2019. Entering 2022, a fresh wave of local epidemic cases and the consequent tightening of social distancing measures have put pressure on local economic activities. The overall economy is expected to maintain its recovery throughout 2022, although its strength and pace will be affected by uncertainties and risks such as the epidemic situation and the normalization of US monetary policy. These adverse factors may also affect labor market prospects following the significant improvement seen in 2021. Although domestic inflation may rise slightly in the near term due to higher import prices, soft domestic rentals and labor costs should help contain overall price pressures. The Hong Kong economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021. On a year-on-year basis, real GDP grew further by 5.5% in the third quarter and by 4.8% in the fourth quarter (Table 3.A), though the pace of growth moderated compared to the first half of the year. For 2021 as a whole, real GDP expanded by 6.4%, marking the first annual positive growth since 2019. Chart 3.1 Real GDP Growth Rate and Contributions of Main Expenditure Components On a quarter-to-quarter basis, economic activity grew modestly by 0.6% and 0.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2021 respectively (Chart 3.1). Domestically, improved labor market conditions, coupled with the Government's Consumption Voucher Scheme, drove up private consumption. However, overall investment spending retreated in the last quarter following strong rebounds in the two preceding quarters. Externally, amid the ongoing global economic recovery, Hong Kong’s merchandise trade performance remained robust, while services trade remained weak, partly due to the continued standstill in inbound tourism (Chart 3.2). In net terms, external trade was a drag on GDP in the third quarter but provided support to GDP growth in the fourth quarter. Chart 3.2 Import and Export Volumes A fresh wave of local epidemic cases and the consequent tightening of social distancing measures put pressure on local economic activities in early 2022. The Government launched the fifth and sixth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund and introduced additional counter-cyclical measures under the 2022-23 Budget to support the economy. To support cash flow, the "100% Personal Loan Guarantee Scheme" and various guarantee products under the "SME Financing Guarantee Scheme" will be enhanced, with maximum loan amounts increased and application and repayment periods extended. The HKMA, together with the banking sector, has also extended the Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme to end-October 2022. The Scheme also offers borrowers an option of partial principal repayment over a one-year period, which is also applicable to loans under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme. The Hong Kong economy is expected to continue its recovery throughout 2022, albeit at a slower pace than in 2021, partly reflecting the slowing global economic growth amid the persistent pandemic and a higher base effect. Specifically, Hong Kong’s goods exports will continue to benefit from global economic expansion. The Government’s push for various capital works and infrastructure projects will also provide support to the economy. The Government forecasts real GDP growth of between 2.0% and 3.5% for 2022, while the average growth forecast by international organizations and private sector analysts is 1.6%. However, the strength and pace of Hong Kong’s economic recovery are subject to numerous uncertainties and risks as outlined in previous chapters. In particular, recent developments in the epidemic, the accelerated pace of US monetary policy normalization, and heightened geopolitical concerns (such as the Russia-Ukraine situation) have cast a shadow over the near-term economic outlook for both Hong Kong and the global economy. On the other hand, if quarantine-free cross-boundary travel with the Mainland resumes earlier than expected, it could boost local economic growth. Alongside the economic recovery, the labor market improved further in the second half of 2021, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate falling to 3.9% by year-end (Chart 3.3). Total employment in December 2021 also rebounded by 2.0% from its recent low in February 2021, though it remained below pre-pandemic levels. In early 2022, official data indicated that labor market pressures re-emerged amid the fresh wave of local epidemic cases. Moreover, the decline in online job advertisements reflected a reduction in new job vacancies. Looking ahead, the fresh wave of local epidemic cases and tightened anti-epidemic measures will exert some pressure on the local labor market in the near term, particularly in sectors involving face-to-face contact. Over the longer term, labor market conditions will depend on the development of the local epidemic and the pace of local economic recovery. Chart 3.3 Labor Market Conditions Domestic inflationary pressures have generally increased in recent months but remain mild. On a year-on-year basis, underlying consumer price inflation edged up to 1.1% and 1.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2021 respectively, remaining at 1.2% in January 2022 (Chart 3.4). The three-month annualized underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, has also picked up in recent months. Specifically, amid recovering domestic demand and rising external prices (Chart 3.5), prices of meals out and certain energy-related items rose at a faster pace. Meanwhile, the housing rental component of the Composite Consumer Price Index continued to trend down broadly, thereby containing overall inflation momentum (Chart 3.6). While real unit labor costs remained soft, they rose slightly in recent quarters, partly due to improvements in real average wages (Chart 3.7). Chart 3.4 Various Indicators Reflecting Consumer Price Inflation Chart 3.5 Hong Kong Import Prices Chart 3.6 Rental Component of CCPI and Market Rentals Chart 3.7 Unit Labor Costs Looking ahead, domestic inflation is expected to rise slightly in the near term amid higher import prices and logistics disruptions caused by the pandemic. However, soft rentals and moderate domestic labor cost pressures should help contain overall price pressures. Market consensus forecasts headline inflation for 2022 at 2.4%, while the Government forecasts headline inflation at 2.1% and underlying inflation at 2.0% for 2022.

Amid a risk-averse sentiment in the local stock market and concerns over the normalisation of US monetary policy, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened during the review period. Thanks to ample Hong Kong dollar liquidity, the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) remained at low levels. Overall, trading in the Hong Kong dollar foreign exchange and money markets continued to be smooth and orderly. Looking ahead, although uncertainties surrounding US monetary policy, the pandemic, and escalating geopolitical tensions may exacerbate capital flow volatility, Hong Kong’s substantial foreign exchange reserves and robust banking system provide it with the capacity to withstand shocks from such fluctuations. On the whole, the Hong Kong dollar traded mostly on the strong side of the Convertibility Zone, with transactions continuing to be smooth and orderly. Since September 2021, the Hong Kong dollar has gradually weakened against the US dollar amid risk aversion in the local stock market (Chart 4.1). Although the Hong Kong dollar saw a slight rebound in October 2021 due to improved market sentiment, its upward momentum subsequently faded, mainly reflecting weak southbound net buying through the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect (Chart 4.2), as well as market expectations that the US dollar would strengthen as the Federal Reserve adopted a more hawkish stance on its monetary policy outlook. During the review period, initial public offering (IPO) fundraising activities continued to provide support to the Hong Kong dollar (Chart 4.3). Total deposits grew moderately during the period under review, with no significant signs of funds flowing out of the local banking system. Meanwhile, the latest Balance of Payments statistics indicate that non-resident direct investment continued to flow into Hong Kong in the second half of 2021, and there were no indications of abnormal cross-border capital flows. Chart 4.1: Hong Kong Dollar Exchange Rate; Chart 4.2: Southbound Net Buying via Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect; Chart 4.3: Equity Fundraising at the Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited (HKEX). Despite the strengthening of the US dollar during the review period, the Nominal Effective Exchange Rate (NEER) index of the Hong Kong dollar remained stable, supported by the appreciation of the Renminbi against the Hong Kong dollar (Chart 4.4). Given the minimal inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners, the Real Effective Exchange Rate (REER) index broadly tracked the movement of the NEER index. Chart 4.4: Nominal and Real Effective Exchange Rates. Looking ahead, uncertainties regarding US monetary policy, pandemic developments, and escalating geopolitical tensions may heighten capital flow volatility. As US dollar interest rates rise, and consistent with the normal operation of the Linked Exchange Rate System (LERS), outflows of Hong Kong dollar funds—the pace and scale of which will depend on prevailing market conditions—could potentially weaken the Hong Kong dollar and trigger the Weak-side Convertibility Undertaking. Hong Kong also possesses ample foreign exchange reserves and a sound banking system, enabling it to withstand capital flow volatility without compromising financial stability. During the review period, Hong Kong’s monetary environment remained accommodative. The Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base increased by 1.4% over the eight months since end-June 2021, primarily driven by an increase in Certificates of Indebtedness. Reflecting additional issuances made to meet banks’ sustained demand for Exchange Fund Bills amid abundant liquidity in the banking system, outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes increased by HK$119.7 billion to HK$1,188.7 billion during the review period, while the Aggregate Balance (before Discount Window operations) correspondingly decreased by HK$119.9 billion to HK$337.6 billion (Chart 4.5). Meanwhile, government-issued banknotes and coins remained relatively stable. Chart 4.5: Aggregate Balance and Outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes. Over the six months since end-July 2021, total deposits of Authorized Institutions (AIs) grew moderately by 4.5%, while Hong Kong dollar deposits edged up by 0.3%. However, it should be noted that monetary statistics can be volatile due to various short-term factors, such as seasonal funding needs related to IPOs, as well as business and investment-related activities; therefore, observing longer-term trends is advisable. For 2021 as a whole, total deposits and Hong Kong dollar deposits increased by 4.6% and 1.4%, respectively. Chart 4.6: Authorized Institutions’ Deposits by Currency. Overall, transactions in Hong Kong’s interbank market continued to be smooth and orderly. Due to ample liquidity in the banking system, HIBORs remained at low levels despite market concerns about tightening US monetary policy (Chart 4.7). Partly reflecting market expectations of higher funding demand towards year-end, HIBORs picked up slightly in December 2021. The average lending rate on newly approved mortgages rose slightly from 1.48% in July 2021 to 1.56% in January 2022. On the other hand, the Best Lending Rates quoted by major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging from 5.00% to 5.50%. Looking ahead, ample liquidity in the banking system provides a sufficient buffer against large-scale capital market activities or financial market volatility. Chart 4.7: HIBORs and USD LIBORs. During the review period, the offshore Renminbi interbank market continued to function normally. Affected by seasonal liquidity demand towards year-end, the overnight offshore Renminbi HIBOR experienced slight volatility in late December 2021, while the 3-month offshore Renminbi HIBOR remained relatively stable, hovering around 3% throughout the review period (Chart 4.8). Chart 4.8: Overnight and 3-Month Offshore Renminbi HIBORs. In the second half of 2021, Hong Kong’s offshore Renminbi funding pool continued to grow steadily. Over the six months since end-July 2021, Renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit (CDs) increased by 30.3%, reaching RMB 1,113.5 billion by end-January 2022 (Chart 4.9 and Table 4.A). Specifically, Renminbi customer deposits rose by 33.5%, mainly driven by corporate fund inflows, offsetting a 48.0% decline in outstanding CDs. Chart 4.9: Renminbi Deposits and Certificates of Deposit in Hong Kong. Over the six months since July 2021, although Renminbi loans decreased by 10.2% to RMB 167.6 billion, Renminbi trade settlement in Hong Kong continued to expand. Between end-July 2021 and end-January 2022, banks in Hong Kong processed transactions totaling RMB 3,763.0 billion (Chart 4.10), representing an increase of 18.3% from RMB 3,181.0 billion in the same period last year. Hong Kong’s sizable Renminbi funding pool continues to support a vast volume of Renminbi payment and financing transactions. For 2021 as a whole, the average daily turnover of the Renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system rose from RMB 1,191.5 billion in 2020 to RMB 1,522.6 billion. Chart 4.10: Renminbi Trade Settlement Remittances. Looking ahead, Hong Kong’s offshore Renminbi business is expected to benefit from the establishment of two-way Stock Connect, Bond Connect, and Cross-boundary Wealth Management Connect schemes, the continued opening up of the Mainland’s capital account, increasing international investor demand for Renminbi assets, and deepening regional economic and financial cooperation under the Belt and Road Initiative and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiative. Major global equity markets continued to rally in the fourth quarter of 2021 but have undergone consolidation since January 2022 amid growing market concerns over the tightening stance of major central banks in advanced economies and the escalation of the Russia-Ukraine conflict. The Hong Kong stock market remained subdued in the fourth quarter of 2021, largely dragged down by a sharp decline in technology stocks. Global risks and uncertainties surrounding the development of the pandemic in Hong Kong caused the Hang Seng Index (HSI) to fall to a nearly two-year low in February. Meanwhile, Hong Kong’s offshore Renminbi bond market continued to grow steadily in the second half of 2021. The residential property market has softened since mid-2021, partly affected by weakening asset market sentiment and a fresh wave of local infections. Major global equity markets generally continued their uptrend in the final quarter of 2021, propelling the MSCI World Index to a record high of 3,262 points on January 4, 2022 (Chart 4.11). Stimulated by government monetary and fiscal policies, the global economic recovery and strong corporate earnings underpinned the rally in major global equity markets, though the pandemic remained a key risk concern for investors throughout the year. However, major global equity markets have consolidated since early January 2022, as markets became increasingly concerned about the tightening stance of major central banks in advanced economies amidst surging inflation risks, soaring commodity prices, and the escalation of the Russia-Ukraine conflict. By contrast, towards the end of 2021, the Hong Kong stock market continued to lag behind other major global markets. The HSI hovered between 24,000 and 26,500 points from September to mid-November, closing 2021 at 23,398 points, down 14.1% from 2020. In early 2022, renewed buying interest from value investors lifted the HSI back to approximately 25,000 points in January. However, uncertainties regarding the pandemic situation in Hong Kong and the escalating Russia-Ukraine conflict dragged the HSI down to a nearly two-year low of 22,713 points by end-February. Over the entire review period from end-August 2021 to February 2022, the Hang Seng Index declined by 12.2%, while the MSCI World Index fell by 5.2% (Chart 4.11). Chart 4.11: Hang Seng Index and MSCI World Index. Following the emergence of the highly transmissible Omicron variant, equity market implied volatility fluctuated significantly in late November 2021 before subsiding somewhat. Although the Skew Index retreated from its historical peak in late June 2021, it remained elevated, reflecting investors' concerns about a potential correction to the prolonged equity market rally since the outbreak of the pandemic, and their consequent willingness to pay a higher premium to hedge against downside risks (Chart 4.12). Chart 4.12: Option Implied Volatility of the Hang Seng Index and S&P 500 Index, and Skew Index. Against a backdrop of ample global liquidity, the Hong Kong stock market has continued to record net inflows from international investors since the last report (Chart 4.13). In contrast, southbound Stock Connect recorded significant net outflows in the third quarter of 2021, mainly due to concerns over the impact of regulatory changes in the Mainland on technology stocks. However, southbound buying via Stock Connect began to recover in December 2021, recording cumulative inflows of HK$98.3 billion by end-February. During the review period, cumulative net buying increased by 5.7% to HK$2,233.0 billion (Chart 4.14). Chart 4.13: Net Inflows into Hong Kong’s Stock Market; Chart 4.14: Net Flows via Stock Connect. After reaching a record high in fundraising during the first half of 2021, Hong Kong’s primary market slowed in the second half. For 2021 as a whole, there were 98 new listings, raising a total of HK$328.9 billion (Chart 4.15), representing a decrease of 17.8% in total funds raised compared to the previous year. In 2021, HKEX ranked fourth globally in terms of IPO fundraising, trailing only Nasdaq, the New York Stock Exchange, and the Shanghai Stock Exchange. Chart 4.15: Hong Kong’s Initial Public Offering Market. The outlook for the local stock market remains uncertain. Easing monetary policy in the Mainland and more Chinese concept stocks seeking secondary listings in the primary market are expected to improve sentiment in the Hong Kong stock market. However, the market still faces numerous headwinds, including uncertainties regarding the local pandemic situation, a faster-than-expected pace of US monetary policy normalisation, and the escalation of the Russia-Ukraine conflict.

The profitability of retail banks in Hong Kong declined in the second half of 2021. The classified loan ratio rose slightly in the second half of 2021, but remained low by both historical and international standards. Underpinned by strong capital and liquidity positions, the Hong Kong banking sector remained resilient. During the period under review, to further assist the economy in navigating through difficult times, the HKMA extended a number of support measures. Looking ahead, the rapid spread of the Omicron variant could pose a threat to the economic recovery, which, coupled with the risk that the pace of US monetary policy normalization may be faster than expected, will present challenges to banks' credit risk management. Banks should remain vigilant and carefully assess the potential impact of relevant risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios. In the second half of 2021, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell by 16.1% compared to the same period in 2020. The weak earnings performance was mainly attributable to decreases in net interest income and non-interest income, as well as an increase in operating expenses. Consequently, the return on assets declined to 0.50% in the second half of 2021, down from 0.61% in the same period of 2020 (Chart 5.1). For 2021 as a whole, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks decreased by 18.6% compared to 2020, while the return on assets fell from 0.77% to 0.59%. Chart 5.1 Profitability of Retail Banks Reflecting the continued impact of the low interest rate environment, the net interest margin of retail banks remained at a low level of 0.98% in the second half of 2021 (Chart 5.2). Chart 5.2 Net Interest Margin of Retail Banks Reflecting year-end funding demand and the decline in the Aggregate Balance following the HKMA's issuance of additional Exchange Fund Bills, the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) recorded a slight increase in the last quarter of 2021. However, given that liquidity in the banking system remained very ample, HIBORs continued to stay at relatively low levels. Specifically, the three-month HIBOR rose slightly by 9 basis points from six months earlier to 0.26% at end-December 2021 (blue line in Chart 5.3). The funding costs of retail banks remained stable during the period under review. Notably, the Composite Interest Rate (a measure of the average HKD funding cost for retail banks) increased moderately by 3 basis points from 0.18% six months earlier to 0.21% at end-2021 (green line in Chart 5.3). Chart 5.3 Interest Rates (a) End-of-period figures. (b) Period-average figures for newly approved loans. (c) Starting from June 2019, the Composite Interest Rate has been calculated based on the newly implemented local "Interest Rate Risk in the Banking Book" framework. Therefore, figures from June 2019 onwards are not strictly comparable with those of previous months. From a broader perspective, the overall HKD and USD funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong increased slightly by 6 basis points in the second half of 2021 (red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4 HKD and USD Funding Costs of Licensed Banks Since June 2019, all licensed banks subject to the new local Interest Rate Risk in the Banking Book framework have submitted returns under the new framework, while exempted licensed banks continue to submit returns under the existing interest rate risk framework. The overall funding cost is calculated as a weighted average of the relevant figures of these two categories of licensed banks. Therefore, figures from June 2019 onwards are not directly comparable with those of previous months. Although the normalization of US monetary policy may herald some improvement in bank profitability, any near-term improvement could be partially offset by two factors. First, despite the Federal Reserve's indication of multiple rate hikes in 2022, past experience suggests that movements in local interest rates may lag behind those of US interest rates (especially when interbank liquidity in Hong Kong remains very ample). As such, it may take more time for improvements in banks' net interest margins to materialize. In addition, the surge in Omicron variant cases could also create uncertainties regarding the pace of economic recovery, thereby putting pressure on banks' asset quality and profitability. The capital position of the Hong Kong banking sector remained robust and well above the minimum international standards. The consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions stood at 20.2% at end-2021 (Chart 5.5), well above the international minimum requirement of 8%. The Tier 1 capital ratio and Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital ratio were 18.2% and 16.2%, respectively, during the period. Furthermore, the leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions recorded a robust level of 7.9% at end-2021, exceeding the statutory minimum of 3%. Chart 5.5 Capital Position of Locally Incorporated Authorized Institutions 1. Consolidated basis. 2. Starting from January 1, 2013, locally incorporated authorized institutions are required to comply with the revised capital adequacy framework, Basel III. Therefore, capital ratios from March 2013 onwards are not directly comparable with data up to December 2012. Measured by the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) requirement under Basel III, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained sound during the period under review. The average LCR of Category 1 institutions remained high at 151.9% in the fourth quarter of 2021 (Chart 5.6), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. Over the same period, the average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio of Category 2 institutions was 59.1%, also well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Chart 5.6 Liquidity Coverage Ratio 1. Consolidated basis. 2. Quarterly average figures. The latest Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) also reflected the stable funding position of authorized institutions. The average NSFR of Category 1 institutions remained high at 135.3% in the third quarter of 2021 (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average Core Funding Ratio of Category 2A institutions also recorded a high level of 150.4%, above the statutory minimum requirement of 75%. These figures indicate that the Hong Kong banking sector is capable of withstanding liquidity shocks. Climate change affects every aspect of our lives, and everyone has a responsibility to contribute to mitigating its impact.
