In this regard, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) has devoted substantial efforts to advancing Hong Kong’s climate goals and contributing to enhancing global climate resilience and sustainable development. Following the inclusion of our first Sustainability Report as a chapter in the HKMA 2021 Annual Report last year, we have published the 2022 Sustainability Report as a standalone publication for the first time this year. I hope this report will provide readers with a deeper understanding of the HKMA’s strategies and priorities in strengthening the Hong Kong banking system’s capacity to address climate change, building a green finance ecosystem, and fulfilling our role as a responsible investor and sustainable organisation. During the year, we made significant progress in integrating sustainability into the HKMA’s key functions. Readers will find details of our specific initiatives and work in this report, with highlights including the following: Banks’ day-to-day operations are exposed to climate risks. As the banking regulator, the HKMA has taken concrete measures to enhance banks’ resilience to climate change. In 2022, we formulated a two-year plan to incorporate climate risk factors into our supervisory processes and explored how technology can assist banks in assessing the impact of physical risks. In light of the increasing launch of green and sustainable products by banks, we also shared good practices with the industry on the proper management of these products to help banks strengthen their climate risk management capabilities. The HKMA actively participates in various collaborative initiatives aimed at addressing climate risks and promoting sustainable finance development. Locally, through the Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group (Steering Group), we are working with other financial regulators to develop a local green taxonomy; this framework will enhance transparency in the financial market and promote greater consistency in green finance policies. At the international level, we are actively engaged with various international organisations to help formulate policies to tackle climate change and assess its implications for financial stability. Hong Kong is well positioned to meet Asia’s demand for green and sustainable financing. Despite 2022 being a challenging year for the global bond market, the volume of green and sustainable debt issuance in Hong Kong continued to record robust growth, increasing by 42% to a total of US$80.5 billion, making Hong Kong the largest centre² for arranging international green and sustainable bond issuance in Asia. Relevant issuers included the Shenzhen Municipal People’s Government and the Hainan Provincial People’s Government, whose issuances once again demonstrated Hong Kong’s unique role in facilitating green and sustainable capital flows between the Mainland and international markets. The vibrant development of Hong Kong’s green bond market is partly attributable to the Government Green Bond Programme. Since 2019, the HKMA has assisted the Government in issuing nearly US$16 billion worth of green bonds, with proceeds allocated to over 40 green government projects, covering areas such as green buildings, waste management and recycling, energy efficiency, and energy conservation. We also assisted the Government in achieving two "firsts": in May 2022, we helped issue the inaugural batch of Government Green Retail Bonds totalling HK$20 billion, which was the largest green retail bond issuance globally at that time. Furthermore, we assisted the Government in issuing the first-ever tokenised green bonds in February 2023. This was the world’s first tokenised green bond issued by a government, marking a milestone that successfully combined our strengths in the bond market, green and sustainable finance, and fintech. Standards, data, and talent are indispensable elements for fostering a robust climate finance ecosystem, and their development requires the concerted efforts and collaboration of various sectors. To this end, the HKMA works primarily through the Steering Group to collaborate with relevant government bureaux, regulators, academic institutions, and the financial sector to advance these elements. In addition to the aforementioned development of a local green taxonomy, the Steering Group, through its Centre for Green and Sustainable Finance, is promoting skills training for the industry and improving Hong Kong’s data resources. Moreover, the Steering Group has made good progress in other areas, including mandatory climate-related disclosures and carbon market opportunities. In 2022, the HKMA further strengthened the Exchange Fund’s responsible investment efforts, notably setting a target for the Exchange Fund’s investment portfolio to achieve net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. Concurrently, we have enhanced our risk management practices to improve the Exchange Fund’s climate resilience and risk-adjusted long-term returns. Furthermore, to fully capture potential opportunities arising from climate change, we are committed to promoting sustainable investment within the Exchange Fund, seeking investment opportunities that support climate transition and mitigation to enhance the portfolio’s long-term returns. By end-2021, the weighted average carbon intensity of the Exchange Fund’s equity portfolio had decreased by 43% compared to the 2017 level. Indeed, the Exchange Fund’s exposure to high-carbon assets has remained consistently lower than that of the broader market. Going forward, we will continue to strive towards our net-zero target by continuously enhancing the integration of Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) factors into our investment management process, exercising active ownership, maintaining ongoing engagement with stakeholders, and focusing on portfolio decarbonisation and transition. Within the HKMA, the Corporate Social Responsibility and Sustainability Committee, chaired by myself, is responsible for formulating the HKMA’s sustainability strategy. Our strategic direction is built upon three pillars: Environment, People, and Community. On the environmental front, we are committed to promoting a green workplace and advocating for a more environmentally friendly marketplace; regarding our people, as a responsible and caring employer, we actively foster a healthy and inclusive work environment; and in terms of community responsibility, we strive to enhance public financial literacy, promote financial inclusion, and give back to society. Compared to the levels recorded when we began tracking our carbon footprint in 2015, our per capita greenhouse gas emissions, energy consumption, and paper usage all achieved double-digit percentage reductions in 2022. More importantly, we have established a roadmap to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050. In the near term, we aim to completely eliminate Scope 1 emissions and reduce Scope 2 emissions by 63% by 2030, using 2015 as the baseline. Addressing climate change and promoting sustainable development require sustained efforts and collaboration from multiple parties. On this critical global issue, we recognise the importance of leading by example and working alongside like-minded peers and international organisations. The next section outlines the HKMA’s short-term plans and priorities in addressing climate change across our key functions. Achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 is an arduous task, but we are fully committed to reaching this goal. We are confident that with the collective efforts of all colleagues, the financial sector, and the wider community, we can successfully rise to future climate challenges. Chief Executive Eddie Yue

In 2023, the HKMA will continue to promote sustainable development in Hong Kong's financial sector and fulfill its responsibilities as a responsible investor and sustainable organization. At the same time, through participation in international and regional organizations, the HKMA will also strive to promote the broad development and best practices of green and sustainable finance. As the banking regulator, we will endeavor to enhance the climate resilience of the banking sector and further refine our green finance ecosystem to support banks' green transition. Specifically, the HKMA will engage with banks to understand their progress in implementing supervisory requirements on climate risk management, incorporate climate factors into our Supervisory Review Process, and revise the Common Assessment Framework on "Greenness Baseline" for the banking sector. Meanwhile, the HKMA will support banks in enhancing their climate resilience and risk management capabilities, such as by exploring various measures and technological solutions to help banks identify, measure, and monitor their climate risk exposures. The HKMA will also collaborate with banks to conduct the next round of climate risk stress testing as part of the 2023–24 supervisor-led regular stress testing exercise. Participating banks will be required to assess their ability to withstand climate risks under an enhanced stress-testing framework covering multiple stress scenarios, including extreme weather events and adverse economic conditions. To foster the healthy development of banks' provision of green and sustainable investment products, the HKMA will keep abreast of local and international market and regulatory developments, maintain communication with the industry, and provide timely guidance on sales processes where appropriate. We will also conduct off-site thematic reviews to gain a comprehensive understanding of the green and sustainable investment products offered by banks. Concurrently, to strengthen the development of the green finance ecosystem in support of the financial sector's green transition, the HKMA is planning to consult the industry on the structure and core elements of a local green taxonomy. On market development, to promote Hong Kong as a regional green and sustainable finance hub, the HKMA will assist the Government in expanding the issuance size of green bonds under the Government Green Bond Programme and broadening the scope of the programme to cover sustainability bonds; meanwhile, it will attract more green financing activities to Hong Kong through the Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme. The HKMA will also assist in implementing the Government-funded Pilot Green and Sustainable Finance Capacity Building Scheme to expand the talent pool for green finance in Hong Kong. In addition, the HKMA will continue to encourage more Mainland local governments, institutions, and enterprises to undertake green financing through Hong Kong, and explore the feasibility of integrating green finance with technology. Separately, we will continue to collaborate with other agencies and departments through the Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group on cross-sectoral topics such as skills training and data, green taxonomy, climate-related disclosures and sustainability reporting, and carbon market opportunities. Through the Alliance for Green Commercial Banks, the HKMA will jointly launch various dedicated initiatives with the International Finance Corporation in Asia, including conducting green finance research, providing unique market insights, offering targeted professional training for banks, and providing practical guidance to assist banks in formulating roadmaps to develop green finance as a core business. Looking ahead, the Alliance will work closely with its cornerstone members, global partners, and knowledge partners to launch a membership programme to expand the Alliance's influence in the Asian region. At the same time, the Alliance will strengthen efforts to enhance the professional capabilities of industry practitioners, facilitate knowledge sharing on green finance, and lead the initiation of projects in new areas. As a responsible investor, the HKMA has set a target for the Exchange Fund portfolio to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050 or sooner, as part of its commitment to participating in global climate action and implementing the recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures. Looking ahead, the HKMA will continue to integrate environmental, social, and governance factors into its investment management process, strive towards the net-zero emissions target, and fully support global climate action. As a responsible and sustainable organization, the HKMA cares about its staff, the general public, and the surrounding environment. We have formulated a sustainability roadmap and established climate targets for our own operations as a commitment to our participation in global decarbonization and climate action efforts. The HKMA will continue to prioritize carbon emission reduction and encourage full staff support in energy conservation and waste reduction. Furthermore, we will provide further guidance to staff on incorporating sustainability principles into procurement processes. To drive digital transformation and enhance operational agility, the HKMA will explore ways to modernize internal systems and applications to further improve work efficiency while minimizing potential risks that may arise during the digital transformation process as far as possible.

Climate change poses a significant risk to the financial system. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) has been committed to strengthening Hong Kong’s financial system to build a greener and more sustainable future, contributing to Hong Kong’s climate goals as well as the global sustainable development agenda. Banks face the impact of various sustainability and climate-related issues in their day-to-day business operations. To continue performing their vital functions within the financial system and to channel more capital toward green and sustainable projects, banks must proactively manage climate risks. As the banking regulator, the HKMA places particular emphasis on building banks’ capacity to address and manage climate risks, and on accelerating their efforts to support the transition to a low-carbon economic model. The HKMA also supports banks in enhancing their capabilities to detect environmental crimes and has participated in the recently published Hong Kong Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Risk Assessment, which covers areas such as environmental crimes and illegal wildlife trafficking. In 2022, the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (Basel Committee)1 issued principles for the effective management and supervision of climate-related financial risks and responded to frequently asked questions, clarifying how the existing Basel framework addresses these risks. In light of these international developments, the HKMA will continue its efforts to incorporate climate-related factors into its supervisory framework. Following the issuance of the Supervisory Policy Manual module GS-1 “Climate Risk Management” in 2021, the HKMA has maintained communication with banks to exchange views on expectations, progress, and challenges regarding the implementation of relevant supervisory requirements. To further strengthen the supervision of banks’ climate risk management, the HKMA has formulated a two-year plan to integrate climate risk factors into the bank supervision process, which was communicated to the banking sector in June. As part of the implementation of this two-year plan, the HKMA issued the revised Supervisory Policy Manual module SA-1 “Risk-Based Supervision,” incorporating climate risk into the risk-based supervision process to enhance the CAMEL2 rating system. Concurrently, drawing on experience gained from the 2021 pilot exercise, the HKMA has refined its climate risk stress-testing scenarios and assessment framework. The HKMA has also developed a plan to incorporate the next round of climate risk stress testing into supervisor-led regular stress tests, enabling a more comprehensive assessment of the banking sector’s resilience under extreme climate scenarios. Under the two-year plan, the HKMA is also enhancing its green assessment framework for banks to reflect the latest developments in sustainability-related issues, including climate risk management and transition planning. At the same time, the HKMA is reviewing the Supervisory Review Process used to assess and monitor banks’ capital adequacy and determine Pillar 2 capital requirements, with the aim of encouraging banks to strengthen their risk management frameworks to address risks associated with climate change and the transition to carbon neutrality. Given the increasing prevalence of green and sustainable products issued by banks, the HKMA conducted a thematic review focusing primarily on banks’ development and ongoing management of these products. During the thematic review, the HKMA identified good practices and issued a circular in December to share them with the industry, facilitating banks’ gradual enhancement of their climate risk management capabilities. The application of technology can improve data availability and strengthen banks’ capacity to manage climate risks. The HKMA has commenced the development of a common platform for banks to assess the impact of physical risks on real estate. Furthermore, the HKMA, together with other central banks and regulators, completed a project under the Bank for International Settlements Innovation Hub to explore how technological solutions can facilitate physical risk assessments. The HKMA also attaches great importance to promoting sustainable and globally leading anti-money laundering (AML) practices; this work leverages advanced analytics and RegTech, complemented by fully automated regulatory data collection. Over the past 12 months, the HKMA has streamlined its AML regulatory data collection processes to reduce banks’ manual workload and paper usage. To enhance transparency across financial markets and promote greater consistency in green finance policies, the HKMA is collaborating with other financial regulators to develop a local green taxonomy. Commonly referred to as a green taxonomy, this framework classifies economic activities as green or sustainable, providing a reference for authorities and market participants to determine whether an activity or its associated products are genuinely green or sustainable. To this end, the HKMA remains engaged with the industry and other relevant stakeholders to discuss in depth the features and challenges of the framework, and is preparing to propose and consult on its structure and core elements in the first half of 2023. Recognizing that climate change may pose potential risks to the financial system, the HKMA has incorporated a broader range of climate factors and scenarios into its financial risk analysis and research to enhance current surveillance efforts. In its ongoing monitoring of financial stability risks, the HKMA takes climate change into account and includes analyses of climate-related risks in various Financial Stability Reports. Through active participation in the Scenario Design and Analysis Workstream of the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS), the HKMA contributes to further enriching climate scenarios, thereby helping central banks and regulators better understand the macroeconomic and financial impacts of climate change. On the research front, the HKMA undertook several applied research projects in 2022, delving into two key topics: greenwashing in the corporate green bond market3 and the role of disclosure in mitigating climate risk exposures4. The findings of these studies help inform policy formulation and supervisory measures to address the impact of climate risks on financial stability. Domestically, this research supports the HKMA’s ongoing monitoring and assessment of the impact of climate risks on financial stability. Internationally, the HKMA has shared its research findings with diverse stakeholders through various channels, including international central bank research conferences and the Authority’s Half-Yearly Monetary and Financial Stability Report. The HKMA’s Liquidity Facilities Framework is a collateralized backstop funding arrangement that provides timely liquidity support to banks in need. The HKMA is currently exploring the incorporation of sustainability considerations into the assessment of eligible collateral under this framework. The HKMA actively participates in international and regional discussions on addressing climate risks and mainstreaming sustainable finance. Through such engagement, the HKMA helps foster international and regional policy dialogue on tackling climate change and its implications for financial stability, while drawing insights to enhance the climate resilience of Hong Kong’s financial system.

To consolidate Hong Kong's position as a regional green and sustainable finance hub, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) has stepped up its efforts to enhance market awareness and participation, provide necessary infrastructure and enablers, and support international initiatives to align with global standards. The Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group (Steering Group), co-led by the HKMA and the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), coordinates the financial sector’s response to climate and environmental risks, accelerates the development of green and sustainable finance in Hong Kong, and supports the Government’s climate strategies1. The work of the Steering Group is primarily guided by its Strategic Plan, which sets out six key focus areas and five action points to strengthen Hong Kong’s financial ecosystem and build a greener and more sustainable future (Figure 1). Strengthen climate-related financial risk management to consolidate Hong Kong’s status as a global risk management centre. Promote the flow of climate-related information at all levels to facilitate risk management, capital allocation, and investor protection. Enhance relevant skills among industry practitioners and raise public awareness and understanding. Encourage product innovation and research measures to channel capital towards green and sustainable projects. Capitalise on opportunities from the Mainland to develop Hong Kong into a green finance centre for the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area (GBA). Strengthen regional and international cooperation. Actions taken to date to advance sustainable finance development in Hong Kong: The Steering Group has made good progress since its inception. Current priorities include skills training and data collection under the Centre for Green and Sustainable Finance (see below), the green taxonomy (see “Establishing a Green Classification Framework to Facilitate Green Financing” in the chapter “Building a Sustainable Financial System” on page 9), climate-related disclosures and sustainability reporting, and carbon market opportunities. Specifically, the Steering Group published a preliminary feasibility assessment on carbon market opportunities in Hong Kong in March, and will support Hong Kong’s development as a regional carbon trading centre, including developing an international high-quality voluntary carbon market and seizing opportunities arising from GBA collaboration. In December, the Steering Group announced a partnership with CDP2 to enhance data availability and strengthen sustainability reporting in Hong Kong. As part of this collaboration, both parties developed a climate and environmental risk questionnaire targeting unlisted companies and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), facilitating corporate sustainability reporting while assisting financial institutions in collecting and analysing company-level data for risk assessment and related business decisions. This marks a significant step by the Steering Group to expand the coverage of its data work to include SMEs, a previously hard-to-reach yet vital segment of the economy. In July 2021, the Steering Group established the Centre for Green and Sustainable Finance to coordinate efforts among financial regulators, government agencies, industry stakeholders, and academic institutions in training and policy formulation, as well as to build resource and data repositories. In the first half of 2022, the Centre launched three repositories focusing on data, training information, and internship opportunities respectively, helping the financial sector and other sectors access data and learning resources related to green and sustainable finance. The resource repository provides data sources for assessing physical risks in Hong Kong. To support talent development in the industry, the Centre assisted the Government in launching the “Green and Sustainable Finance Training Pilot Scheme” in December, providing subsidies to practitioners, students, and graduates participating in training and upskilling programmes related to green and sustainable finance. Other measures to promote skills training include the launch of the “Sustainable Finance Internship Programme” to create more internship opportunities for students, and the introduction of a new Module on “Green and Sustainable Finance” under the HKMA’s “Enhanced Competency Framework for Banking Practitioners”3. “Green and Sustainable Finance Training Pilot Scheme” The HKMA has also been actively supporting regional green and sustainable finance development. In November 2020, the International Finance Corporation and the HKMA launched the “Alliance for Green Commercial Banks”4, bringing together financial institutions, banking industry associations, research institutions, and innovative technology providers in the region to jointly develop a collaborative platform for green commercial banks. The Alliance aims to enable commercial banks and other financial institutions to fully realise their potential in mainstreaming green finance as a core business, and to facilitate the financial system’s engagement in global climate change initiatives. It operates by providing a one-stop peer-learning platform for financial institutions to acquire the knowledge, tools, and information needed to formulate their own green finance roadmaps and transform into credible green financial institutions; convening green finance leaders and connecting green financial institutions across different emerging markets to foster communication and explore frontier topics; and advancing the global green finance agenda to unlock vast green and climate-related investment opportunities. In June, five globally leading financial institutions5 became Cornerstone Members of the Alliance, working closely with the International Finance Corporation and the HKMA to encourage clients to adopt green strategies, promote best practices for green products and services, and unlock new business opportunities to facilitate the transition to a green economy. Additionally, three Global Partners and one Knowledge Partner6 committed in 2022 to providing climate expertise in areas ranging from innovation and standardisation to academic research. Details of the Alliance and its membership structure are available on the relevant webpage (English version): Cornerstone Members, International Finance Corporation and HKMA sign Memorandum of Understanding. Meanwhile, since March 2021, the Alliance has organised 18 training sessions and roundtables, attracting over 6,000 participants from around the world, including the Asia-Pacific region, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and the Americas. Furthermore, in June 2022, the Alliance, in conjunction with the Hong Kong Institute for Monetary and Financial Research (HKIMR)7, published its inaugural frontier topic research report titled “Climate Risk: Definition, Measurement, Current Practices and Regulation”. The HKMA has been promoting green and sustainable debt issuance and fostering a local ecosystem of related professional services. Total green and sustainable debt issued in Hong Kong in 2022 (including bonds and loans) reached US$80.5 billion, representing a 42% increase. +42% Green and Sustainable Debt Issuance (US$80.5 billion) To demonstrate the Government’s commitment to tackling climate change, promoting green finance, and striving to make Hong Kong a more sustainable and liveable city, the Government launched the “Government Green Bond Programme” in 2018, with the HKMA assisting in the implementation of related green bond issuances. To date, the Government has issued nearly US$16 billion equivalent in green institutional and retail bonds, with proceeds allocated to over 40 green government projects, covering green buildings, waste management and resource recovery, energy efficiency and conservation, among others. To enhance the transparency and accountability of the Programme, the Government publishes an annual “Green Bond Report”, detailing the allocation of proceeds raised from green bonds and the expected environmental benefits. To enable citizens to participate in Hong Kong’s sustainable development through investment and share in the resulting benefits, the first batch of green retail bonds totalling HK$20 billion was issued in May, receiving enthusiastic public support and becoming the largest-ever green retail bond issuance globally at that time. This issuance also diversified Hong Kong’s range of green and sustainable financial products, reinforcing Hong Kong’s status as a premier regional and international green finance hub. The Government continued its regular issuance of green institutional bonds in the 2022-23 fiscal year, issuing US$5.75 billion equivalent in green bonds in January 2023. This triple-tranche issuance covered US dollars, euros, and renminbi, with tenors ranging from 2 to 30 years, continuing to serve as an important benchmark for potential issuers in Hong Kong and the region. The issuance was well received by the global investment community and successfully attracted new investors who had not participated in previous Government green bond issuances, reflecting investors’ confidence in Hong Kong’s long-term credit profile and economic fundamentals. Responding to investor demand, the Government doubled the issuance size of the renminbi tranche to RMB 10 billion. The share of international investors and Mainland investors participating via Bond Connect Southbound also increased, demonstrating Hong Kong’s role as a premier offshore renminbi business hub and further consolidating its leading position as an international financial centre. In February 2023, the HKMA also assisted the Government in issuing tokenised institutional green bonds to test the use of distributed ledger technology for bond issuance and settlement. These were among the first tokenised green bonds issued by a government globally. This primary issuance was settled on a T+1 basis on a private blockchain network, with subsequent processes—including coupon payments, secondary market trade settlement, and redemption at maturity—also digitised. The experience gained from this Government issuance can serve as a reference for market participants interested in conducting similar bond issuances in the future. To provide the industry with credible and accessible market information, the HKMA continues to collaborate with the Climate Bonds Initiative and the International Capital Market Association to publish annual reports on the green debt markets in Hong Kong and the region respectively. According to the International Capital Market Association’s report, in 2022 Hong Kong became the largest hub for arranging international green and sustainable bond issuance in Asia, with total bonds arranged through Hong Kong reaching US$27.8 billion, accounting for more than one-third of the regional total. Largest Arranging Hub for Asian International Green and Sustainable Bonds US$27.8 billion Following its inaugural issuance in 2021, the Shenzhen Municipal People’s Government issued another RMB 5 billion offshore local government bonds in Hong Kong in November 2022, including RMB 2.6 billion in green and blue bonds8. In the same month, the Hainan Provincial People’s Government also made its debut offshore bond issuance in Hong Kong, totalling RMB 5 billion, including blue and sustainable bonds. These bond issuances once again underscore Hong Kong’s unique role in facilitating green and sustainable capital flows between the Mainland and the rest of the world, as well as its enduring status as the region’s premier fundraising platform. The HKMA continues to promote and implement the “Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme” launched in 2021, leveraging the scheme to attract more related professional service providers—including financial institutions, green advisory firms, and external reviewers—to establish and expand their businesses in Hong Kong. The scheme has been well received by the industry. By end-2022, the scheme had covered expenses for pre-issuance, post-issuance, or both types of external review services for over 180 green and sustainable debt instrument issuers, helping issuers ensure and demonstrate strict adherence to market best practices and international standards. Starting from March, the scheme was enhanced by lowering the minimum loan size threshold for applying for external review fee subsidies from HK$200 million to HK$100 million, facilitating smaller enterprises in obtaining green financing. Following the successful completion of the proof-of-concept for tokenised retail green bonds under Project Genesis in 2021, the HKMA and the BIS Innovation Hub Hong Kong Centre collaborated again under Genesis 2.0 to explore the technical feasibility of digital carbon forwards (also known as Mitigation Outcome Interests, or MOIs), aiming to enhance transparency, objectivity, and green credentials in the green bond market. Completed in October 2022, the project successfully developed two prototypes that utilise blockchain and other relevant technologies to track, deliver, and transfer digital MOIs.

As one of the world’s largest asset owners and managers, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) plays a pivotal role in promoting green and sustainable finance to support the global climate change agenda. The HKMA is also a pioneer in responsible investment, having taken the lead in investing in green and sustainable assets as early as 2015. It requires its external investment managers to adopt the Principles of Responsible Ownership promulgated by the Securities and Futures Commission, and to integrate environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors into the investment management of the Exchange Fund. Adhering to the principle of "Capital Preservation First, Long-term Growth Second," the HKMA invests prudently, believing that emphasizing ESG factors can unlock long-term sustainable value and mitigate associated risks for its investments. In the face of increasingly severe climate change challenges, the HKMA continues to advance on its responsible investment journey, including setting a "Net-Zero Emissions by 2050" target in 2022 and refining risk management strategies to enhance portfolio resilience, thereby seeking better risk-adjusted long-term returns for the Exchange Fund. The HKMA also actively participates in building a green and sustainable finance ecosystem, partnering with like-minded investors and regulators to jointly promote responsible investment, and collaborating with international organizations to develop ESG investment standards. Transparency of climate-related information plays a crucial role in managing climate risks. To fulfill its commitment to supporting the Glasgow Declaration issued by the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) at the 2021 UN Climate Change Conference and to greening the global financial system, the HKMA has made climate-related disclosures for the Exchange Fund in accordance with the recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) under the Financial Stability Board. a. FCLTGlobal — Focusing Capital on the Long Term b. PRI — Principles for Responsible Investment c. NGFS — Network for Greening the Financial System d. TCFD — Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures The Exchange Fund Advisory Committee, chaired by the Financial Secretary, establishes the responsible investment framework and guiding principles, which are implemented by the Exchange Fund Investment Office (EFIO) in the investment management of the Exchange Fund. The primary guiding principle is for the HKMA to prioritize ESG investments that offer risk-adjusted long-term returns comparable to other options, consistent with the investment objectives of the Exchange Fund. Details of the HKMA’s responsible investment framework are available on the HKMA website: The Investment Committee under the Exchange Fund Advisory Committee, chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, is responsible for overseeing ESG and climate-related risks associated with the Exchange Fund’s investments. The Investment Committee reviews the responsible investment framework and risk management approach, and monitors the progress of ESG integration and the ESG profile of the Exchange Fund through regular meeting reports from the Risk Management and Compliance Division of the EFIO. As shown in Chart 1, the ESG Committee established under the EFIO, chaired by the Chief Risk Officer, is responsible for coordinating and overseeing various ESG initiatives within the EFIO. Motions discussed and work progress at each ESG Committee meeting are reported to the Chief Executive Officer of the EFIO. Governance Structure for Responsible Investment Oversight The dedicated team within the Risk Management and Compliance Division works closely with various investment teams of the EFIO on ESG integration, and assists senior management of the EFIO in managing ESG and climate-related risks and opportunities across different types of investments: Public Market Investments The Credit, Regulatory and Compliance Committee, composed of senior management of the EFIO, monitors the ESG profile of the fixed income portfolio through regular reporting by the Risk Management and Compliance Division. In addition, the Risk Management and Compliance Division participates in the selection, appointment, and monitoring processes of external investment managers for equity portfolios from an ESG perspective (see the section "Striving for Active Ownership" under "Risk Management" on page 27). Private Market Investments The Investment Committee, chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, considers ESG-related assessments made by the Risk Management and Compliance Division and the private markets investment team for each investment proposal. Mounting evidence² continues to indicate significant impacts from climate change and related risks. According to the latest report³ under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), even assuming full implementation of announced Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) across regions, global temperature rise is still estimated to reach 2.1 to 2.4 degrees Celsius by 2100, making it difficult to achieve the goal of the Paris Agreement to limit the increase in global average temperature to well below 2 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels. If regions adopt more aggressive policy measures to close the temperature gap, the resulting transition risks⁴ and market repricing of assets based on anticipated future trends, coupled with inherent physical risks, will exacerbate pressure on asset valuations. Given updates to global warming trajectories and model assumptions, the HKMA leveraged the expertise of external consultants to further assess the resilience of the Exchange Fund's "Portfolio" under a "Rapid Transition" scenario (Chart 2), beyond the scenarios assessed in 2021. The "Rapid Transition" scenario incorporates higher transition risk factors over the short, medium, and long term, assuming that policy changes and technological developments jointly drive a rapid decline in carbon emissions, while multiple assets face sudden divestment to maintain average temperature rise below 1.5 degrees Celsius before 2100. This scenario broadly aligns with the disorderly transition scenario recommended by the NGFS for forward-looking climate impact assessments. The "Portfolio" maintains strong resilience over the medium to long term due to its relatively high allocation to sovereign bonds, which have lower sensitivity to transition impacts. Sector distribution is key. Low-carbon power and renewable energy assets stand to benefit from the relevant transition. Transition risks and asset repricing may cause short-term shocks to performance, particularly for equity assets. Over time, the overall "Portfolio" will be subject to increasingly intensified impacts from gradually manifesting physical risks. Energy and traditional utilities remain the most vulnerable sectors. Like other modeling approaches, climate scenario analysis has its limitations. The analysis is based on market benchmark sector allocations at the strategic asset allocation level and does not account for the effects of active security selection within specific sectors. More granular research indicates that investments within the "Portfolio" are generally more resilient to transition shocks or suffer milder impacts compared to the market benchmarks of the strategic asset allocation. These findings reaffirm that the HKMA’s climate-focused responsible investment enhances portfolio resilience. The trajectory of climate change remains uncertain, and scenario analysis methodologies will continue to evolve alongside improvements in data quality and policy developments. The HKMA will regularly review relevant scenarios and refine assessments to better ascertain the Exchange Fund’s resilience to climate change. As a long-term investor, the HKMA fully understands the risks and opportunities presented by climate change. The HKMA is committed to further expanding sustainable investments and seizing opportunities related to climate transition, climate risk mitigation, and enhancing long-term portfolio returns. Building on strong momentum in 2022, the HKMA increased its holdings of green, social, and sustainability bonds by another 50%. Regarding equity investments, the HKMA invested in actively managed equity portfolios with a governance theme and adopted a decarbonization strategy favoring low-carbon companies for passively managed equity portfolios. Furthermore, the HKMA is exploring the establishment of a dedicated private equity portfolio with specialized partners of the Exchange Fund’s "Long-Term Growth Portfolio" to promote green and sustainable development in Asia (Chart 3). Chart 3 Continued Implementation of Measures to Increase ESG Investments The HKMA has invested in a Pan-African wind farm operator which, in addition to generating clean energy, places great emphasis on social and biodiversity factors. Prior to the establishment of the wind farm, local villagers used poisoned bait to prevent predators from attacking their livestock, inadvertently endangering certain endangered vulture species. Recognizing livestock as vital assets to local villagers, the operator constructed livestock shelters within the wind farm to protect animals from natural predators. Additionally, the operator employs bird monitoring teams to issue warnings when vultures are attracted by carcasses occasionally left by predators, enabling the shutdown of wind turbines to prevent vultures from being struck by blades. Reducing livestock predation creates a win-win situation: safeguarding villagers' livelihoods on one hand, and reducing vulture fatalities caused by wind turbines on the other, thereby protecting endangered species. Sound ESG practices can create additional business opportunities and open new revenue streams for companies, as illustrated by the following supply chain-related example. The investee company is an integrated logistics and warehousing operator in Mainland China, specializing in cold chain logistics for pharmaceuticals, chemical products, and high-end consumer goods. Facing rising ESG operational standards driven primarily by multinational corporate clients requiring service providers to meet ambitious decarbonization targets aligned with the Paris Agreement, the company engaged external consultants to help formulate a "Three-Year ESG Plan" aimed at reducing carbon emission intensity by 50% by 2030. This comprehensive decarbonization plan yielded significant results in 2021 alone. These ESG initiatives earned the company a "Low-Carbon Green Management Case Study" award from the China Federation of Logistics & Purchasing. Such achievements and recognition have enabled the company to secure substantial business opportunities from multinational clients in the consumer and chemical product sectors who place particular emphasis on ESG practices. The growth of ESG investment is intrinsically linked to the development of the green and sustainable finance ecosystem. The HKMA actively collaborates with like-minded investors and partners to promote responsible investment and enhance industry capabilities. In 2022, the HKMA successfully hosted the 4th Annual ESG Workshop, exchanging best ESG practices with nine participating private market institutions (including general partners, limited partners, and corporates), and promoting sustainable investment opportunities in the Asia-Pacific region and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area. On the public market side, the HKMA urged counterparties (primarily investment banks) to expand their ESG staffing and research capabilities, particularly in Hong Kong. Mr. Darryl Chan, Chief Executive Officer of the Exchange Fund Investment Office, delivered opening remarks at the 2022 HKMA ESG Workshop At the international level, the HKMA actively participates in developing industry ESG investment standards and practices: As one of the earliest central bank signatories to the Principles for Responsible Investment (PRI), the HKMA participated in a PRI-coordinated collaborative initiative among signatories to develop standardized responsible investment due diligence questionnaires for private equity and venture capital investments⁵,⁶, assisting private market investors in conducting ESG assessments of general partners and investment proposals. The HKMA participates in several working groups to support FCLTGlobal’s research; this research aims to explore mainstream market practices for long-term portfolios and decarbonization of private assets, as well as their applicability to long-term investors. As a member of the NGFS and a supporter of the TCFD, the HKMA contributed to the NGFS Guide to Climate-Related Disclosure for Central Banks, demonstrating its commitment to adopting sound ESG practices. The HKMA also leads a workstream under the NGFS "Central Banks’ Net Zero" workgroup, participating in the development of sustainable and responsible investment guidelines for the central banking community. The HKMA continues to participate in various industry forums and seminars, sharing insights on responsible investment and climate change strategies. Ms. Carmen Lau, Chief Risk Officer of the Exchange Fund Investment Office (center), spoke at an ESG Investment Opportunities Sharing Session Building internal capacity is essential to advancing the ESG journey. In addition to encouraging staff to take sustainability-related courses and obtain relevant qualifications, the HKMA has acquired relevant knowledge and practical experience through the process of engaging external consultants in 2021 to advise on mainstream industry practices for portfolio climate transition. Meanwhile, the HKMA utilizes ESG data compiled by reputable external data providers to supplement its ongoing portfolio analysis, helping reinforce the ESG resilience of the Exchange Fund.

The HKMA is committed to reducing its own carbon footprint, with the aim of achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 or sooner, and contributing to Hong Kong’s overall climate goals. While striving to promote environmental sustainability, the HKMA also upholds its commitment to caring for staff well-being, promoting financial inclusion, and fulfilling its social responsibilities. The HKMA is dedicated to conducting its daily operations in a responsible and sustainable manner. To this end, the HKMA implements sustainability initiatives under three pillars: Environment, People, and Community (Figure 1). The Corporate Social Responsibility and Sustainability Committee is responsible for leading the formulation and implementation of the HKMA’s sustainability strategy. Chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, the Committee comprises three Deputy Chief Executives and representatives from the Risk Management and Compliance Department and the Corporate Development and Operations Department, and reports regularly to the Governance Sub-Committee of the Exchange Fund Advisory Committee. Under the leadership of the Committee, various teams and working groups are responsible for planning and implementing measures within their respective areas. In 2022, the Corporate Social Responsibility and Sustainability Committee approved climate targets for corporate operations and reviewed the transition roadmap towards achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 or sooner. During the year, the Committee continued to review progress on the HKMA’s green initiatives, including proposals to enhance the HKMA’s sustainable procurement policies, procedures, and methodologies. Sustainability Governance Framework; The HKMA’s Corporate Sustainability Journey. In recognition of the HKMA’s dedication to caring for the environment, its people, and the community at large, the Hong Kong Council of Social Service has awarded the HKMA the “15 Years+ Caring Organisation” logo for the 16th consecutive year. The HKMA attaches great importance to its own carbon footprint and has established internal Green Office Guidelines to manage the environmental impact of its operational processes. Environmental considerations have been integrated into the interior design, operations, and maintenance of the HKMA’s offices. In 2022, BEAM Plus awarded Gold certification to certain renovated office areas of the HKMA. This marks the second green building certification received by the HKMA, following the LEED Gold certification obtained in 2021. Awarded BEAM Plus Interior v1.0 Gold Certification. The HKMA has implemented various energy-saving measures. Total energy consumption in 2022 was 4,996.4 MWh (2.8 MWh per capita), representing a decrease of 24.4% compared to 2015 (Chart 1). Total Scope 1 and Scope 2 greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions in 2022 amounted to 2,996.4 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (tCO2e) (1.7 tCO2e per capita), a reduction of 38.2% compared to 2015 (Chart 2). Chart 1; Chart 2 GHG Emission Intensity (Scope 1 and 2). The HKMA encourages paperless operations internally. In addition, the HKMA has implemented a print management system requiring staff to log in at printers to confirm each print job, helping to reduce unnecessary printing and toner usage. Where printing is necessary, double-sided printing and black-and-white printing are encouraged. The HKMA is also preparing to implement an internal electronic recordkeeping system. Total paper consumption in 2022 was 20.5 tonnes (0.0114 tonnes per capita), a decrease of 65.3% compared to 2015 (Chart A). Chart A: Paper Consumption Intensity. The HKMA continues to adhere to the “4R” principles in waste management. In addition to conventional waste, the HKMA reduces electronic waste through technological solutions such as server virtualization and private cloud infrastructure. In 2022, the HKMA engaged an external company for the first time to conduct a waste audit to analyze the composition of waste generated by its offices. The audit revealed that food waste constituted a significant portion of total waste, prompting the HKMA to launch a food waste recycling programme (see page 41, “Enhanced Waste Management”). Total non-hazardous waste generated in 2022 (including general refuse and recyclables) was 242.0 tonnes (0.135 tonnes per capita), a decrease of 4.8% compared to 2015 (Chart 3). Fluctuations in the trend were mainly attributable to work-from-home arrangements during peak periods of the COVID-19 pandemic and the resumption of office operations after the fifth wave of the epidemic. Chart 3 Non-Hazardous Waste Intensity. The HKMA prioritizes waste reduction at source and is committed to reducing, reusing, and recycling. In 2022, the HKMA engaged a company for the first time to conduct a waste audit to gain a better understanding of waste composition in daily operations (plastics, paper, metals, glass, wood, electronics, etc.) and to provide recommendations for waste reduction. Based on the findings of this audit, the HKMA launched a food waste recycling programme in November, installing food waste collection bins in all pantries. Food waste collected daily is transported to an organic resources recovery centre in Hong Kong for conversion into renewable energy for power generation. Residues from the conversion process can also be turned into compost for landscaping and agricultural use. Furthermore, recycling bins are conveniently located throughout the office. The HKMA shares recycling tips with staff and places greater emphasis on improving source separation of recyclables, as well as highlighting precautions when handling items such as cardboard boxes, food containers, and beverage bottles. In addition, we continue to organize events to raise staff awareness of environmental protection, explain waste management policies, and encourage staff to make good use of recycling facilities in the office. Daily collected food waste is sent to the Organic Resources Recovery Centre; Recycling plastic items. The HKMA operates two data centres (primary and backup). As these account for a major portion of the organization's overall energy consumption, the HKMA has adopted green designs and various energy-saving measures, including rack-mounted air conditioning systems, LED lighting, and 24-hour monitoring of power efficiency. Following the completion of a consultancy study on the green performance of the aforementioned data centres in 2022, the HKMA is preparing to implement recommendations to enhance overall energy efficiency. Preparations have also commenced for obtaining green data centre certification. Recognizing the importance of fostering a culture of sustainability, the HKMA regularly launches various programmes and activities to educate and encourage staff to adopt habits conducive to sustainability and embrace green and digital working practices. The HKMA shares green living tips and annual office-wide energy and paper consumption statistics with staff, reminding them to contribute to addressing environmental issues at an individual level; staff are also encouraged to submit suggestions on sustainability matters. Led by a Senior Manager of the Administration Division, a task force brings together staff from different departments to brainstorm ideas and concrete measures to promote a green workplace. Task force members also serve as ambassadors when new green initiatives are rolled out. The HKMA encourages the wider community to adopt more environmentally friendly practices and has introduced various measures to improve operational efficiency across the HKMA, the financial sector, and the economy as a whole, minimizing resource consumption. The HKMA’s Electronic Submission System (STET) is a one-stop platform enabling banks to submit documents electronically to the HKMA, covering various types of regular returns required on a weekly, monthly, quarterly, or annual basis. Another system, the e-Delivery System, provides a secure electronic communication channel for the HKMA to disseminate information such as circulars and guidelines to banks. Both systems help save substantial amounts of paper annually. Regarding bank complaint handling and enforcement work, the HKMA has taken measures to support paperless submissions, allowing bank customers to lodge complaints via electronic channels and online forms. The HKMA is also developing a next-generation management information system to facilitate complaint handling and the transition from paper-based to digital records. To reduce paper usage, the Central Moneymarkets Unit (CMU) has adopted digital signatures in its daily communications with participants, including the issuance of circulars, account opening and closure letters, and responses to audit confirmations. Looking ahead, the CMU will continue to explore further green initiatives, including the adoption of automated electronic processes for both internal and external communications. By promoting the use of the Faster Payment System (FPS) and stored value facilities, the HKMA encourages the public to adopt electronic payments in place of cash and physical cheques. Further information on FPS and stored value facilities can be found in the chapter “Hong Kong as an International Financial Centre” of the HKMA Annual Report 2022. Sending e-Hongbao is simple and convenient, reducing the use of physical red packets and banknotes, thereby supporting Hong Kong’s sustainable development. To this end, the HKMA continues to actively promote this practice across various social media and traditional platforms, encouraging the public to send e-Hongbao via internet or mobile banking services using FPS or other e-wallet services during the Lunar New Year. Major banks and e-wallet operators have also organized various campaigns to attract users to e-Hongbao, such as offering festive user interfaces, enhancing functionality for greater convenience, and launching lucky draws or cashback promotions. HKMA promotes e-Hongbao on social media. For those who choose to give physical red packets during the Lunar New Year, the HKMA continues to encourage the use of “Good-as-New Banknotes,” which are fit but previously used notes, for packing red packets. Good-as-New Banknotes reduce the need for printing new banknotes, thereby lessening environmental impact. Feedback from note-issuing banks indicates growing public acceptance of Good-as-New Banknotes in recent years. The Coin Collection Programme reflects the HKMA’s efforts to promote coin recycling. Coins collected through the programme are recirculated to meet public demand, improving coin circulation efficiency and reducing the need for minting. The programme operates two coin collection vehicles and has served over one million person-trips to date, collecting more than 800 million coins with a total face value of approximately HK$1.3 billion. In 2022, about 78% of users chose to top up their stored value facility accounts with part or all of the collected value. The HKMA maintains ongoing collaboration with the Hong Kong Council of Social Service, deploying coin collection vehicles on NGO flag days to collect coins in support of social services. Coin counting machines on board the coin collection vehicles. Launched in 2014, the Coin Collection Programme is the world’s first systematic coin collection programme utilizing a mobile vehicle concept. It has won numerous local and international awards over the years, gaining recognition for its innovative and environmentally friendly approach to coin processing. The programme operates two coin collection vehicles, each equipped with two high-speed coin counting machines to collect coins exchanged by the public. Users may choose to exchange coins for banknotes, top up stored value facility accounts (such as Octopus cards or e-wallets), or donate the proceeds to the Community Chest. In addition to collecting coins, the vehicles are occasionally deployed for various educational activities (e.g., student visits).

Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency has conducted an independent verification of the Climate Targets (the "Climate Targets") of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority ("HKMA"). The Climate Targets were developed with reference to the requirements of the SBTi Corporate Manual (the "SBTi Corporate Manual"). The objective of this verification engagement was to verify whether the Climate Targets were developed with reference to the SBTi Corporate Manual. This verification engagement was conducted in accordance with the International Standard on Assurance Engagements 3000 (Revised), "Assurance Engagements Other Than Audits or Reviews of Historical Financial Information," issued by the International Auditing and Assurance Standards Board. The verification procedures were specifically designed to express an opinion and conclusion to obtain a reasonable level of assurance. The verification process was conducted in accordance with the requirements of the SBTi Corporate Manual. The HKMA is responsible for the collection and presentation of the data. Our verification work was conducted with absolute independence and impartiality. Based on the results of this verification, Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency provides reasonable assurance and concludes that: • The Climate Targets were developed with reference to the SBTi Corporate Manual. Shen Xiaoyin, Audit Manager, Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency, March 2023. Verification Statement: Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency has conducted an independent verification of the 2022 Environmental Data (the "2022 Data") of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority ("HKMA"). The 2022 Data includes total energy consumption, Scope 1 and Scope 2 greenhouse gas emission intensity, paper consumption intensity, non-hazardous waste generation intensity and recycling rate for 2022, as well as the changes in these data compared to 2015 levels. The HKMA's greenhouse gas emissions data were compiled in accordance with the Greenhouse Gas Protocol ("GHG Protocol") jointly published by the World Resources Institute ("WRI") and the World Business Council for Sustainable Development ("WBCSD"). The verification scope covered relevant data for the period from January 1, 2022, to December 31, 2022, as well as relevant data for the period from January 1, 2015, to December 31, 2015, used for annual performance comparison. The verification scope encompassed a total of six office and warehouse assets: four offices located at 1) Two International Finance Centre, 2) Hopewell Centre, 3) One Pacific Place, and 4) Kowloon Commerce Centre; and two warehouses located at 5) Lok Sing Industrial Centre and 6) Chung Lee Centre, situated in Kwai Chung and Tsuen Wan respectively. The objective of the verification was to provide reasonable assurance regarding the accuracy and reliability of the 2022 Data and to confirm the adequacy of the HKMA's data collection mechanisms. Within the verification scope, Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency examined representative data and supporting evidence selected from the six assets. This verification engagement was conducted in accordance with the International Standard on Assurance Engagements 3000 (Revised), "Assurance Engagements Other Than Audits or Reviews of Historical Financial Information," issued by the International Auditing and Assurance Standards Board. The verification procedures were specifically designed to express an opinion and conclusion to obtain a reasonable level of assurance. The verification process was conducted in accordance with the requirements of the GHG Protocol. The verification process tested the completeness and accuracy of data by tracing selected sample data back to their sources, and reviewed the underlying procedures for data collection, aggregation, estimation, calculation, and internal checks, and performed reliability testing. The verification process also included validating internal data collection and management mechanisms, conducting interviews with representatives responsible for preparing the 2022 Data, and selecting representative data and information for examination. Relevant raw data and supporting evidence were also reviewed in detail during the verification process. The HKMA is responsible for the collection and presentation of the data. Our verification work was conducted with absolute independence and impartiality. The Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency verification team was not involved in the preparation of the 2022 Data. Based on the results of this verification, Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency provides reasonable assurance on the 2022 Data and concludes that: • The 2022 Data are materially accurate and reliable; • The HKMA's overall data collection mechanisms are adequate. Shen Xiaoyin, Audit Manager, Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency, March 2023.

Scaling up and accelerating climate action has become the most pressing issue of our time. We are now nearly halfway through the critical decade for addressing the climate crisis. To have any hope of limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius, we must reduce global carbon emissions by more than 40% within this decade. Yet greenhouse gas emissions continue to hit record highs. The latest climate science indicates that the window of opportunity to limit global temperature rise to 1.5 degrees Celsius is rapidly closing. The impacts of a 1.1-degree Celsius temperature increase are already being acutely felt worldwide—record-breaking heatwaves and droughts, severe flooding, storms, and other extreme weather events are occurring with increasing frequency and intensity. Hong Kong is no exception. Last September, following a ferocious super typhoon, we were immediately struck by a once-in-a-century rainstorm. Despite our robust infrastructure and rapid disaster response capabilities, the impact was still severe, causing widespread flooding, transport disruptions, and extensive road damage across many areas. All these serve as stark reminders that decisive and proactive climate action is urgently needed. Asia faces particularly significant challenges in its low-carbon transition, especially in balancing economic development with sustainability. We need credible transition strategies that appropriately balance climate action with economic growth and social inclusion. This is by no means an easy task. Driven by rapid economic development and population growth, the region accounts for more than half of global carbon emissions. Meanwhile, due to its high population density and geographical location, the Asia-Pacific region is also highly vulnerable to sea-level rise and extreme weather. Given the varying stages of economic development across the region, while the low-carbon transition will bring new opportunities for some economies, raising the necessary transition financing remains a formidable challenge for others. Market estimates suggest that the Asia-Pacific region will require annual investments exceeding US$3 trillion over the next 30 years to support its low-carbon transition. As an international financial centre, Hong Kong has both the capability and the responsibility to leverage the power of finance to support the low-carbon transition across Asia. As a banking regulator, market facilitator, and responsible investor, the HKMA has made substantial efforts towards the sustainable development agenda. Readers can learn about the specific measures and initiatives launched by the HKMA over the past year in the various chapters of this report. Furthermore, to strengthen the HKMA’s internal governance structure and better coordinate sustainability efforts across different functional areas, we established the Green and Sustainability Steering Committee last year. For detailed information on the Steering Committee, please refer to the newly added chapter on "Governance for Sustainability." Banks in Hong Kong play a vital role in supporting Asia's transition to net zero. In addition to fulfilling our traditional functions as a banking regulator—ensuring banks properly manage climate risks in our day-to-day supervision—we also act as a facilitator, supporting the banking sector in providing financing for the low-carbon transition. One example is the development of a green taxonomy framework to help banks and other financial institutions identify environmentally sustainable activities, thereby aligning their business decisions with global climate goals. We launched a prototype of the green taxonomy framework for consultation in May and are currently refining it based on feedback received during the consultation period. Moreover, as stakeholders increasingly demand higher-quality and globally comparable sustainability disclosure information, the HKMA is working with other regulators to develop a clear roadmap for adopting the disclosure standards issued in June by the International Sustainability Standards Board—a comprehensive global baseline for sustainability reporting. The HKMA’s role as a facilitator extends beyond setting frameworks and rules; we are also committed to addressing pain points faced by the industry. Currently, many banks face difficulties in conducting physical risk assessments due to data constraints. In light of this, the HKMA will soon launch a cloud-based physical risk assessment platform. By simply entering property addresses, banks will be able to assess the impact of physical hazards on residential and commercial buildings in Hong Kong under different climate scenarios, thereby assisting them in managing relevant climate risks. As a leading international financial centre and sustainable finance hub in Asia, Hong Kong has consistently served as a bridge, channelling international investment into sustainable development projects across Asia to support the region's low-carbon transition. In recent years, the total volume of international green and sustainable bonds arranged in Hong Kong has accounted for more than one-third of the Asian market, significantly outpacing other regions. Notably, the Shenzhen Municipal Government and the Hainan Provincial Government issued green and sustainable bonds in Hong Kong in 2023 for the third and second consecutive years respectively, reaffirming Hong Kong’s pivotal role as a green gateway connecting the Mainland with the rest of the world. The vibrant development of Hong Kong’s sustainable bond market is partly attributable to the demonstration effect of the Government Green Bond Programme. Since 2019, the HKMA has assisted the Government in issuing approximately US$25 billion worth of green bonds to institutional and retail investors. With each issuance, we have seized the opportunity to innovate and expand the features of green bonds—including currency, tenor, and distribution channels—laying the foundation for other public and private green bond issuers in the region. Following the issuance of the world’s largest government retail green bond in 2022, we issued the world’s first tokenised government green bond in February 2023. In February 2024, we completed the second issuance of tokenised green bonds; denominated in four major currencies and issued in digital native format, these represent the world’s first multi-currency digital green bonds. At the same time, we have proactively introduced various measures to enhance the vibrancy and competitiveness of Hong Kong’s sustainable finance ecosystem. These efforts cover multiple areas, including skills training, data enhancement, green fintech, and transition finance. Specifically regarding talent development, we launched a new "Green and Sustainable Finance" module under the Banking Professional Qualification Scheme in 2023, offering systematic courses to banking practitioners to deepen their understanding and professional knowledge of green and sustainable finance. Transition finance is another key area of focus for us. It provides funding for decarbonisation activities in high-carbon-emitting and hard-to-abate sectors, preventing these industries from failing to transition due to lack of financial support. To support the robust development of transition finance, the HKMA will expand the local green taxonomy framework to include transition activities. We will also extend the scope of the "Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme," which provides funding to eligible bond issuers and borrowers, to cover transition bonds and loans, encouraging regional enterprises to raise transition capital in Hong Kong. Furthermore, we will strengthen engagement with relevant stakeholders, leveraging public-private partnerships and blended finance models to attract private sector investment into sustainable development projects that have traditionally struggled to secure financing. Some of the aforementioned initiatives require cross-sectoral collaboration and are primarily coordinated by the Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group, co-chaired by the HKMA and the Securities and Futures Commission. Regional cooperation is equally important. In addition to our long-standing partnership with the International Finance Corporation on the Alliance for Green Commercial Banks, the HKMA’s Infrastructure Financing Facilitation Office became a founding member of both the Sustainable Investment Capacity Building Alliance and the Green Development Investment and Financing Partnership in 2023. Additionally, the Glasgow Financial Alliance for Net Zero announced plans to establish a chapter in Hong Kong. Through these partnerships, we aim to promote skills training and knowledge sharing, thereby supporting the channeling of capital towards sustainable development projects both regionally and globally. To foster new business development and knowledge exchange, the HKMA helped organise the inaugural "Hong Kong Green Week" earlier this year. The event attracted over 1,600 participants from nearly 30 jurisdictions, including top decision-makers from the global business and financial communities, who gathered to discuss ways to scale up climate finance in the region and forge new partnerships. Chief Executive Mr Eddie Yue delivered remarks at the flagship event of Hong Kong Green Week, the Asia-Pacific Climate Business Forum. As the manager of Hong Kong’s official reserves and a significant global asset owner, the HKMA leads by example as a responsible investor. Since 2015, the HKMA has been at the forefront of investing in green and sustainable assets, progressively expanding the Exchange Fund’s ESG and green asset portfolios across both public and private markets. In line with the goal of achieving net-zero emissions for the Exchange Fund’s "Investment Portfolio" by 2050 or sooner, the HKMA added a new actively managed global equity portfolio themed around sustainability and climate transition last year, while extending the application of customised low-carbon equity indices to another public market portfolio. Furthermore, the green, social, and sustainability bonds prioritised in the HKMA’s investments have outperformed their benchmarks, demonstrating the principle of "doing good while doing well." In the private market, we continue to pursue green-related investment opportunities and have become an anchor investor in two Asia-focused transition investment funds. By end-2022, the weighted average carbon intensity (WACI) of the Exchange Fund’s equity portfolio had decreased by 6% and 46% compared to 2021 and 2017 levels respectively, remaining consistently below the overall market level. As a sustainable organisation, the HKMA remains committed to continuous improvement, formulating our sustainability goals and plans based on three pillars: environment, people, and community. Specifically, throughout our low-carbon transition journey, we continuously strengthen our resilience to climate change by assessing our environmental performance and implementing various internal measures. These measures encompass emission reduction, energy efficiency enhancement, and waste management, all aimed at ultimately achieving our commitment to reach net-zero emissions by 2050 or sooner. We have formulated plans to completely eliminate Scope 1 emissions in the near term and have made good progress towards our interim target of reducing Scope 2 emissions by 2030. To attract and retain top talent essential for fulfilling the HKMA’s key functions, we are dedicated to promoting the physical and mental well-being of our staff alongside our green objectives. Additionally, we contribute to building a caring society by collaborating with stakeholders to promote financial inclusion, enhance public financial literacy, and raise awareness against financial fraud. The climate challenge is immense and exceptionally urgent. Economies around the world are moving towards a more sustainable future, a process expected to bring profound changes to financing activities and asset allocation. While this transformation entails significant risks, it will also present unprecedented opportunities. As a leading global sustainable finance hub, Hong Kong has a responsibility to take the lead in addressing these challenges. At the same time, we are well-positioned to seize the momentum. The HKMA will fully support the industry in financing the low-carbon transition; continue to lead by example as a responsible investor and sustainable organisation; and collaborate with like-minded partners to advance this critically important global agenda. Chief Executive Eddie Yue

Climate change risks and other sustainability issues are of global concern. The HKMA’s objective in its sustainability efforts is to demonstrate leadership through its own policies and operations, ensuring that both the Hong Kong financial system and the HKMA itself are resilient to climate change risks, while supporting the transition towards more sustainable economic development. Through active participation in international and regional organizations, the HKMA will also strive to contribute to the formulation of green and sustainable finance policies and standards at both regional and global levels. As the banking regulator, the HKMA will further strengthen the banking sector’s climate resilience and climate risk management capabilities. Specifically, key priorities include: launching a new round of thematic reviews on banks’ climate risk management practices and conducting a new round of consultative meetings as part of the assessment of banks’ progress in implementing supervisory requirements on climate risk management; continuing work on integrating climate factors into the HKMA’s Supervisory Review Process; completing the second round of the industry-wide Climate Risk Stress Test, providing guidance to participating banks throughout the process, and sharing observations and lessons learned with the industry; enhancing sustainability disclosures, including collaborating with local relevant authorities to align related requirements with the global baseline IFRS Sustainability Disclosure Standards, and preparing for the implementation of Pillar 3 of the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision’s framework for climate-related financial risks; and sharing guidance with the industry on best practices for transition planning. To promote the sound development of banks’ provision of green and sustainable investment products, the HKMA will continue to keep abreast of local and international market and regulatory developments, and maintain engagement with the industry to ensure that banks adopt appropriate sales processes. In addition, the HKMA will act as a facilitator, striving to foster the development of the green finance ecosystem and support banks in financing the economic transition. We will soon launch a local green taxonomy and continue to expand its coverage to encompass a broader range of activities, including transition activities.
